en: In the Śrīpāñcarātra Paramasaṃhitā:
Devala approached the highly wise Mārkaṇḍeya as he was seated in a hermitage adorned with various trees. 1.1
Having bowed to him according to the prescribed rule and being greeted by him in return,
the learned man proceeded to ask about the supreme sphere of knowledge:
"O Blessed One, the Vedas have been studied by me, along with their limbs, sub-limbs, and in full detail."
I have studied the Aṅgas and the Vākovākya scriptures; yet,
among all these, I do not see anywhere a path to the highest good that leads to perfection, except through the resolution of doubt.
I do not see the supreme benefit in any single one of the scriptures;
rather, my doubt increases regarding those very many [texts].
Therefore, O Blessed One, tell me the means for cutting through my doubt.
"And I see no one other than you who is skilled in the path to the highest good.
(1.6) Thus addressed by Devala, Mārkaṇḍeya, the great ascetic, overcome with wonder, replied to Devala as follows: (1.7)
I have obtained a long life, yet my memory has not failed me;
I have witnessed many dissolutions, as well as creations and the periods of the Manvantaras.
I have seen many teachers and thousands of scriptures.
I did not find anything among them that was exclusively beneficial.
Thereupon, deeply despondent and with a burning heart,
I reached Sālagrāma and worshipped Viṣṇu alone.
Eight thousand years have passed since he himself arrived and made his decision;
by whatever means, provided one is endowed with faith and devotion, according to that rule.
Then that Blessed Lord, whose eyes resemble lotuses—
"I beheld him of dark complexion, serene and compassionate toward his devotees.
As that king of gods was being praised by me with hymns after I had prostrated before him,
O ascetic, he spoke these words to me with compassion."
"O Mārkaṇḍeya, I am pleased with you because of the long-lasting propitiations performed by you according to the rules and filled with devotion. (1.14)
"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever dwells in your mind: long life, wisdom, sovereignty, or whatever else you desire, O observer of noble vows.
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, I replied with palms joined in reverence:
"May I possess pure knowledge, free from doubt and free from agitation.
Thus addressed, the God of gods, smiling, spoke this:
"If you desire such knowledge, go from here to Śvetadvīpa."
Situated in the midst of the ocean of milk, the sole abode of yogins—
there, having worshipped the highly wise Siddhas according to the prescribed rite,
accomplish the desired knowledge whose object is total liberation.
"And your movement through various regions shall be uninterrupted.
Furthermore, O observer of noble vows, by my grace your lifespan shall be long.
Having spoken thus to me, that god vanished on the spot.
Then, O Devala, having become filled with wonder, I set out for Śvetadvīpa;
after a long time, I reached that island again, having crossed over mountains and oceans, and was not hindered anywhere along the way. 21.21-22ab.
There dwell perfected beings (siddhas) composed of light, possessing four arms,
their own hands marked with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
they are single-mindedly devoted, meditating upon Puruṣottama alone as their sole refuge.
"Seeing those who were single-mindedly devoted, filled with joy, free from the pairs of opposites, without possessions,
whose impurities were fully ripened, and always intent on meditation,
I bowed down to them with wonder and spoke as was appropriate."
Then I arrived at the hermitage of the perfected sage Sanaka. Having honored him there, I spoke these words:
"Know me to be Mārkaṇḍeya, returned from another continent."
"O you who have reached the further shore of knowledge, instruct me, for I have approached you for the sake of wisdom.
Thus addressed by me, the wise and high-minded son of Sanaka,
bowing to the Supreme God, replied, "So be it."
Then, by that tantra which was proclaimed to me by him who was pleased,
my doubts were severed and the darkness in my heart was destroyed; O Creator, resolve has arisen within me and my mind has become serene.
Long-standing anxiety has vanished and desire for everything has ceased.
O Devala, this Tantra was obtained by me in a previous Manvantara;
yet, over such a long period of time, it was not revealed to anyone.
This tantra was [taught] in its entirety, yet due to the vastness of its textual extent, many ascetics departed by resorting to only a single portion;
consequently, this tantra became divided into many parts throughout the world. || 1.31–1.32 ||

"This *Pañcarātra* has been proclaimed as unaccomplished, insubstantial, and mutually contradictory; yet this supreme *Yogatantra* was fashioned by the Supreme Person himself, O you whose wealth is asceticism. (1.33)
It is consistent with the truth and brings supreme benefit to the world;
it is accepted by yogins, and especially by Vaiṣṇavas. This alone is established as the sole authority among the Āgamas.
In every creation, by the command of the God of gods,
those wise ones who know this tantra in its entirety without interruption—
for them, no doubt ever arises regarding the paths of merit.
Their birth is not fruitless, and for them nothing remains difficult to attain.
They never grieve, they never become angry, and they never despair;
for them there is the successful fruition of their actions and the arising of the fruit of knowledge.
In this tantra, the conjunction of both is proclaimed;
the five qualities of the great elements are known as the "five nights" (pañcarātra) for embodied beings.
Because of that connection or because of their cessation, it is remembered as Pañcarātra.

The subtle elements, ego, intellect, and the unmanifest—these are said to be the nights of Puruṣa; therefore, it is remembered as Pañcarātra. If this entire system [tantra] is [studied] with attentiveness by anyone... 1.41–1.42ab.
For him, there is only a slight purpose in studying other treatises; however,
if you also wish to abandon entirely your doubt regarding the path to merit, then listen to this tantra.
"For one who stands in doubt on all sides, this tantra is considered the supreme [remedy].
Upon seeing you in such a state, wonder has arisen within me;
therefore, listen with an undistracted mind to the Pañcarātra as it was heard by me. (1.43–1.44)
By the grace of the God of gods,
this hundred thousand chapters, containing the accounts of creation and dissolution,
endowed with wondrous powers and various fruits of ritual action, was [received] formerly from the mouth of Sanaka.
But this entire tantra cannot be heard, O Devala,
even after one has attained a long life;
having extracted the essence of the mantras, I shall speak it to you, O Devala.
Prefacing this with an introduction concerning the deeds of Vaikuṇṭha:
This [universe] was then composed of darkness, unperceived, without defining marks, inconceivable, unknowable, and as if entirely asleep. (1.48)
There, having resorted to a sleep consisting of yoga, the Supreme Person, who is self-luminous, then set his mind upon creating for a long duration; there,
the Lord again assumed a form composed of yoga.
In the beginning, he created the seed of the world: a white-lustred lotus,
with a thousand petals spread wide, containing a circle of filaments within,
joined with a central pericarp, and originating from the circle of his navel.
In him he created the Creator, the four-faced Ordainer,
the source of all ignorance, the Lord whose self was purified.
Having created the five elements, that Lord created the worlds.
Having thus created the entire world— both the stationary and the moving— along with all the manifest elements, the Grandfather, the Great Yogin,
entered into motionless meditation and prepared to depart.
Then, doubt arose within his heart on all sides. And as knowledge was being produced by that [doubt], his mind wandered;
then he beheld the Supreme God reclining upon the Ocean of Milk.
The lotus-eyed one, reclining upon a bed of infinite splendor,
with four arms bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; dark-complexioned, clad in yellow garments, and graced by Śrī at his feet.
He bore the Śrīvatsa mark, possessed a serene luster, and his chest was radiant with the Kaustubha gem;
he was attended by Vainateya, who was seated at his side.
Having seen that best of persons, [he fell] at the two lotus-feet of the Lord.
"By me, the supreme... [is attained].
There is no higher measure than that; such is the established state of one who has become Brahman.
In the final moment, his measure quickly becomes like that of an insentient stationary being."
One who is terrified by the latent impressions of saṃsāra, liberated from the bonds of karma,
self-satisfied, and indifferent, realizes nirvāṇa.
Explain this to me in detail, for my curiosity is great.
The activity of all embodied beings is twofold: supreme knowledge and action.
From the preponderance of knowledge comes liberation; from the preponderance of action (or knowledge-action), however, comes transmigratory existence.

Action accompanied by a limited measure is considered to have a measurable fruit; knowledge has a fruit that is both beginningless and endless because it is free from the desire for measurement. 1.64 Brahmā.
How is it that for transmigrating persons who perceive the excellence of the senses, cognition arises even for yogins through the measurement [of objects]? 1.65.
Supreme.
The knowledge of those wandering in saṃsāra does not at all operate toward liberation;

rather, it operates toward the means for that [liberation], which are the causes for severing bondage. When those bound objects and instruments have been severed, [knowledge abides in liberation]. (1.66)
The supreme knower remains motionless by himself alone.
By what quality, O Brahman, are your liberated embodied beings distinguished?
Tell me this, O God, for it is the supreme secret among secrets:
"I myself am the Supreme; these beings are none other than I; there is no difference whatsoever therein."
"Just as I dwell, so do liberated embodied beings.
"O Supreme Person, tell me the causes of bondage for embodied beings," [said Brahmā].
In what form do the causes of bondage bind the person?
O Brahmin, the Supreme [Self] is bound by the three qualities alone, through their modes of operation both in summary and in detail.

Sleep is divided into three types, and by it men are bound. For one of *sattva*, sleep consists of happiness; for one of *rajas*, it is crowded with activity; for one of *tamas*, it takes the form of heavy lethargy. Thus, the connection [to these qualities] is said to be threefold.
The union of the person with the three qualities alone persists;
how, then, can there be separation for the yogin who desires liberation? (1.73)
O Lotus-seated One, even these three qualities are not supreme for the Puruṣa;
they come into being and cease to be according to the influence of the objective world.
"O best of gods, what is that object which has been described as that through whose conjunction these qualities arise for men, and through whose [absence] they cease to exist? 1.75 Paramaḥ.
Nature (prakṛti), composed of the three qualities (triguṇā), should be known as residing within the objects of the embodied soul.
Bound by union with it, they are liberated when separated from it.
The Puruṣa always knows Nature as it abides in the three qualities.
And she constantly gives birth to his various kinds of sleep.
One should resort only to beloved sleep, which exists as if independent; for it is held that this connection causes a man to forget his own true splendor.
O God, tell me this: by what cause does the conjunction of Brahmā with Prakṛti arise? This is a supreme secret, so it is considered. (1.79)
Supreme illusion alone was ordained by me as its cause in the past;
furthermore, it remains like a fire within the wood of illusion, solely through the power of karma.

But as for this illusion created by me, there is no cessation of it anywhere in this world without my grace; no deliberation need be made on this point. (1.81) As long as this illusion does not cease through my grace...
So long is there saṃsāra for a person, but liberation occurs upon its reversal.
O Lord, what is the basis for this grace toward you, who are already perfectly complete, that Brahmā [should exist]?
I do not know the cause of that; tell me that, O Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
The highest faith, devotion, and meditative concentration have been directed toward me by these people.

Know from me that it is only the auspicious that is being distinguished; understand that to be my clarity. Devotion offered to me, even if devoid of scriptural tradition, will bring only auspiciousness to a person—even a fool—of this there is no doubt.

Therefore, O Grandfather, for transmigrating beings, there is nothing else anywhere that brings about the supreme good except through my grace; this should be sought. Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Response to the Question," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the second chapter.
"O Lord, O God, O Lord of gods, O you whose eyes resemble the lotus!
I consider all this to be a sacred vow; you alone are the Lord of the worlds. (2.1)
"Tell us the means by which those people who desire to worship you according to the prescribed rules may then attain that which they seek. (2.2) Supreme.
Those entities in which my sport consists— both in creation and in withdrawal—
you, endowed with devotion, should always remember them in their proper sequence.
Of these, primordial nature (prakṛti) and the material elements (dravya) are the root of conflict.
The unmanifest and ignorance—these alone are said to be the manifest. (2.4) The unmanifest, intellect, ego, and the five subtle elements;
the eleven organs and the five gross elements. (2.5)
"The field is twofold—the gross and the subtle—and likewise the Knower of the Field is the Supreme.
Thus, O sinless one, all the principles have been proclaimed to you.
These [beings] are endowed with these very three qualities residing in primordial nature."
All these beings exist as superior, middling, and likewise inferior.
(2.7) The superior ones are known to abound in *sattva*, the middling ones consist of *rajas*, and the inferior ones are characterized by *tamas*; such are their respective conducts. (2.8)
In that regard, worship with dispositions consisting of *sattva* brings about my grace;
with those of *rajas*, there is the attainment of enjoyments; and with those of *tamas*, it is a cause of delusion.
Therefore, one who approaches me through the sequence of all these dispositions [attains the goal].
One should act with the quality of purity (sattva) alone, having destroyed passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas).
Having resorted to the sequence of dissolution, one should effect destruction everywhere;
having resorted to the sequence of natural creation, the re-origination [of all things] is prescribed.
In that process of creation and dissolution, one should know that all things are dependent upon me;
the sequential evolution of entities is not intended to be established otherwise. (2.12) Brahmā.
From what source is the arising of phenomena, or where is their destruction held to occur? If you say that both of these happen at the final moment, then speak! 2.13 Paramaḥ.
Nature gives birth to all states of being, and Nature again devours them.
Upon the emergence of Brahman there is creation; upon his departure, however, there is dissolution.
A period measuring a thousand yugas constitutes a single day of Brahmā, and his night is of equal duration.
By that measure, his lifespan is also one hundred years.
In this way, O Grandfather, by my command, creation and dissolution continually revolve through the duration of a Brahma-day.
What is the nature of that primordial matter (prakṛti), and how is it brought forth?
What is the relationship between her and the Supreme Person? (2.17)
Supreme, insentient, beyond the reach of others, eternal, and constantly changing;
composed of the three qualities (guṇas) and the field (kṣetra) for those who act—such is said to be the nature of Prakṛti. (2.18)
The relationship between that [prakṛti] and the person (puruṣa) is one of pervasion;
for it exists as beginningless and endless in the ultimate sense.
Just as sound is established by pervading all this space, so too does it abide.
In the very same way, having pervaded the unmanifest, the Supreme Self remains established [within it].
Just as oil is in sesame seeds and as taste is in water, so too here, by pervading [the unmanifest], the relationship of the pervader and the pervaded is maintained. (2.20–21)
In that regard, the pervasive form is the Supreme, the Person who is the subject;
having pervaded the unmanifest, He exists as the object of the Supreme.
Just as existence and non-existence cannot be shown separately from one another, [so too are they inseparable]. (2.22)

Likewise, pervasiveness is not other than that which is pervaded by everything; it is so designated because of that [pervasion]. Therein, the non-conscious is unmanifest, while the conscious is considered supreme.
Both of these, though distinct from one another, exist as if non-different from Him.
O Brahmā, how did all this—the three worlds—come to be from him? What are men like, and how is cyclic existence established within this world? (2.25)
By the command of the Supreme Person alone, primordial nature (prakṛti) always produces the worlds and also withdraws them at the end. (2.26)
But Nature (prakṛti), being insentient, does not produce otherwise;
therefore, the Supreme Person (puruṣa) effects these two: creation and dissolution.
In this regard, O Brahmin, listen with a concentrated mind to this account of creation first.
I shall further describe to you both its maintenance and its dissolution.
There are five renowned powers of the Supreme Self,
by means of which the Supreme Lord abides in the supreme ether.
Parameṣṭhin, Pumān, Viśva, Nivṛtti, and Sarvasaṃjñita—
these are said to be his five powers, known by the name of the five Upaniṣads.
The Lord, the Supreme Self, the Master of the World, consists of these five powers.

The union of the five senses experiences the fivefold knowledge. Parameṣṭhin is said to reside in sound; Puruṣa is said to reside in touch. Viśvātman is declared to reside in light; Nivṛttyātman is said to reside in taste. (2.31–2.32)
The Supreme Person is said to be the universal self within the sense-object of smell;
indeed, these five selves are recorded as being established in subtle forms.
They transcend the objects of worldly existence, are accessible through yoga, and are eternal.
This subtle body is said to be the cause of liberation.
Through its connection with primordial nature (prakṛti), fifteen powers—five groups of five—are known in succession as the sources of the qualities (guṇas). || 2.34–2.35 ||
Jyeṣṭhā, Vidyā, Kānti, Śānti, and Śraddhā as the fifth—
these five stainless powers (śaktis) have arisen as the cause of Sattva.
Vāgīśvarī, Kriyā, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, and Sṛṣṭi as the fifth.
Among them, *sā* (the power of *sattva*), *jñāna* (knowledge), and *amalā* (purity) are considered the causes of *rajas*.
Furthermore, the first of these [powers] is *mohinī* (deluding); then there is *avidyā* (ignorance) and *tamovatī* (possessing darkness).
*Mṛtyu* (death), *māyā* (illusion), and *malinā* (impurity)—these are the sources of *tamas*. || 2.37–2.38 ||
In this regard, know that *sattva* is illuminating, *rajas* is of the nature of activity, and *tamas* is to be known as obscuring; such is the definition of the qualities (*guṇas*).
By these very qualities, this world—both stationary and moving—is constituted.
Diversity has been attained in its manifold forms through association and separation.
The intellect (buddhi) arises as eightfold from the qualities (guṇas), which consist of the three *guṇas* themselves:
from *sattva* it is born as consisting of happiness, and from *rajas* it is joined with suffering. (2.40–2.41)
Now hear these distinctions therein, which are mixed with darkness and delusion: four are characterized by goodness (*sattva*), this one form is characterized by passion (*rajas*), and furthermore,
there are three characterized by darkness (*tamas*), which I shall name.
Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—these, according to the followers of Sattva, are the qualities of Sattva.
(2.43) In Rajas, however, the form is considered the opposite of dispassion; know that those which are the opposites of dharma and the rest belong to Tamas. (2.44)

From the intellect (buddhi) is born the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), which is threefold and composed of the three qualities (guṇas); by means of this, a living being perceives what is not the self as the self. From the ego-sense known as the "transformative" (vaikārika) arises the "pure" (sāttvika); from the "passionate" (rājasa) arises the "fiery" (taijasa).
From the *tāmasa* form of *ahaṃkāra*, known as *bhūtādi*, the threefold [ahaṃkāra] arises.
From the *vaikārika* *ahaṃkāra*, however, the five sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) are produced, by which knowledge is accomplished for the person (*puruṣa*) in this world. (2.46–2.47)
The five organs of action, which initiate activity, arise from the Taijasa [ego];
and from that [Taijasa] arises the mind, which possesses a twofold form and is the means for forming volitions.
Furthermore, Time, characterized by its specific functions, is born from the Taijasa alone.
From Time, the directions—beginning with the East—were produced and established in their respective order.
And from the elements (bhūta), the subtle elements (tanmātra) were likewise born in due sequence:
first the subtle element of sound, and second that which is preceded by touch.

The third consists of the subtle element of form alone, the fourth of taste alone, and the fifth of smell alone, for the sake of accomplishing a subtle body. The five [subtle elements] beginning with smell, as well as space, time, and the mind, [are the constituents].

Egoity (ahaṃkāra), intellect (buddhi), and primordial nature (prakṛti)—these are the twelve forms of the Supreme Self, whose body is yoga. Having established Vāsudeva [as the goal], those desiring perfection worship these forms. (2.52–2.53)
From the subtle elements (tanmātras), however, the five gross elements arise in succession:
ether, wind, fire, water, and earth as the fifth.
From these, the gross body of embodied beings is produced. (2.54)
The ear, the eyes, the tongue, the nose, and the intellect are the organs of perception (buddhīndriya).
The organs of action (karmendriya) are traditionally said to be speech, the hands, the genitals, the anus, and the feet.
Together with the effects and the instruments, this is called the gross body (sthūla-śarīra).

Thus, O Brahmin, I have described to you the creation, ending with the body, according to its subtle and gross divisions. Now I shall speak of the powers of the Supreme Person himself, which are like inner sheaths.
They appear as if distinct due to the differences in their birth, names, and forms.
Having acquired a material body through their own accumulated actions, those transmigrating beings wander for a long time in saṃsāra. || 2.58–2.59 ||
By pure action they go to an auspicious upward-facing state;
by impure action they likewise go to a downward-facing state. Men, though their own nature is of the form of consciousness, are submerged in the undifferentiated.
Incapable of knowing themselves or others, and devoted to darkness, they take refuge in it.
Attachment, aversion, and the like are their defects, born of their very nature;
what else can they do for embodied beings within the sphere of saṃsāra? (2.61–2.62)
Due to the predominance of the qualities (guṇas) through their own auspicious and inauspicious actions,
embodied beings go to high, low, or middling states of existence.
Among them, when the quality of sattva predominates, the state of being a deity is desired as their destination.
Human birth is said to arise from *rājas* [quality], and the state of animals likewise from *tamas*.
Thus all embodied beings go to various destinies;
mounted upon the wheel of time, they revolve through the illusion of ignorance.
"O Brahmā, O God of gods, you have spoken to me of the Kālacakra; O Lord,
if it is possible, I wish to hear its true nature."
Supreme Time creates all beings; Time destroys all creatures.
Time remains awake within all things, for Time is indeed insurmountable.
Time divides all human aims into higher and lower;
the past, the present, and the future—all proceed from time. The movement and revolution of the planets, constellations, and zodiacal signs [are likewise governed by it].
The differentiation of these two [days and nights] occurs in many ways for him.
Its division is proclaimed through twelve distinctions:
the solstices, the seasons, the months, the fortnights, and likewise the lunar days. || 2.69–2.70 ||
Likewise, the *savana*s, the watches (*yāma*s), the moments (*muhūrta*s),
the *nāḍī*s, the *kalā*s, the *vināḍī*s, and the twelve *prājā*s are recorded [as its parts].
The year is their lord, whose nature is time and who arises from the fiery principle (*taijasa*).
They say its two rims are what has been called the two solstices (ayana).
Furthermore, the three seasonal sacrifices (savana) are declared to be the three hubs;
the spokes are to be known as the months, and the principles (tattva) as the fortnights, O Lotus-born One.
The six seasons are proclaimed as his limbs, and the feet and so forth are enumerated as his [lower] parts;
the muhūrtas are proclaimed as the fingers on his hands and feet.
His veins are said to be the nāḍīs, and his hairs are established as the kalās.
The pores of the skin are the *vinaḍya* and the vital breaths are the exhalations.
(2.75) Having mounted this wheel, the world of the moving and the stationary undergoes rising and setting, just as do the planets and the stars. (2.76)
The Supreme Person himself, having become Brahmā and Kāla, remains established;
for the sake of worldly transaction, he causes the wheel to revolve perpetually.
By this very [wheel], he causes the entire world to revolve through the power of the *guṇa-māyā*.
The eternal God remains intent on his creative acts, as if at play.
O Lotus-seated One, those twelve forms which have been proclaimed of him—
from them alone, in due order, the twelve Śaktis were born again.
Yogeśvarī, Sukhā, Prajñā, Tuṣṭi, Smṛti, Dīpti, Āgā, Vāṅnīti, Kānti, Amṛtā, Śakti,
and Sarvātmikā— these twelve are proclaimed.
Having attained this world, these [energies] remain present at all times.
Furthermore, from these twelve guardians of the forms (*mūrtipāla*) arose;
likewise, by their power, they became renowned here in the worlds.
And know, O Lotus-born one, that they themselves are the lords of the months:
Viṣṇu is to be known as the first in Madhu; in Mādhava, he is Madhusūdana;
in Śukra, he is declared to be Trivikrama; and in the month of Śuci, he is Vāmana.
Śrīdhara is to be known in Nabhas, and Hṛṣīkeśa in Nabhasya;
Padmanābha is in Iṣa, O Brahmin, and the Lord Dāmodara in Ūrja.
Keśava is said to be in Sahas, and the Lord Nārāyaṇa is in Sasya.
Mādhava is to be known as presiding over the month of Tapa, while Govinda presides over Tapasya.
Thus, these twelve lords of the months are established month by month;
they have been proclaimed according to their sequence, possessing great heroism and great qualities.
That very Blessed One, the God, the Supreme Self, the Teacher of the World,
remains established as differentiated by the divisions of deities and so forth,
just as [the one space] appears distinct when residing within substances of various colors. || 2.87–2.88 ||
Just as the form of a crystal gem appears to be one thing and then another,
so too the single, supreme Puruṣa appears to be manifold through states composed of the qualities (guṇas),
wherein the world— bound and liberated— is born in diverse forms.
He alone should follow the conduct [of the moon], like the moon even more than sandalwood.
He is called Yama because of his restraint, and Śakra because of his power;
he is to be known as Vāyu because of his movement, and indeed as Vahni because of his carrying [the oblation].
Hara is so called because of his taking away, and Brahmā because of his Brahminical activity;

thus, these various divine forms should be understood as the powers (śaktis) of that very [Being]. It is impossible to enumerate the powers of the Great Soul, owing to his manifold nature (vaiśvarūpya).
Among them, three are preeminent and renowned throughout all the worlds;
they have been celebrated from of old as the persons Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu.
Even among those, [Viṣṇu is distinguished] by his mode of being characterized by *sattva* and by his protection of the worlds.
And because he delights in liberation, Viṣṇu alone is distinguished;
for since he is thus distinguished above all other persons, and because he is the cause of all that is auspicious, he is therefore the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). || 2.95 ||
They say that both [the individual soul and the Supreme Soul] consist of Nārāyaṇa, as they are the sources of ultimate liberation. He alone is skilled therein; therefore, he is indeed Nārāyaṇa.
Vāsava is so called because of dwelling (vasana) in the body, as are all embodied beings.
Among them, he is remembered as the common deity Vāsudeva;
because the world is pervaded by him, he is therefore remembered as Viṣṇu.
Because of the taking away of sufferings, he is designated as Hari.
That God, manifest in four forms, presides over the worlds.
Having attained supreme perfection in dharma and the other goals, out of a desire for the welfare [of beings],
Vāsudeva is known as Dharma, and Saṅkarṣaṇa is known as Knowledge.
Likewise, Vimukta, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and Sakaleśvara—
wherever these four manifest qualities are present,
there the four gods, who are affectionate toward their devotees, become pleased. (2.101)
But those four [kings] who act unrighteously, in whom faults are established, forcibly seize that [kingdom] and plunge it into calamities;
[they bring ruin] to the Vedas, the stages of life (āśramas), the social classes (varṇas), and likewise to the quarters of the world. || 2.102–2.103 ||
"These four lords of the world perform the division [of their functions].
Thus, this path of creation has been described by me in brief;
because of the abundance of those who desire to know it, a detailed exposition cannot be given.
But that which is contrary to the process of creation is known as the equilibrium of dissolution (pralaya).
When the end of dissolution has arrived again, the Supreme Person,
being beyond all activity and consisting of a mass of pure consciousness, abides in the supreme ether.
"Know me, O Grandfather, to be that very Puruṣa Viṣṇu,
lying upon the king of serpents in the Ocean of Milk through my *māyā*, O Brahmā.
All men worship me alone in many ways with sacrifices."
Yogis who have conquered their senses meditate upon me alone;
they praise me alone with hymns of praise and worship me with devotion;
and the heads of the branches of the Vedas proclaim me alone. (2.108–109)
I alone am the Virāj Self, abiding as the soul of all worlds;
all worlds abide in me, and therefore I am the Lord of the universe.
Those men who are possessed of devotion always take refuge in me alone.
They will possess accomplishment and have fulfilled their purpose; of this there is no doubt.
O Brahmin, two desires arise within me toward living beings:
one is regard, and the other is indifference, by which I am eternally sustained.
By means of this [power] acquired previously, I favor those who perform auspicious deeds and are devoted;
furthermore, by this same [power], I restrain those who are unrighteous and undevoted.
For it is precisely because of me that they have obtained a body, which is the instrument for all accomplishments.
Embodied beings must perform pure actions for my propitiation. When I am pleased, O Grandfather, heaven or even liberation shall be attained by all men; of this there is no doubt.
"Thus, O Brahmin, this has been told, having extracted the essence from everywhere;
it is the measure of the world, the supreme secret. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Sequence of Creation," in the glorious *Paramasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
[The Dispassionate One?
Now begins the third chapter.
O Brahmā, regarding that Supreme God whom you have described as the cause of creation—
how can his worship or meditation be accomplished by human beings? (3.1)
For he is never delimited by any causes whatsoever,
nor is his form determined by the nature of direction, place, or time. (3.2) Now, how should worship be performed for him by one desiring spiritual accomplishment?
Tell me this: how is it right, O God of gods, for that which is supremely beneficial?
This most secret matter, asked by you, I shall speak out of a desire for your welfare.
Listen to that kind of worship which is due to the God of gods.
He is to be worshipped as one possessing form; there is no worship of the formless.
His forms exist for the sake of accomplishing tasks and for the purpose of bestowing grace upon the worlds.

Therefore, having conceptualized that Acyuta in the form of a person and having worshipped him with supreme devotion, human beings attain perfection. But in the case of the Lord of Gods, who is formless, worship is not possible for men.
There is neither meditation nor praise; therefore, one should worship with a mental image (sākāra).
For worship, praise, or even meditation performed upon a mental image according to the procedure seen in the scriptures, becomes as if performed upon the God himself.
Drawn by supreme devotion by those yogins, the God of gods assumed a four-armed form for the sake of bestowing grace upon them. Therefore, one should worship the God of gods in that very form.
Because of the difference in their fruits, his worship is prescribed by the scriptures as being twofold.
(3.10) The first fruit is worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), while the supreme fruit is liberation (*nirvāṇa*).
Furthermore, because these two are distinct—the lower and the higher—the deity also differs between them. (3.11)
One person is to be worshipped for the sake of worldly prosperity (*udaya*), while the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*) is to be worshipped for the sake of liberation (*nirvāṇa*).
Therein, one who seeks prosperity should worship [the deity] having visualized him with eight arms, possessing a beautiful vehicle, equipped with weapons, and accompanied by his retinue.
[He is] resembling a great sapphire, lotus-eyed, and clad in yellow garments.
(3.13) The time for worship is the forenoon; the duration is one year; and there must be no interruption in the worship until the attainment of the fruit. (3.14)
The worship of this [deity] during times of great prosperity has been proclaimed.
O Brahmin, listen now to how the worship is performed for one seeking the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).
One should bear the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus with four arms.
The supreme deity, resembling pure crystal, is worthy of worship.
Likewise, the lotus is the seed of creation; the discus is the basis for maintenance;
the mace is the seed of dissolution; and the conch is the basis for liberation.
This worship at midday and other times should be performed according to one's ability;
it consists of being indifferent toward fruits [of action] and continues as worship for as long as life lasts.
This very worship, joined with all the principles (tattvas), proceeds by way of the path of withdrawal (saṃhāra).
Thus has the worship for one desiring liberation been proclaimed to you.
Of these two forms of worship, O Brahmin, the worship for liberation is superior because its fruit is ultimate, whereas the other is not, due to the opposite being the case.
There is no destruction of an action performed, even in hundreds of births;
through its convergence, there is indeed nourishment, though it may not manifest as a specific fruit due to a lack of connection.
Liberation is unsurpassed happiness, yet even that is impermanent insofar as it is free from suffering.
Therefore, with every effort and without sloth for the sake of liberation, one of great mind who desires the goal should worship Vāsudeva;
his worship is threefold: through action, through speech, and through the intellect.
It is established that each succeeding one of these yields a greater fruit than the preceding.
With pure substances such as perfumes and flowers, which are approved by the virtuous,
their application with a mantra is known as the sacrifice of action (karmayajña).
Having become pure and composed, whatever recitation one performs with devotion through hymns and mantras is traditionally known as the sacrifice of speech (vāgyajña).
Having abandoned all external [rites], one should perform it mentally according to the rule.
When one worships the Lord of Gods, that is called the mental sacrifice (manoyajña).
O Brahmin, each of these is traditionally held to have a threefold division according to the influence of the powers (śakti):
it is sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasī.

The *sāttvikī* [type of speech] is for the sake of liberation; the *rājasī* is for the accomplishment of desires; and the *tāmasī* is for the purpose of harming others. Each preceding one is more weighty than the following.
[This applies to] Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and women as well.
Endowed with devotion by their very nature, they should perform the worship of the God;
both the prosperous and the poor, as well as the young and the elderly—
whether they be scholars or yogis— should perform the worship of the God.
There is nothing more supremely beneficial than the worship of Hari’s feet.
Therefore, with every effort, one should become a Vaiṣṇava;
for there is no one in this world who bestows fruit except for Puruṣottama.
By His will, actions and their fruits proceed;
no man is capable of bringing about the accumulation of prosperities nor of averting calamities. Therefore, one should take refuge in the Divine. (3.33–3.34)
How is Brahmā to be worshipped, that Lord of the Gods? What kind of worshipper should he be? And what is his ritual practice, and of what nature would its fruit be? (3.35)
O Brahmin, with a concentrated mind, I shall describe to you the supreme procedure for worship,
according to which a devotee of the Lord should perform the sacrifice to Lord Hari. 3.36
"Right time, proper conduct, self-study, accumulation of materials, purification, sacrifice, praise, and meditation—thus the rule is eightfold.
He who abides by this rule is called a Bhāgavata. (3.37)
Through merits performed in previous births, a man becomes a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata).
O Brahmin, there are two kinds of persons: the initiated and likewise the uninitiated.
The initiated should perform the practice in its entirety, while the uninitiated performs it in part.
The commitment (*samaya*) of both [the teacher and the disciple] is equal; therefore, one should observe the commitment.
The Blessed One alone—and no other—is to be meditated upon as the cause of the universe, always by virtue of his being the master, the guru, and the friend. (3.40)
One should know that [this consists of] the study of His vidyā, a devoted interest in hearing of His qualities,
trust in His devotees through deed, mind, and speech,
and the cultivation of sattvic substances, actions, and qualities. (3.41–3.42)
One should never set one's mind upon attending to those who are dependent on others;
one should keep a temple nearby and circumambulate the deity.
One must never step over, eat, or touch the remains of offerings (nirmālya).
One should neither give [it away] nor smell it, but should protect it...

|| 3.44 || Having become pure oneself, one should constantly recite hymns there, having meditated upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa in the evening, in the morning, at midday, and during the five watches of the day. || 3.45 ||
Whether rising from sleep, walking, bowing,
falling, receiving, or giving, one should recite the eight-syllable mantra.
[One should avoid those] who abide by heretical doctrines and those who subsist on the treasury of the gods.
One should not touch nor converse with atheists, those who are censured, or the wicked.
One should not occupy a seat, a bed, or a vehicle that is unsightly;
nor should one place one’s feet upon any place where the form of Hari resides.
One should always listen to accounts of the abodes of Viṣṇu and especially of his sacred fords (tīrthas), as well as of his devotees and perfected ones (siddhas), treating them like kinsmen.
One should not eat food consisting of impure substances, nor that which has been gathered by unholy means.

One should avoid meat and intoxicants, nor food that has been mentally intended for those who drink intoxicants. One who is initiated should avoid the food of a funeral feast, a multitude of people, or a woman in childbirth. He should never be impure; he should be steadfast and a devotee of the Lord.

He should always deliberate with distinguished Vaiṣṇavas who are experts in the Pañcarātra, being intent on resolving doubts regarding ritual actions. He should not speak of his own accord unless asked, nor should he respond to one who asks in an improper manner.
For even though he knows, the wise man should behave toward the world like one who is dull-witted.
(3.53) When sitting, when in the company of others, and when danger has arisen, he should constantly mutter either the eight-syllable mantra or the twelve-syllable mantra. (3.54)
"In case of negligence, or an offense, or the transgression of the rule,
one should perform a penance consisting of a recitation (japa) of either a thousand or a hundred [times].
Thus, O Brahmin, has the rule been declared to you in brief."

Furthermore, one should observe whatever is ordained in the Vaiṣṇava dharma. Now I shall describe the conduct that must always be practiced by the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas). Conduct is proclaimed as the daily ritual (nityakarman) prescribed by the scriptures.
At the time of dawn, having voided excrement and washed himself,
remaining silent and pure, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and recite the five Upaniṣads during the twilight prayer—
either a hundred times, a thousand times, or ten times in times of distress.
Having paid homage to the Sun with the Kāla-mantra and to the directions in sequence with his own mantra, being pure, he should mutter the eight-syllabled mantra,
or even the twelve-syllabled one, daily as appropriate.
Having recited the hymns of praise, he should at the conclusion meditate upon the God of gods;
then, having conversed with his devotees, and especially with Brahmins,
he should constantly perform his own duties as prescribed by the Dharma.

One should listen to the mantras of Viṣṇu and to those stories which destroy sin. One should associate with his devotees and avoid dispute with them. One should worship Puruṣottama three times a day, or once a day, according to one's ability.

Having bathed, one should worship the God with devotion, remaining untiring in one's daily duties; especially during the solstices and other such times, and particularly on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī). One should worship with special care in sacred places and at holy fords (tīrthas).
Or, with diligent effort, he should perceive other forms of Viṣṇu;
having paid homage here and there, he attains that very [Lord]. He should never make his speech false before the feet of the God.
Even in times of distress, O King, one should not stand over the image of the deity;
a wise man should never speak of his reliance upon the God of gods in a secretive manner.
When a specific cause arises, he should not say, "It must not be spoken."

One should give a handful of fodder to a cow even before the time for one's own meal. One should not eat without having first obtained permission from ascetics (yatis) or devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas).
O Grandfather, I shall describe to you the proper conduct for those who have been initiated (dīkṣitas).
Just as eternal perfection indeed comes to the devotees of the Lord,
so too one who has risen early in the morning, observing silence and mentally reciting everything,
and desiring to go while facing the east, should place his left foot upon the ground.
One should enter with the left foot and utter the mantra *nivṛttyātmānaṃ*.

(3.71) Having performed the cleansing of impurities with earth and water according to the scriptures, one should touch the water with the *viśvātman* [mantra] and sip it with the *puruṣātman* [mantra]. (3.72)
Having sprinkled water upon his head or indeed his entire body while identifying with the *parameṣṭhin* self,
and having performed the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*) according to the rule and recited [the prayers] in due order,
he should mentally resolve upon the imperishable Supreme Self by means of the mental mantra.
Having touched each of the sense organs once with the Ahaṃkāra-mantra, he should salute and touch a tawny cow with the Buddhi-vidyā-mantra. Then,
having touched the supreme mantra, he may perform his worldly duties.
Having offered scent to the gods and to the Brahmins with the *vidyā* of the "mere-scent" (*gandhamātra*),
and having touched that very scent [to himself], he should perform the purification of his hands.
He should consume medicinal herbs with the *vidyā* of the "mere-taste" (*rasamātra*).
One should [offer] forms, flowers, and ornaments with the mantra of sight;
garments, auspicious items, and likewise a seat with the mantra of touch;
and one should hear auspicious speech with the vidyā of mere sound.
One should contemplate all the great elements (mahābhūtas) as being merely their subtle essence (tanmātra).
Upon contact with impurities, upon eating contemptible food,
and upon other unwholesome things, a person should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having collected them in a pure vessel in sequence with the Upaniṣad mantras—
cow urine, cow dung, clarified butter, curd, and milk as the fifth—
one should drink them with the [mantras] beginning with *parameṣṭhin* and then consecrate one's body with them.
In this way, one shall be liberated from evil and the purity of one's purpose arises.

Having bathed according to the ritual with mantras, one who has performed the protection rite should daily worship Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world, whose form is manifested through those very mantras.

For the sake of purification, having first bathed, one should perform the ritual bath with mantras (mantrasnāna). Taking earth with the *sarva* mantra, one should purify the water with the *nivṛtti* mantra; having invoked the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) with the *viśva* mantra, one should apply the earth with the *puruṣa* mantra.
One should bathe with the *parameṣṭhi* mantra and then sip water again according to the prescribed rule;
having sprinkled all the limbs with the five *upaniṣad* mantras, one should purify oneself. Having entered into the water, one should mutter the five mantras in their proper sequence.
Having performed three, two, or even one breath-control (prāṇāyāma), or having disciplined himself with a single [repetition],
and having bathed, put on two garments, sipped water (ācānta), and become composed,
he should face the east and remain steady. || 3.86–3.87 ||

One should mutter the *paramahaṃsa* mantra, as well as the *praṇava* consisting of three measures (*trimātra*), a thousand times or a hundred times; likewise, one should also mutter the twelve-syllable and eight-syllable mantras.
Having first offered a handful of water, one should worship the Sun.
With these very great mantras, at the appropriate time, with palms joined in reverence,
one should meditate upon the supreme Lord, subtle and consisting of light, seated within the mandala; thereafter,
one should satisfy the deities with water in the proper sequence.
[He worshipped] Indra and the others, preceded by Viṣṇu, as well as those beginning with Vāsudeva;
the twelve forms and the twelve Śaktis, and the Supreme Self alone;
the elements beginning with earth, and the sages together with the ancestors.
First, the name [of the deity] in the accusative case, followed by "I satisfy" (tarpayāmi) as the latter part;
this is the mantra prescribed for the libation exactly as it is.
Having performed the libation and sipped water again, one should proceed to the place of sacrifice.
"Where a Vaiṣṇava man, subsisting on withered food, worships the Supreme Lord according to the prescribed rule, attains supreme perfection in no time at all.
Thus ends the third chapter, named "Discipline," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
O Lord, I desire to hear about the supreme worship of Viṣṇu;
how is that Puruṣottama, the devotee of Viṣṇu, to be adored? (4.1)
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme method of worshipping Viṣṇu,
by the practice of which a devotee attains the state of Viṣṇu. 4.2
Having reached the place of sacrifice, having washed himself and sipped water, and being restrained in speech,
he should look upon the house and the sacrificial altar or mound with the mantra.
Having circumambulated the altar clockwise and paid homage to it with a concentrated mind, [he should proceed].
Having arranged his garment over his left shoulder like a sacred thread (*upavīta*), being pure and facing the east, he should sit down; then, having touched both hands with the *praṇava*,
he should place the five *upaniṣads* in order upon the fingers beginning with the little finger.
One should perform the six-limbed rite with one hand using the mudrās and mantras;
having performed the binding of the directions in all quarters with the weapon-mantra (astramantra),
one should likewise surround the interior of the fire-wall on all sides with the fire-mantra (tejomantreṇa).
Having thus performed the protection of oneself, one should practice the sequence of concentration (dhāraṇā).
Having first formed the "yogic casket" (yogasaṃpuṭa) joined with three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma),
through the filling or the exhaling of the vital air, or even through the careful exhaling of it— 4.7–4.8.

That which is performed by means of the vital breath is called *prāṇāyāma* for a person. Then, having contemplated the wind within the navel-lotus as being of the nature of the Puruṣa, one should especially fix the consciousness there, having become one with that wind.
Then, having meditated upon the Fire as the soul of the universe and the Sun within the heart,
one should maintain there the consciousness that has become fire on all sides;
thereafter, one should maintain with the whole [self] that Bhava, who is of the nature of Indra, in the throat.
Through withdrawal, one should hold Varuṇa at the head in the form of water;
the concentrations (dhāraṇās) are black, red, yellow, and white in form.
Each one is said to be accomplished by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) as previously described.
With all forms of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and with unwavering meditative absorption (*samādhi*),
one should contemplate the entire world as being endowed with those [divine] qualities,
following the sequence of inhalation (*pūraka*), exhalation (*recaka*), retention (*kuṃbhaka*), and the state free from effort (*nirmaya*). || 4.13–14 ||

And it should be understood that this practice must be performed by men who are devotees of the Lord. When one has thus been rendered with all impurities burnt away by means of these meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās),
he should then resort to meditation consisting of yoga, which bestows purity of the self.
By means of unwavering meditative absorption, one should dissolve the elements, beginning with earth,
into the Supreme Self by following the order of their dissolution;
thereafter, one should contemplate the entire creation up to the gross body.
Having emanated [the deities] with the right hand and recited the mantras in sequence,
and having meditated upon the causal principles themselves, one should install them in their respective places:
in the center of the face, in the heart, in the secret place, and likewise in the soles of the feet.
One should then install the elements, beginning with space, by means of the five mantras.
Having thus become composed of mantra through the meditative absorption of great yoga,
[one should perform the rite] with golden jars filled with nectar-like water.
One should consecrate oneself with the waters held in the hands of the women of the quarters,
while visualizing within the heart the radiant sun in the form of a disk; and having visualized the moon within that [sun], one should likewise visualize the circle of fire within the moon.
Having thus visualized the body, both internally and externally, as being fashioned by mantra,
the practitioner is fit to perform the worship of Hari;
having himself become [the deity] even once, he should worship the God of gods.

Even in the context of ordinary worldly interaction, one is neither the worshiped nor the worshiper; for the body is merely material. Therefore, having withdrawn it through the process of dissolution and having produced another, pure [body], one should worship the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
One should worship the God on a sacrificial mound, in an image, in water, or even in fire; or one may worship Him mentally in the space of the heart, or in a mandala,
or within the center of the solar orb, according to what is possible.
Having first gathered pure substances from all sides,
one should sprinkle the sacrificial pedestal with the *parameṣṭhin* mantra and prepare it.
Upon that perfected pedestal, the Lord Hari is worshipped.

Vāsudeva and the others are established as the feet of the sacrificial pedestal (yāgapīṭha). Furthermore, the four beginning with Adharma are proclaimed as the footstools. Vāsudeva, the embodiment of Dharma, is installed in the south-eastern quarter.

In the southwest stands the god Saṅkarṣaṇa, whose form is knowledge; in the northwest direction is Pradyumna, established as the embodiment of dispassion. In the northeast is stationed Aniruddha, whose form is sovereignty.
The four bamboo poles are indeed the cognitions beginning with unrighteousness (adharma);
the three hammers are the three types of egoism; and the three qualities (guṇas) are the supports. The elements are its coverings, and it is said that Rudra is the lid. (4.31–4.32)
Within that [egg] is the lotus born of Brahman, perfected with twelve petals,
filled with filaments within, and possessing a broad pericarp in the center.
Virāj, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), whose form is the world, is its presiding deity.
The twelve forms, beginning with Mohinī, are to be known as being on the lotus petals in sequence; these fifteen Śaktis are on the filaments,
while the three Guṇas and the three Yonis are on the root of the pericarp in order.

The triad of qualities and powers (guṇa-śakti) is established in the center in their proper sequence: fire, moon, and sun; above these they are situated. Having thus prepared this according to the rule with the mantras of the seats (pīṭha-mantra).

One should perform worship of the divine seat with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. Upon that [seat], one should meditate on the form of the Supreme Self, four-armed and as pure as clear crystal, by means of the supreme powers (parā śaktayaḥ).

One should invoke the Lord, the Supreme Self, the Infallible One, who is marked by the four symbols of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, into that [liṅga]. First, one should mentally conceive a throne within the hollowed palms.
Then, for the sake of the ritual preparation, one should invoke the omnipresent God there—
the conscious, eternally satisfied one— into the *praṇava* by means of the *parameṣṭhin*;
one should call upon Him who is established in the *praṇava* through His nature as the *puruṣa*.
Then, one should meditate upon the Supreme as the Universal Self (viśvātman) seated upon the throne held in the hollowed palms;
having uttered the mantra "nivṛttyātmā," one should cause Him to enter the body.
One should contemplate Him as conjoined with the entire self and the physical body.
Having bowed slightly, stood up, and offered a welcome once more,

and having requested the presence [of the deity] through the knowledge of the qualities of sattva and the mantra of power belonging to rajas, one should offer the water for the feet and the other offerings in due order. || 4.43–44 ||

One should offer the *arghya* according to the rule with the eight-syllable mantra; then one should offer mouth-perfume (*mukhavāsa*) with the *vidyā* of the essence of flavor (*rasamātra*). Having offered incense, garlands, and so forth, and having received permission, one should perform a circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*).
Having performed the fire-ritual and prepared the sacrificial oblation according to the rules,
one should approach the side of the deity in the prescribed manner and perform the bathing of the deity with the *tamasaḥ śakti* mantra.
Having performed the rite of pacification with the *pañcopaniṣad* mantra and pure water,
one should offer two garments and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) while reciting the *guṇamantra*. One should likewise offer ornaments according to one's means, as if they were offered mentally.
And one should offer auspicious perfumes with the *vidyā* of the element of smell (*gandha*).
One should offer flowers and garlands with the *vidyā* of form (*rūpa*), as well as a mirror;
and one should offer incense and a lamp with the mantra of touch (*sparśa*) and the *vidyā* of form.
Having offered the *arghya* according to the rule with the twelve-syllable mantra,
he should again offer oblations consisting of liquids, as well as foods to be chewed and eaten,
and water for rinsing the mouth, using the same mantra as before.
Having offered the hymns by means of mere sound and having prostrated,
one should circumambulate with the *diṅmantra*, perform a clockwise circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*), and,
according to the proper time, perform the auspicious recitation (*japa*) for as long as desired.
Having meditated upon the Japa-paramahaṃsa, the twelve-syllable mantra,
the eight-syllable mantra, the Lord of Gods, or indeed the Praṇava itself,
one should then offer the Arghya with the Paramahaṃsa and bow down.
Having offered oneself as a servant, one should then dismiss [the deity].
One should remember that just as [the deity] was invoked previously, so too is it dismissed;
one should worship with the thought, "It should be forgiven," following the sequence in reverse order.
This indeed is the procedure for the hero, which has been told by me in brief.
Having worshipped the Supreme Self, the pure devotee of the Lord,
his soul purified of all sins, attains the path of liberation.
He obtains all desired objects in every way, both in this world and the next;
he crosses over to liberation and is not oppressed by enemies. Having been consecrated according to the ritual, he understands the procedure known from the Tantras.
By applying oneself in this way, one attains accomplishment; otherwise, one becomes a sinner.

One should worship the image after having prepared the pedestal according to the prescribed sequence, meditating with the mind upon the form of the deity composed of yoga, even though it is but a physical image.
Having established Hari within that [image], one should invoke him and worship according to the prescribed rite.

There is no difference whatsoever in the sacrifice even when performed in the midst of water. However, in the case of a fire sacrifice, one should fulfill all those requirements that are absent in the water ritual.
Within the expanse of the heart, however, one should perform everything mentally during the sacrifice;
the patron of the sacrifice should arrange such a ritual procedure within the maṇḍala.
One should [visualize] the powers, such as the sovereign power of yoga and others, in all directions, part by part.
The practitioner should place them on the outer enclosure of the yoga-pīṭha.
Outside of those as well, he should place the lords of the twelve months in the cardinal directions;
outside of them, he should place the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the directions, beginning with Indra.
Having meditated upon everything in due order along the path of the wheel-mandala,
and having meditated on the seat situated on the level of the axle, one should worship the deity.
This procedure for the sacrifice is also prescribed for the center of the solar mandala.
Thus, one who is skilled in the worship of the deity should worship Vaikuṇṭha in these places of worship according to the proper method and at the proper time,
following the sequence beginning with the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and having obtained [the fruit] through conviction once again.

Sacrifices must be performed in other locations; otherwise, there would be great fault. For the sake of protecting the sacrifice from obstacles, one should station the guardians of the quarters outside all the sacrifices dedicated to the Supreme Self.
Among all sacrifices, the mental sacrifice is the most excellent.
For when the mind is not serene, even the application of ritual action is fruitless.
Contemplation preceded by affection is designated as devotion (bhakti).
For worship performed even if it is done without devotion becomes as if unperformed.
Eightfold devotion is prescribed, especially for a Vaiṣṇava;
having attained which, one reaches supreme perfection without delay. (4.72)
Constant worship of the Lord, the preservation of the sacred pledge (samaya),
trust in fellow Vaiṣṇavas, great reverence for the ritual worship, personal effort in performing worship oneself, and devotion to listening to his stories. (4.73–4.74)
Indifference toward the suffering of others and not depending on their worship—
this eightfold devotion belongs to that embodied being who hears this tantra and is worthy to speak it. (4.75–4.76)
Now tell me that worship of the other, the primordial God, which you have described for one who desires worldly prosperity. (4.77)
This very method of propitiation for the other Viṣṇu is supreme;
I shall now describe the specific tantra, while all else remains as previously stated.
Then Janārdana, with eight arms, was to be worshipped upon a red lotus,
accompanied by his vehicle, weapons, and retinue.
Ananta the serpent was in the east, and the king of birds in the west.
To the left of the God is Lakṣmī, and to his right is Sarasvatī.
In the southeast is Vṛddhi, while in the southwest Siddhi is said to be located.
Mati is indicated in the northwest, and Śānti resides in the domain of the northeast.
O Lotus-born One, the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the sword, the shield, the arrow, and the bow— these are the weapons held in the eight hands of the God;
and upon his chest he bears the Kaustubha jewel and the Śrīvatsa mark.
Assuming manifold forms for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of the world,
the Lord is to be worshipped through his twelve manifestations for the sake of spiritual power.
One should employ the *haṃsa* everywhere in the place of the *paramahaṃsa*.
One should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the principles (*tattva*) according to the order of emanation.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should make a resolve for the fulfillment of desires and ensure that the ritual service remains uninterrupted at the proper time.
With all one's power, one should provide food for those who have been invited and for the Vaiṣṇavas.
Thus, various kinds of gifts and the honoring of teachers;
the accomplishment through the instruction of Vaiṣṇava mantras;
and the maintenance, without interruption, of the vows associated with their proper times.
Thus has this rule for one desiring worldly prosperity been proclaimed:
one should worship the God for a year, or indeed for twelve years.
Prosperity is said to be of two kinds, based upon the worship of the Deity.
The first resides in the present life; the other relies upon a future birth.
(4.89) Here, the first is said to be light, while the second is called heavy.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods with desire, he passed away without attaining his goal. (4.90)
Then, in another birth, he shall obtain that desire even more abundantly.
But those who worship the God for the sake of prosperity throughout their lives will become kings, lords of the realm with all their desires fulfilled.
Alternatively, one should not perceive any distinction created by time:
for men possessed of intense devotion, success occurs, and not otherwise.
This has been declared in brief, O Grandfather, regarding the other [means].
"The worship of the God of gods is proclaimed in many ways.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Worship," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Which substances are desired for inclusion in this worship?
And what kind of purity is required for them? O Blessed One, tell me this. 5.1 Supreme.
The place of worship, the vessels, darbha grass, water, and even the images; perfumes, flowers, ornaments, incense, lamps, and unbroken grains (akṣata);
the arghya offering, the food offering (naivedya), and so forth—O Grandfather, these are the materials for worship.
Having purified these, one should first worship Puruṣottama.
In that regard, there is great purification for oneself through bathing and sipping water (ācamana);
O Lotus-born One, listen as I describe the procedure for bathing, which was previously mentioned by me.
The base of the palm of the thumb is indeed remembered as the *brahmatīrtha*.
One should drink [water] three times using the *brahmatīrtha*, and then rinse the mouth again;
furthermore, one should sprinkle water upon the left hand and upon the soles of both feet.
Having touched the heart with the palm, and likewise the face with the fingers;
having placed the ring finger on the thumb and touched the eye with water;
having likewise placed the index finger on that same [thumb], and similarly on both nostrils.
Having likewise performed the *kaniṣṭha* [mudrā], one should touch the two ears with that same [hand].

Having likewise performed the *madhyamā* [mudrā], one should touch both the regions of the arms. With that same [hand], one should touch the region of the navel; and joined with all [the fingers], one should touch the head.
This is declared to be the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), especially for one who has been initiated.
Having recited the five mantras in sequence, having drunk [the water] and wiped the mouth again,
and having sipped water once more in that same manner, one should sprinkle oneself with the five mantras.
One person should undertake the worship of Hari, while another performs other duties;
through bathing with water and clay, as well as by sprinkling and sipping water,
the body of a person is purified both externally and internally.
The purity of speech is ordained through utterances most dear to the truth;
the causes of mental purity are knowledge, clarity, and contentment.
He who possesses these three always remains pure, O embodied being.
In that very way, the God is constantly pleased by his worship.
This is declared to be the purification of the self; now hear about the purification of the place.
The place for gambling and eating, as well as the place for excrement, [should be avoided].
An altar site located in a cremation ground, or likewise presided over by a caṇḍāla;
one infested with worms and insects, or filled with husks, ashes, and bones; and one crowded by many people—such a place of worship is censured. (5.15–5.16)
One should always smear even an auspicious ground with cow dung. One should take fresh cow dung that has fallen upon the earth from a cow;
one should avoid that which comes from a calf, that which is too thin, that which is white, or that which is infested by insects. (5.17)
Then, having smeared [the vessel] with the weapon-mantra and having purified the jar, one should set it aside.
Having washed his hand with water, the knower of mantras should again touch it with his hand,
sprinkling it with the wind-mantra and the water-mantra.
One should scatter unbroken rice grains upon it with the eight-syllable mantra;
in this way, the purification of the site is accomplished. Now hear about the purification of the vessel:
one should cleanse gold and copper with water containing mango bark.

One should purify silver with house-soot or with extinguished charcoal; or, if it is alloyed with iron, one should purify it with water mixed with ashes. As for objects made of conch or mother-of-pearl, their purification is by means of salt.
Objects made of fruit or leaves are purified by earth and water;
purity comes through the removal of stains and odors, and not otherwise. (5.23) One should fill a single vessel with water mixed with fragrant flowers.
One should sequentially place the five upaniṣads upon him (or it) with the five mantras.
With that, one should sprinkle all the vessels, either individually or together—
[the water] which is free from salt, unclouded, pure, filled with fragrance, and endowed with flavor.
Water that has not been touched by wicked people is sufficient for all ritual acts;
through it, the purification of materials is accomplished. Now, hear concerning the purification of the image: the purification of one made of metal is indeed like that of a metal vessel.
The purification of a stone [image] is prescribed by covering it with a full [quantity of water].
Likewise for one made of wood; however, for those made of jewels, there is cleansing.
Having thus purified [the image], having collected [the water], and having touched [it], thereafter one should follow the opinion of Śakra.
One should understand that the purification of kuśa grass and similar items is by means of wiping;
for all other things, non-use is the highest form of purification.
Having prepared a seat with darbha grass and remaining below the place of worship, [one should proceed].
With darbha grass in hand, one should purify the water by consecrating it with a strainer.
The finest fragrance is said to be that produced by kuṅkuma, agaru, and candana,
which have been quickly incensed, finely ground, and mixed with camphor.
Whether the fragrance be artificial, the auspicious green [fragrance] is authoritative;
even pure sandalwood alone is auspicious and pleasing to Viṣṇu.
[So too are] both types of *karavīra*, the two kinds of *padma*, *ketakī*, *jāti*, and *mallikā*.
Likewise, three types of blue lotuses, tagara, and campaka; droṇa, vānīra, śamyāka, śvetārka, and kuṭaja;
as well as kandalī, bakula, tulasī, and the fresh mallikā. || 5.33–5.34 ||
The *asanastabaka*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, *maruta*, *śamī*,
*punnāga*, *vaṃśa*, *punnāga*, and *kṣudrapunnāga*; the *mālatī*, white *kumuda*, *devadāru*, and the two types of *utpala*.
The *kovidāra*, the *nāga*, the *sadābhadra*, and the *priyaṅgukā*; the *bilva* and the *navamālā*, as well as two maidens and two elephants;
the *āvīra*, the *karṇikāra*, the *vaiṣṇavī*, and the *śaṅkhapuṣpikā*.
Two *aśoka* trees and a *kunda*, with buds full of fragrance;
*śephālikā*, *kuravaka*, and the yellow *koraṇḍa*; two *nandyāvarta* trees and also the small *ketaka*.
Having thus gathered the flowers, one should worship Puruṣottama.
Worship with flowers gathered during the day is for worship during the day; likewise, worship with flowers gathered at night is for worship at night.
In times of distress, one may act as appropriate, though each preceding method is recommended over the following.
Muktapuṣpā, Varā, Māyā, and likewise Māyā [and Yātayāmā], as well as Sṛkkarā—
these should be especially avoided, and one should avoid them even in that context.
Koraṇḍa, black-colored [fruits], Kāpittha, and Harikarṇikā.
Ājñā, vibhītaka, śirīṣa, and madayantikā;
nirguṇḍī, sindhuvāra, kiṃśuka, śalmalī, and japā; arka, kanaka, unmatta, karañja, and the poisonous tree (viṣapādapa). || 5.42–5.43 ||
The bandhūka, mādhavī, nīpa, arjuna, and likewise the pāṭala;
as well as the caṇḍā, kośātakī, alābu, and śigru—
one should especially avoid these among trees and creepers.

That which is torn or cut, as well as a bud, and likewise that which is withered or stale; that which has reached the ground, that which is heavily bound, that which has fallen, and that which is devoid of a vessel;
that which is the remains of a meal, that which is faded, and that which has been touched by one who is untouchable.
Even if flowers have been prepared, one should avoid them even in times of distress; however,
having washed one's hands with water, a wise man should take the flowers in a vessel and afterwards place them where they are not exposed to the heat.
One should not offer barley, mung beans, millet, or flat beans of any kind;
nor should one take sprouts of dūrvā grass, bhūstṛṇa grass, or māṣa beans, unless they are fresh, combined with the first fruits [of the season], and free from defects.
One should avoid leaves and sprouts that are contrary to what is prescribed for the God.
Lāmajja is highly recommended among all roots for the Supreme Self.
Incense made from *devadāru* wood, mixed with sandalwood and *agaru*, [is likewise offered].

One should not offer incense produced from smokeless charcoal during the worship of the gods. One should present incense from *sāla* wood, resin of the *sarja* tree, or *daṇḍa* wood mixed with artificial *agaru*, or any other [incense] excluding animal products, from a vessel.
One should offer a lamp made with cow’s ghee or even with oil,
provided with a wick of thread and ignited by the fire of one's mouth. [The wicks] may be made of fine silk, linen, or subtle cotton.
One should present newly washed garments, perfumed, to the deity.
One should also give ornaments made of gold and gems;
however, one should not give those that are defective or have previously been worn by men.
One should avoid rice grains that are mixed with animal parts, chaff, ashes, bones, wood, or stones, and those that are broken or deficient in their preparation.
[One should offer] well-prepared Śāli rice grains, which possess the luster of jasmine, the moon, pearls, and conch shells.
One should offer cooked milk-rice that has been washed six times.
One should also offer cakes made from *śāli*, *ṣāṣṭika* rice, wheat, barley, mung beans, and so forth—prepared without alkaline salt, ground, and fried in ghee. || 5.57–58 ||
One should entirely avoid sacrificial oblations that are to be consumed when they are excessively hot or excessively cold,
as well as those that are undercooked, overcooked, or improperly cooked. All fruits that have ripened in their proper time are sweet.

At the time of worship, one should offer flowers that are free from worms and insects. Having offered fresh ghee, strained through cloth and mixed with the juice of *gandhaparṇa* leaves, for the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), one should likewise accept [the remainder] produced from cow's milk.
Having first spread clarified butter [upon the vessel] and having placed the sacrificial offering (havis) in two parts within the bowl,
one should sprinkle it again with that [butter] and then present the food offering (nivedya).
The worship of the retinue is performed by the offering of scents and flowers.
One should offer the arghya, pādya, naivedya, and other articles to the Deity alone.
[The twigs] produced from the palāśa, udumbara, aśvattha, plakṣa, and nyagrodha trees,
or likewise from milk-exuding trees (kṣīravṛkṣa), should be twelve finger-breadths in length.
The wise practitioner should offer fuel-sticks with the *pīṭha* mantras while the assembly is complete;
[the sticks] should be curved, scented, sharp, and split from poisonous trees.
For rites such as killing (*māraṇa*), one should offer fuel-sticks that are perforated and dry.
The fuel-stick (*idhma*) should be one cubit long, and the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) should be one forearm in length.
Water, however, should be kept constantly, or obtained from a Vaiṣṇava temple;
thus, with these auspicious materials belonging to himself, he should worship the Lord.
He will remember seven successive births in ever-increasing detail; furthermore, there shall never again be any loss of his past impressions (saṃskāra).
Then he attains that state, having reached which he does not grieve.

But those people who worship Janārdana with the wealth belonging to others—whether for the sake of money or for the sake of fame—their labor is fruitless. As for those who offer their own wealth for the purpose of worship, [their effort is not so]. (5.69–5.70)
When offerings are being performed, they become partakers of the share;
therefore, with every effort, one should employ for worship wealth acquired by oneself, and never that acquired from others, even in times of distress. (5.71–72)
If one lacks material offerings for worship, one should honor [the deity] even with flowers;
if flowers are lacking, then with water; if water is lacking, then with the mind alone.
Or, if there is delusion regarding wealth, one may have another devotee of Viṣṇu perform it.
A wise person should not enjoy [the fruits] themselves without having propitiated the deity.
For those who do not eat and do not drink without having honored the deity,
there is nothing whatsoever difficult to attain for them, both in this world and in the next.
Whatever one performs with auspicious materials, whatever one performs day after day,
and whatever one performs with personal devotion— by that, Viṣṇu is pleased. Thus, O Lotus-born One, [I have explained] the materials, the purification, and the ritual procedure for you.
"Everything has been told in brief; what more shall I say to you?
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Ordinance of Substances," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Explain correctly the treasury of mantras belonging to the Supreme Self,
as well as their characteristics, applications, and various fruits. 6.1 Paramaḥ.

"Come, I shall tell you the supreme characteristics of mantras, their seed-syllables, and their application; this secret I reveal to you. All ritual actions preceded by mantras accomplish the desired fruit."
The deity is summoned by mantras, and by mantras alone is he dismissed.
(6.3) Because they are produced from *mantraṇā*, they are called mantras; therefore, one should not reveal them.
One should not write down their true forms, nor should one proclaim their characteristics. (6.4)

The *praṇava* is the seed-syllable of all mantras, certainly the primordial light; it is considered the supreme means for both sustaining and withdrawing the life-force of all things. (6.5) Having worshipped the deity with that very syllable, one should constantly recite it.
For one who is constantly devoted to the *praṇava*, such perfection comes to pass.
O Grandfather, there is no mantra superior to the *praṇava*;
the syllable *Oṃ* consists of three morae (*mātrās*), while the letter *M* is half a mora.

The seed-syllable (bīja) of mantras is remembered as being variously [derived], but it is superior to the Praṇava; it is certain everywhere that the salutation (namaskāra) is superior to the seed-syllable. Know that the word "Parā" is likewise superior to the salutation.
Therefore, relying upon that very Lotus-Seated One...
