[6.9] The names "born of sattva," "born of rajas," and "born of tamas" end in the fourth case (genitive) and are used in the plural; the word *para* is likewise treated in the same manner. [6.10]
The first [seed-syllable] consists of eleven forms with *bindu*s and *visarga*s;
and for the five [deities] beginning with Jyeṣṭhā, there are five seed-syllables with the letter *i* (the wind).
With the third and fifth vowels, and with the twelfth [vowel], [these are formed].
On the fourteenth day, joined with the letter *la* itself in five ways,
those five seed-syllables belong to Vāgīśvarī and the others in sequence;
joined with the five beginning with the sixth [vowel], they are traditionally taught for Mohinī and the others.
But the name of all these, O Lotus-born one, is indeed as previously stated:
the letter *ma*, having become a *bindu*, is to be known as ever abiding in all beings within their bodies like the vital breath (*prāṇa*). (6.14)

The letter *da*, however, is said to represent quality (*guṇa*); remember it as the source of all qualities. (6.15) The letter *ba* represents the seed of the intellect (*buddhi*); therefore, hear now concerning its various distinctions.
It becomes joined with the four letters beginning with *ma*, namely *dharma* and the others. (6.16)
In the case of unrighteousness (*adharma*) and the others, it should be known that he is joined with four [syllables].
However, in their subdivisions, the vowels are the qualities (*guṇas*).
The syllable *pa* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the mind and is also the name of volition (*saṅkalpa*).
The seed-syllable of Time is the letter *ha*, while the seed-syllable of the Directions is with the *visarga*.

The five letters beginning with *na* are recorded as being in the subtle elements of sound and the rest; those beginning with *ṇa* are in the organs of perception, and those beginning with *ta* are in the other [organs of action].
O Lotus-born One, the five seed-syllables of the elements beginning with the letter *ña* were created according to their respective order as the names of Vāsudeva and the others,
due to the conjunction of their qualities and powers.
The wise one, proficient in the Pañcarātra, should arrange the seed-syllables (bījas);
their application in the outer enclosure is prescribed according to the sequence.
Therefore, I shall now declare the mantras of the wheels for the construction of the wheel-maṇḍala.
The seed-syllable of Akṣa is the letter CA, situated in the center of the wheel;
the seed-syllable of Kāla is the letter HA, joined with the twelve vowels.
The seed-syllables of the zodiac signs beginning with Aries are to be known as being upon the [twelve] spokes.

The seed-syllables of the lunar days (tithis) for the zodiac signs are traditionally taught as being arranged in left-to-right and right-to-left order; they are considered peaceful and are regarded as consisting of both the bright (śukla) and dark (kṛṣṇa) fortnights.
They are joined respectively with their own initial vowels and with the faces ending in the nasal bindu.

In the bright and dark fortnights, ending with the *visarga*, the beloved lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī are situated in order starting from Aries (*meṣa*) and the others, with the letters beginning with *ra* in the middle of the *ara*s. Thus they say they are established according to their sequence.
The houses beginning with *ha* and ending with *ma* should be known as being arranged in reverse order, starting from the uncreated sequence (*akṛtakrama*).
Within the vowel groups, there are seven houses by virtue of the positions of Rāhu and Ketu;
the short vowels are the first, while the seeds of Śrī reside within the [consonant] groups.
The letter *sa* and the letter *ma* are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the two rims;
likewise, the seed-syllables of the [other] principles (*tattva*) have been proclaimed in their entirety.
These are declared to be the mantras of the wheel, as they truly are in the construction of the wheel.

Now hear, in order, the seed-syllables and the names of the six limbs as well. The letter *ha* joined with the qualities (*guṇa*), the vowels (*svara*), the syllable *e*, the visarga, and the bindu is proclaimed as the seed-syllable for the six limbs.
The heart, the head, the crest, the armor, as well as the weapon and the eye— these, O Lotus-born One, are designated as the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
They are used everywhere for self-protection, at the commencement of worship, and during the two twilights.
Whether lying down or having eaten, one should always perform the six-limbed [prayer].
(6.33) In the case of releasing the *añjali* toward a woman in her courses, in the purification of all places, and upon touching weapons, the weapon-mantra is prescribed. (6.34)
In the sprinkling of oneself, in the circumambulation of the deity,
and in the ritual attendance during the twilight prayers, the directional mantra is prescribed.
By the recitation of the elemental mantras, one may bring all beings under one's control.
By constantly reciting the Kāla-mantra, one shall obtain a long life.
By reciting the mantra of Prakṛti, one always dwells in heaven;
likewise, by the constant recitation of the mantras of Vāsudeva and the others.
Success regarding dharma and other goals arises for the person who constantly recites either the eight-syllabled or the twelve-syllabled mantra;
at the end, having placed the *praṇava* [Om], the seeker of liberation should remain with his senses restrained.
The placement of the *praṇava* at the end is not prescribed for one who desires a specific fruit. One should employ the utterance *svāhā* at the conclusion of all oblations (*homa*).
[As for food], it may be milk, barley-gruel, alms-food, vegetables, or even fruit.
Having become pure, one should consume [the substance] and accomplish the desired mantra.
At the confluences of rivers, at sacred fords (tīrtha), and in mountain sanctuaries,
one should first worship the deity and recite the mantras day after day.

A thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, and twelve hundred thousand—by reciting [the mantra] this many times, the mantras are perfected; and through fire-offerings (homa), they become bestowers of fruit.
The sacrificial materials include fuel-sticks, clarified butter, fruits, lotus petals, and other oblations.
One who desires results should offer oblations day after day for the sake of attaining those fruits.
For one of great [power], it is Mahākāla; but for one who is small and weak, it is Kāla.
When the desired goal is accomplished, the wise one should practice that very desire mentally.
A Vaiṣṇava should never invoke the Supreme Lord at an improper time, nor should he ever perform rites for the purpose of harming others;
indeed, all calamities perish by themselves for one who sacrifices to Viṣṇu.
And his perfections increase constantly, even though he is free from desire;
for even one who seeks a fruit, provided he is devoid of longing and mental constructs, certainly obtains that fruit by worshipping the Supreme God. (6.47)

Even when worshiped with great effort, Govinda does not become pleased by the thought, "Give this to me," even while performing actions for the sake of human fruits. This is so even if a desire for an object to be attained remains in the heart of a Vaiṣṇava. (6.48–6.49)
Then one should worship the retinue of that very deity;
for the sake of sovereignty, one should worship the great wheel with twelve spokes,
radiant and resembling the sun, adorned with a hub and a rim.
The seed-syllable of this [conch] is *im*, and its name is Sudarśana.
One who desires fame should worship the great conch Pāñcajanya;
the seed-syllable of this [conch], which is filled with sound, is *śam*. || 6.51–6.52 ||
For the purpose of subduing enemies, one should worship the mace alone—
[the mace] which appears as if wrathfully destroying [all], and which is unassailable by gods or asuras.
The seed-syllable (bīja) of this [mudrā] is "ṢaṬ," and its deity is the goddess in female form.
O Grandfather, his names are Kṛtyā and Durgā.
One who desires the accumulation of wealth should worship Vaiśravaṇa with supreme devotion; what seed is there for him that its fruit would not be accomplished? (6.54–6.55)
But one who desires to enjoy wealth should worship Agni every day;
his seed-syllable is the letter *ga*, and his lunar mansion is Kṛttikā.
O Grandfather, I shall now describe the honors due to him on the lunar days (*tithi*) and astrological conjunctions (*yoga*).
O Brahmin, these few seeds of desire have been shown to you merely by way of summary for the benefit of practitioners;
indeed, because desires are innumerable, their full expansion cannot possibly be described. (6.57–6.58)

Even in hundreds of divine years, neither the speaker nor the listener can truly [grasp] all the desires of every embodied being, for they are indeed manifold. No one succeeds through desire; therefore, desire is useless.

Therefore, with every effort, having abandoned the longing for desires, one should worship the Blessed Lord; by that alone everything is accomplished. Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Treasury of Mantras," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the seventh chapter:
O Blessed One, this Vaiṣṇava sacrifice which has been proclaimed by you is indeed [the sacrifice of] Brahmā.
It is possible for one who has been initiated alone, and not for anyone else, to perform [these rites] with mantras.
(7.1) In that regard, explain the initiation of the Vaiṣṇavas in due order:
in what place does initiation take place, or for what kind of person? (7.2)
What kind of distinction exists in initiation, and what is the conduct prescribed therein?
Explain all of this to me, for my curiosity is indeed great. (7.3) Supreme.
At the confluences of rivers and sacred fords, in temples of the gods,
on mountain peaks, in granaries, or in a place that is very beautiful,
one should designate a site for sacrifice on ground previously examined.
The ground of a Brāhmaṇa is white; that of a Kṣatriya should be reddish-brown;
that of a Vaiśya is yellow in color, and that of a Śūdra is declared to be black.
Furthermore, there may be a portion according to one's desire; the first [white] is the destroyer of sin.

A ground that is inclined toward the east and north, elevated in the remaining directions, free from thorns, and devoid of enemies, is suitable for auspicious rites. It should be broad and untouched by wicked people. (7.7)
Having thus understood the desired ground and having first performed the removal of thorns,
the wise man should have it cleared of living beings, insects, chaff, ashes, bones, and the like; then,
having moistened it again with clay, he should construct the central altar.
One should have a boundary established all around it, level with the water, fixed in every direction,
so that others standing outside cannot enter the center of the altar.
Furthermore, one should construct a covering above even without pillars,
so that the rays of the sun never fall upon the sacrificial altar (vedī).
Having established the doorways in due order, one should prepare fire-pits (vahnikuṇḍa) in the four directions.
One should prepare garments of various colors using diverse materials,
as well as various types of jars and various kinds of vessels.
Furthermore, whatever Vaiṣṇavas there may be who desire initiation should be gathered here.
All of them should strive here together with equal devotion and concentration.
(7.14) Whose fruit shall be greater according to the Dharma: his who excels in enthusiasm, in the giving of wealth, or in bodily exertion? (7.15)
When the teacher initiates his disciples solely for their benefit,
then all of them should likewise serve him according to their ability.
In that very place prepared for the rite— free from defects and free from disturbances—
At a distance from both city and village, completely surrounded on all sides,
provided with all necessary implements and endowed with materials for worship,
he was previously authorized by skilled Vaiṣṇavas who had been initiated.
Resembling the surface of a mirror, adorned with yellow garments and canopies,
beautified in all directions by jars filled with flowers, medicinal herbs, fruits, and the like;
untouched by those who have not received initiation, and situated near water.
The preceptor should perform the initiation for the wise Vaiṣṇava on the twelfth lunar day,
or on the full moon, or at the equinox, or at the solstice,
or under the Śroṇā constellation, according to the prescribed rule.
A householder devoted to Viṣṇu, skilled in the rites of initiation,
intent on helping others, and likewise bearing the marks of the discus;
one who does not make a profession of the initiation-tantra, but is solely devoted to his duty.
One who is endowed with the knowledge of the scriptures and has desisted from worldly activities is proclaimed as an *ācārya*.
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are traditionally held to be the three castes fit for initiation;
likewise, Śūdras and women may also be so, provided they are endowed with noble birth, good character, and virtuous qualities.
One should not initiate a seeker who is an atheist, cruel, devoted to unrighteousness, deceitful, unrefined, ignorant, ungrateful,
or one who acts for the sake of hypocrisy or merely for the purpose of testing [the teacher]. (7.25)
The preceptor should not perform the supreme Vaiṣṇava initiation for him either; rather,
he should grant initiation to one who is always wise and possesses knowledge of the ritual procedure for the worship of the deity, for in this way his dharma increases.
The preceptor himself should enter the ground prepared by the disciple,
having meditated upon the deity in his mind and being accompanied by those who have received initiation;
having eaten food free from pungent spices and salt on the previous day, they should remain perfectly composed.
Having sipped water in the morning, he should prepare that ground according to the prescribed measurement.
The measurement for the altar (vedi) is ordained as twelve aratnis for Brahmins and Kṣatriyas; for Vaiśyas, it should be reduced by one-sixth.

For women and Śūdras, one should fashion [the image] reduced by one-third according to the laying out of the threads; on the altar, one should fashion the axle from the center using a twelfth part. That same measurement applies to the navel, while for the nostrils it should be double.
One should know that there is a celestial palace (*vimāna*) within the navel-lotus and a covering (*saṃstarana*).
Having struck a peg at the center, one should apply a cord there, marked with measurements, perfectly circular, well-positioned, and fastened.

There, being fully prepared, one should smear all the fields with pigments, circular in form on all sides, according to the proper measurements and in due order. One should divide the ground of the axle into three parts by means of three equal circles.
A lotus is conceived wherein the primary [lotus] has twelve petals.
The pericarp is in the central circle, and the filaments are in the second;
in the third are its petals, which are equal and graceful.

One should fashion all the parts as thick in the middle and gradually thinner toward the tips; the spaces between the petals should be made uniform everywhere. Likewise, one should prepare the region of the navel provided with three lines.
Furthermore, one should divide the non-spoked field into twelve equal parts;
within those, one should arrange the spokes and the spaces according to their respective proportions.
It is prescribed that the measurement of both be identical in all directions.
One should place the directions within the intervals between the spokes, and the intermediate directions within the range of the vowels.
One should imagine the thick forms of the spokes at the base and at the head,
and in the middle, circular forms on all sides with a measure of half [the total].
Furthermore, one should draw two circles, equal on all sides, within the *nemikṣetra*.
Their widths there are considered to be in the form of lower and upper [segments];
these are to be known as twenty-four in all directions, in successive order.
One should arrange the junctions of all the spokes at their tips and middles.
This much is declared to be the wheel, circular on all sides. One should also fashion its outer enclosure with the measurement of the hub.
For the purpose of admitting those seeking initiation, one should arrange a circle on all sides.
Therein, one should designate the places for the guardians of the directions within the cardinal points;
all of these should be square, measuring half a cubit on each side.
Even if the ground outside is seen to be low or high,
one should level it by the measure of a cubit for the successful establishment of the gates in the cardinal directions.
One should construct square gates facing the cardinal points.
In the center they should have open spaces and be broad on both sides;
the doors, starting from the north and so forth, should be determined according to the sequence of the Brahmins and the other castes for entry, exit, or initiation. || 7.47–7.48 ||
One should draw the outer circle, provided with five mandalas,
wherein the great elements, beginning with space, are situated on all sides.
Having thus measured it well with a cord, one should fashion the wheel on every side.
Then, the preceptor skilled in ritual should draw [the design] with five pigments:
white, black, red, dark blue, and yellow—or iron [pigment].
For the drawing of the lotus-born [deity], the lotus-colored [pigments], and the circle of the wheel (cakramaṇḍala), [these are used].
One should first draw the pericarp (karṇikā) entirely in yellow;
one should then draw the filaments (kesara), which are strewn with red and white [pollen]. The petals, however, should be drawn in white alone, and the space between them in dark blue.
One should then draw the three-fold rim (nemi) as white, red, and black.
The spokes (arā) should be yellow in color, and their center should be drawn white.
Within the area of the rim, however, one should draw the various [colors] in reverse order.
Both the white and black colors [should be used], while the yellow color is for the junctions.
Having thus drawn the wheel, one should then draw the cities of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in various colors upon the outer enclosure.
On the outer mandala, one should apply five colors in sequence:
black, yellow, red, dark green, and white as the fifth.
One should fashion the gates, made beautiful, with red and white [colors].
Having thus performed the drawing of the wheel, O Lotus-born One,
one should cause the disciple to receive the pledge (*samaya*) of the high-souled Vaiṣṇavas.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the procedure for the scattering of colored powders (*rajas*).
By means of which color they create the circle of the wheel with powders;
it is taught by me that the filling of whichever color is specified for drawing should be done with that very same colored powder.
The wise man should have powders prepared by skilled artisans using herbs, stones, leaves, wood, and likewise fruits, through appropriate methods.
The arrangement of their mandalas is prescribed for all locations.
One should skillfully level out depressions, elevations, and other irregularities.
By means of some mechanical fastening, one should make the pericarp (karṇikā) elevated,
and likewise the petals and the spokes (arāṇi) from within their respective spaces.
Elsewhere, the wise man should scatter powders of uniform color;
having thus drawn the supreme wheel-mandala with these powders,
the preceptor, being well-composed, should initiate the disciples who seek it.
Having had it drawn with pigments either upon a wall or on a cloth,
one should install the wheel of Īśvara out of sight of people;
but one should personally behold it at the proper time, meditating upon the Supreme Lord.
Its measurement is prescribed there precisely according to its capacity;
however, one must not omit any of the positions up to the edge of the rim.
Thus, I have explained to you everything regarding the drawing of the wheel.
By the mere recollection of whom all sin is shattered.
Piśācas, pannagas, yakṣas, grahas, pretas,
and rākṣasas do not remain near him, even in a house where he is merely depicted in a painting.
Mounted upon this discus is Vāsudeva, the Lord of the universe;
he should be worshipped with diligent effort by Vaiṣṇavas desiring perfection.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, named "The Discus," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Paramasaṃhitā.
Now begins the eighth chapter, the supreme one; hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme characteristics of initiation (dīkṣā).
Having attained which, the Vaiṣṇava of purified soul reaches perfection.
(8.1) For one whose mind is unstable and who finds no path to the highest good, those expert in initiation declare initiation to be the means for liberation from bondage. (8.2)
She, however, by the power of devotion, is established in three activities for men:
first in the observance of the rules (*samaya*), then in the knowledge of the tantras, and thereafter in worship.
Those possessed of intense [devotion] should be employed in these three activities by the wise.
For the sake of increasing the Dharma at all times in due succession,
one should first establish the entire covenant and then listen to it;
furthermore, having been initiated, one should take up the Tantra through the initiation of the text.
Furthermore, one who has been initiated into the mantra-initiation should worship the deity;
he who is intense and endowed with devotion should apply himself to the initiation.
By the grace of the deity, everything desired by him is accomplished.

Having drawn the maṇḍala together with its retinue using pigments, the preceptor should show it to the disciple; he shall then be one who has received the initiation of the pledge (samayadīkṣita). Having first drawn the maṇḍala with powders, he should afterwards [draw it] with pigments according to the rule.

One should show the disciple according to the prescribed rite; there, the initiated one comes into being. Having offered all the mantras into the fire and having invoked the Supreme Lord, he who shows the maṇḍala is to be known as an *upāsaka*.

First one should hear the Tantra, secondly one should master the Mantra, and thirdly one should worship the Deity; such is the threefold sequence. Hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for initiation in general.
O Brahmin, listen with a well-composed mind to that which brings about all accomplishments:
having first ascertained the directions and having drawn a wheel according to the scriptures,
one should place jars filled with water in all the directions.
The knower of mantras, having offered [the trees] whose necks are wrapped in cloth and which are endowed with flowers, sprouts, and fruits— twelve, eight, or four of them— with the water-mantra,
and having offered a canopy with the space-mantra and a lamp with the fire-mantra; || 8.13–14 ||
Having fashioned a fly-whisk with the *vāyumantreṇa* mantra and a parasol with the *kṣitividyā*,
and having prepared a fire-pit within the *vāruṇī* [direction] of Vāsudeva,
he should dissolve the clarified butter and purify it for the sake of accomplishing the extensive *homa*.
Having washed the vessels and gathered the sacrificial wood and *kuśa* grass,
having churned the fire-drill (*araṇi*) or produced fire by means of a gem,
one should cause a faithful and disciplined disciple to dwell in the tantras.
Having withdrawn [the elements] by means of the path of reabsorption, he himself, facing eastward,
should generate them again by way of emanation and establish [the disciple], with his senses restrained.
Having performed all this first, the initiation teacher himself [should proceed].
Having performed the protection and the placement [of mantras], one should perform the placement of the seed-syllables (bījanyāsa).
One should place the seed-syllable of the axle on the axle, and the seed-syllables of the hubs on the hubs.
The deities (mūrtis) are to be joined with the petals, while the powers (śaktis) are placed upon the filaments.
One should place the seed-syllables of Time (kāla-bīja) and the seed-syllables of Power (śakti-bīja) within the spokes;
at the tips [of the spokes], one should place the principles (tattvas) of the guardians of the forms (mūrtipālas) in order;
and one should place the seed-syllables of the fortnights and the lunar days (tithis) in their respective sequence.
On the right side of the Purāṇas, they are established in Vāmana;
likewise, they are in Nairṛta and in the abodes of the other guardians of the directions.
Having cast the seed-syllables of the elements into the outer mandalas, [one should proceed].
One should invoke the supreme deity upon the lotus within the mandala;
having invoked him, one should worship him mentally according to the path of the scriptures.
Having meditated upon the Supreme Self seated upon the throne and having offered the arghya water, [one should proceed].

Having received permission, he should circumambulate [the teacher] while offering salutations and keeping him to his right. For the sake of accomplishing the fire-rite (agnikārya), he should take recourse to a fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) measuring one cubit in size and circular in shape on all sides.

There, having performed the ritual actions beginning with the marking (*ullekha*) and ending with the application of *cakravāka* fat, one should rise and worship the Supreme Deity according to the prescribed method.
Having offered [the offerings] up to the collyrium (*añjana*) through meditation, one should then take up the mirror.
Rising again, having offered a third portion of the sacrificial porridge (caru) contained in the vessel,
one should present the collected foods, both solid and soft;
and having performed self-protection up to the offering of a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), one should proceed.
Having received permission, he should perform the fire-offering (homa) beginning with the encircling lines (paridhi).
Having invoked the Deity seated upon a lotus in the center of the fire by means of his splendor,
and having worshipped him and performed the offering of fuel-sticks (samidh), he should take up a new sruva ladle.
Having offered oblations in sequence with the *pīṭha* mantras, it is taught that one should constantly offer them in a continuous stream.
Furthermore, for a fortnight, the Paramahaṃsa should offer oblations using a ladle;
the Guru should likewise offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter with that very same ladle.
One hundred times he should offer oblations with the *pīṭha-mantras*, as well as with the five *upaniṣads*,
and also with the *śaktis*, the *mūrtis*, and the *śaktis* of the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipālas*).
Ten times, however, he should offer clarified butter with the *akṣa-mantras* and the others.
Having thus performed the expiation and surrounded the mandala, he should summon the disciple.
Having touched [the disciple] with three threads consisting of the three qualities (guṇas) on the navel, heart, and head respectively, the Guru,
taking one-third of the sacrificial oblation (caru), stands to the west of the fire.
Having sprinkled it with the three qualities, he should offer it with the nature of the Puruṣa;
and there, remaining silent, he should consume the Vaiṣṇava oblation.
Having consumed it and sipped water as appropriate, he should take refuge with the teacher.
And he should give him a tooth-stick according to his [spiritual] quality. When the disciple has sipped water, the preceptor should perform a protection ritual at the time of dusk;
he should place a triple-stranded thread, consecrated with mantras, upon the tip of the disciple's hand.
Having touched [the image] with the Vāsudeva mantra, one should lay it down upon a bed of *darbha* grass;
having touched the eyes with the Rūpa-mantra for the sake of attaining success in dreams,
one should observe the dream while remaining self-controlled and seated.
Engaging in conversation about Vaiṣṇava topics with the initiated disciples outside,
the teacher should pass that night without succumbing to sleep.
If he is unable [to remain awake], he should dismiss the deity into the fire and into the maṇḍala itself.

Having risen at dawn, well-bathed and embodying the mantra, and having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the mandala— having completed the consecration of the wheel— he should generate the mandala anew.
Having summoned the disciple and purified him, he should make him newly composed of mantra.
Having offered oblations with all the mantras in the proper sequence as before,
he should take a single garment, bind it around the disciple’s face,
and taking him by the hand, enter the mandala through his own entrance.
Having led [the disciple] around in circumambulation, one should cause him to prostrate before the guardians of the directions.
That flower, by whatever chance it may fall upon a particular flower,
that mantra is prescribed for his protection and for his success.
Having produced two eyes, he should show him the circle of the wheel (cakramaṇḍala).
He should explain the principles (tattvas) in their proper order and according to their divisions, and instruct him: "Meditate upon this form of reality with your intellect. || 8.46–8.47 ||
One should offer oneself with supreme devotion, as well as one’s entire possessions;
one should also offer jewels, ornaments, and garments. One should cause a gift of affection to be given and cause the Vaiṣṇava vow to be undertaken.
Then he should grant permission for the rite of worshiping the deity;
he should cause [the disciple] to hear the instruction and the secret [teaching] transmitted through the lineage.
In this very same way, he should impart [these] to all others as well.
If one sees a bad dream or another ill omen,
then a hundred oblations with the five Upaniṣads are prescribed there.
Through the connection of knowledge and austerity, the teacher [protects] the disciple who has taken refuge in him.
One should initiate [the disciple] even by means of a brief rite within the solar mandala.
Having sent forth the Lord of Gods from the disciple and dismissed him from the edge of the mandala,
and having released the fire situated in the center, one should then purify everything.
But for that disciple who is endowed with virtues and whom the teacher wishes to make an *ācārya*,
the knower of mantras should perform his consecration according to this rite:
with perfumes, flowers, fruits, milk, *śāli* rice, beans, barley, and so forth.
One should fill twelve jars with jewels, elements, and gold; then,
with pure water from sacred fords and the form-mantras in their proper sequence,
one should place them in the directions, adorned with perfumes and flowers.
Having made the disciple face the east and initiated him according to the path of the Tantra—
one who is faithful, humble, learned, and free from greed— the preceptor,
facing the east himself, [should worship] the Lord, the God seated upon the throne.
Having worshipped with the mind, one should present this request.
Having received permission, the Guru, remaining standing, should perform the consecration again,
taking the jars upon his head in the order of emanation while reciting the mantras.
Having performed the consecration with all [the materials], the Guru himself should provide the seat (*bṛsi*).
He too, having put on clean garments and remaining silent, should sit upon it.
And he should give the Vaiṣṇava discus as well as the meditation-band (*yogapaṭṭaka*).
"O teacher, may you be beloved by all living beings in the Vaiṣṇava Tantra.
Let disciples approach you; conduct yourself toward them according to the scriptures.
You should not act out of greed for wealth, nor out of desire for fame, nor out of fear."
"One should constantly remember the Lord according to the specific rules of the Pañcarātra.
Having been told this, he should rise, perform a circumambulation of the teacher,
place [the teacher's] feet upon a seat, and wash them with water.
Having sprinkled himself with water from the [teacher's] feet upon his head with devotion,
he should satisfy the guru with gifts of wealth according to his capacity and devotion—
namely, gold, vehicles, land, clothing, and ornaments.
"Whatever he gives to his guru, by that the king of the gods is pleased.
Today I have sought refuge in you, both with my body and my wealth.
Having said this, he should prostrate at his feet.
"May you be well and auspicious; may you prosper in life and wealth.
Having spoken thus, he should dismiss that disciple of the guru with affection.
And this applies to the disciple who has received initiation within the Vaiṣṇava maṇḍala.
With palms joined in reverence, he should satisfy the teacher with wealth;
having satisfied him, he should clasp his feet with both hands and request permission from the guru for the worship of the God of gods.
"He too should say, 'Worship the God,' thus granting permission.
(8.70) And having received permission, the disciple, from that time forward knowing the mantra, should worship the Supreme God; in this way he shall obtain the fruit of the worship. (8.71)
The God of gods is not pleased by the worship of that man who performs worship without being authorized by the preceptor.
Therefore, [one should worship] the deity situated in the center of the mandala as indicated by the preceptor.

Having seen [the deity] and obtained the permission of the guru, one should worship Puruṣottama. He who thus performs the Vaiṣṇava initiation, or causes it to be performed, both of them go to heaven; but in the opposite case, they go to hell.

He who performs the Vaiṣṇava initiation solely out of greed for wealth shall become a sinner, as shall the teacher of one who has taken refuge [in the path] while being an atheist. He who, through ignorance, should disregard his teacher and devotee...
He should be known as one who has committed a transgression against the Tantra; for him, initiation is fruitless.
At the conclusion of the initiation, he should cast all of that into abundant water, or otherwise bury it in a pure place far from the road.
Having first laid out the mandala and offered oblations with the mantras in their proper sequence,
and having consumed the sacrificial food, taken the tooth-stick, and performed the preliminary rites,
one should perform the consecration of the wheel and observe a dream on the following day.
Having become intent on fasting, on the following day he should draw the entire mandala, accompanied by recitation and fire-offerings;
then, having entered it at sunset and having dismissed everything in this manner, [he should proceed].
At dawn, one should go to the avabhṛtha bath where the supreme sacred ford is located;
there, one should especially cause Brahmins endowed with devotion to pronounce auspicious blessings.
Thus, O Lotus-seated One, the sequence of rites for initiation has been described.
"For the sake of favoring my devotees, what more shall I tell you? (8.82).
Thus ends the eighth chapter, named "Initiation," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
O Janārdana, how should the practitioner recognize the signs of both the auspicious and the inauspicious? Tell me that which is known.
9.1 Supreme.
One should discern the auspicious or inauspicious fortune of the practitioner by the falling of the tooth-stick and by the visions in dreams, as well as by signs of fire.
[One should also consider] the *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *plakṣa* trees, as well as *darbha* grasses sacred to Viṣṇu.

One should have a tooth-stick made from *ātmāgata*, *apāmārga*, *añjana*, *dhātakī*, or *śamī*; or other pure substances. It should be exactly twelve finger-breadths in length, straight, and free of knots. (9.3–9.4)
The wise man, having rinsed [the tooth-stick] with water and remaining silent, should eat it from the root;
looking toward the northern, eastern, western, and southern directions respectively,
those of the various castes should chew the tooth-stick.
Having cleaned the upper and lower teeth with it in due order,
the wise man should break it in the middle, rinse it again with water,
and throw it outside; he should observe its fall.
If the tip points eastward, there will be prosperity; if it points southeast, ascetic power and strength.
If it points southward, there will be death; if it points southwest, the loss of wealth. If it points westward, there is supreme peace; if it points northwest, the onset of disease.
If the tip points north, there is the acquisition of wealth; if it points northeast, supreme happiness.
If it stands with the tip pointing upward, great prosperity is desired.
One should recognize these as the signs regarding the cleansing of the teeth.
Especially at the time of initiation, at great undertakings,
and whenever one wishes to know for oneself what is auspicious or inauspicious,
one should, having fasted according to rule, observe [the omens] correctly.
I shall explain the auspicious and inauspicious [results] for the practitioner even through dreams.
Having seen a dream according to its form, one should report it to the guru.
A dream occurring in the first watch of the night yields fruit within a year.

In the second month it lasts for eight months, in the third for three months, and in the last month it occurs at dawn with haste; the fruit [is obtained] from the rays reaching the end of the sun and the moon surrounded by stars. 9.14
A blazing *agnihotra* fire, or even one that is radiant and glowing;
[the sight of] mother, father, wife, sons, brothers, and friends; and the eating of raw human flesh, starting with the feet and so forth. (9.15–16)
The drinking of milk, Soma, wine, blood, sugar-cane juice, curd, and clarified butter;
the drinking from the ocean and from rivers, and the eating of milk-rice (pāyasa); [the sight of] men, elephants, and so forth, as well as palaces, palanquins, and fruit-bearing trees. 9.17–18ab.
Ascending easily, as if with pleasure, onto a wagon, a seat, or a bed;
crossing over oceans, rivers, and other great bodies of water;
and meeting with gods, twice-born brahmins, teachers, the wise, and the virtuous. || 9.18–9.19 ||
A conch, a discus, a banner, and so forth; a city of the Gandharvas, a bull; a parasol, Indra’s banner, rain, a mirror, and a jewel;
a fly-whisk, a palm-leaf fan, a water-jar, blood, and meat.
Anointing the body with flour-paste, hearing sounds of merit, O serpent,
approaching those who should not be approached, being bitten by scorpions and the like, being bound in all one's limbs, and likewise being assaulted by kinsmen— these are the signs. || 9.21–9.22 ||

Having seen such dreams as these, and various others as well, one should know that auspicious prosperity has arrived before long. (9.23) But in a dream, seeing oneself naked, devoid of clothing, and acting in such a manner—

One who sees a broken carriage, or one mounted upon it, or one with a broken umbrella, banner, or weapon; or who sees a Caṇḍāla, a washerman, a painter, a hunter, a mleccha, a wandering bard, or an heretic— no good fortune arises for him.
Likewise, climbing upon a donkey, a camel, a buffalo, a tiger, or an anthill;
being anointed with oil and likewise mounting [a vehicle] while traveling toward the south;
obtaining silver or gold; and drinking honey and oil.
Dancing while smeared with mud, as well as performing a marriage ceremony;
being swiftly carried away by a current, the eating of cooked meat,
the falling out of teeth, and likewise the shaving of the head.

Emerging from water, climbing a withered tree, seeing bad dreams, or witnessing other such inauspicious sights—a man does not attain what is auspicious; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (9.29)
But he who, being in the middle at that time, should eat ghee and milk-rice;
and he who, having become situated on a mountain, climbs a tree;
and he who, staying upon a palace, crosses the ocean himself. (9.30–9.31)
He indeed attains sovereignty and consumes the very earth;
for whatever the gods, brahmins, cows, ascetics, ancestors, and kings say to a man in a dream, it shall come to pass exactly so. (9.32)
During initiation and during the installation [of an image], one should carefully observe dreams regarding great persons and their transformations.
And in the fire-ritual, if the fire blazes up without effort, [it is auspicious].
Or it may proceed clockwise with its crests blazing;
or it may emit a heart-pleasing fragrance or a most enchanting form. The prosperity of that practitioner increases, without a doubt.

If the fire brought for the sake of the *homa* should perish without cause, calamities will arise for that practitioner; of this there is no doubt. Or else, the consumer of oblations (*hutāśana*) may emit a sign of Viṣṇu or a foul odor.
Or if it does not ignite, or if that auspicious [fire] turns counter-clockwise;
or if, while the mandala is being drawn, there should be heavy rain,
or a violent wind, or a halo around the sun.
The death of kinsmen or likewise the displeasure of the deities—
O Grandfather, for the practitioner there is nothing auspicious in that,
even if there are other great and auspicious omens. (9.39–9.40)
When the time is auspicious and favorable, one's prosperity increases;
even that which is difficult to attain may present itself spontaneously,
or the grace of a deity may be its far greater cause.
If misfortunes should arise regarding the materials that have been obtained,
or if there is agitation caused by the gods, that is considered an ill omen.
Thus, by these signs, the practitioner [knows] that the desired accomplishment will not occur.
One should awaken within oneself whether it be auspicious or inauspicious.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Knowledge of Omens," in the Paramasaṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the tenth chapter:
O Janārdana, explain the path of yoga in detail;
I have a supreme longing for all the limbs of yoga therein. (10.1)
Indeed, among all forms of knowledge, the knowledge of yoga is preeminent;
through the knowledge of yoga, one attains absolute liberation and supreme bliss. 10.2

But action performed by men alone, without the knowledge of Yoga, cannot produce great accomplishment; therefore, one should take recourse to Yoga. That [Yoga], as enjoined in the scriptures, is of two kinds due to the distinction between knowledge and action.

And due to the distribution of actions as well as the diversity of the mind, one is known as the yoga of knowledge and the other as the yoga of action. That which constitutes the concentration of the mind upon some particular object is [the former]. (10.4–10.5)
Unperturbed and undisturbed, that is proclaimed as yoga;
if a man’s mind remains unswerving even while performing actions,
this becomes the yoga of action (karmayoga), which destroys all evil.
But if one binds the mind to the object that is knowledge itself, free from distress,
that should be known as the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), which brings about all perfections and is auspicious—
that [yoga] wherein the mind experiences no affliction in either of the two yogas.
He attains that station which is the celebrated station of Viṣṇu;
for the Lord alone is the foundation of both types of yoga.
That worship must be performed through both knowledge and action.
Restraint (*yama*) and observance (*niyama*) are determined to be the means for the yoga of action (*karmayoga*);
detachment (*vairāgya*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*) are said to be the means for the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*).
Through compassion, the organ of speech [is restrained], and by not performing what should not be done, the hand [is restrained].
From approaching those who should not be approached, from treading upon a dance floor,
and from union with a censurable woman, one's own groin organ [is lost];
and from excreting by mere wish, the secret organ becomes ill-behaved.
And by not forming intentions toward harmful things, he protects his mind;
this righteous discipline is proclaimed as *yama*.
In the practice of vows, fasts, giving, and so forth, it is that which restrains these [actions]. 10.13–10.14
Therefore, that [practice] should be known as *niyama*, the means for accomplishing *karmayoga*.

Having performed an action through *karmayoga*, that action should then be offered at the end once more at the feet of the Supreme Self, like water for honor (*arghya*) and water for the feet (*pādya*). || 10.15 ||
Even when performing actions for the sake of their fruit, the knower of yoga,
being deeply apprehensive, should contemplate only service to the Lord.
This applies whether an action is joined with knowledge or devoid of knowledge.
"The distance between the two [ears] is great"—this is the conclusion of the treatise;
even regarding sweet sounds, the sense organ of hearing is required. Likewise, regarding visible forms, the sense organ of the eye is required. 10.18
The skin is fickle, yet it is soft to the touch; the nose brings you auspicious fragrance. The tongue is attached to great flavors, and the mind likewise to the affairs of the world;
that by which one restrains these through knowledge is known as dispassion (*vairāgya*).

Stability in the Supreme Self through non-deviation is to be known as *samādhi*; it should be understood as the highest limb of yoga, which is knowledge. Having first firmly restrained the senses through dispassion, one whose mind is steadfast [attains this].
One who is single-mindedly resolved should fix the mind equally upon the Lord of Gods.
As if seeing Him close at hand, as if bowing down and touching Him,
and as if hearing His words, one should contemplate Him without hesitation.
One should practice yoga; by that, the God of gods is pleased. Brahmā [said]:
"The minds of men have for a very long time been possessed by the latent impressions of worldly existence."
How can it be restrained in a single moment by the yoga of knowledge?
(10.25) Even when the mind has been made stainless through the meditative absorption of the yoga of knowledge, at its conclusion, it does not transcend that [same] nature once again. (10.26)
At times he considers his mind as if it were brought under control and well-restrained;
yet, when the cause arises again, it transgresses its boundaries. (10.27) Supreme.
Thus, this binding of the mind according to its true nature is difficult to accomplish;
however, through long-term practice, one should bring about detachment.
Then, his latent predispositions (vāsanās) begin to disintegrate somewhat on all sides.
While the latent impressions (vāsanās) are being exhausted, one should practice firm meditative absorption (samādhi). By the power of samādhi and through the relinquishing of attachment,
having ascended to the palace of Vaikuṇṭha, one protects the fruit of one's own performed actions.

By means of many methods, one should gradually bring the activity of the mind under control in solitude; never by means of haste. Furthermore, he who desires to bring the mind under his own control through haste—

Misfortunes or various kinds of diseases will overwhelm him. Just as one might bring a corrupted limb under control through a sequence of gentle methods over a long period, so should the high-minded man bring his mind under control.
In a secluded, uninhabited place, free from disturbances and delightful,
devoid of the hardships of food and recreation,
he remained unperturbed by cold, heat, wind, or even frost.

In a field of merit rich with water, having established himself in unwavering being and having practiced the science of yoga, he— concentrated at the proper time— discriminates [the self] by means of the non-injury of the body. || 10.35-36 ||
One should contemplate one's own birth, maintenance, destruction, and so forth;
as he contemplates in this way and seeks refuge in the Lord,
faith and devotion arise for the application of the path of yoga.
In that regard, one should train one's own mind with an undistracted mind. Wherever one's latent impression (*vāsanā*) is intense, one should observe that object;
having applied discernment right there, one should eliminate the seed of passion.

Knowing that to be a source of harm for himself, the practitioner of yoga must certainly awaken from it, even if he is attached to it; having steadied his mind, he should diligently resort to a solitary place. 10.40
Due to impossibility, due to lack of union, due to agitation, due to seeing defects, and due to the transformation of age, dispassion toward sense objects arises. 10.41–42.
Brahmā.
By these causes, the enjoyment of men ceases;
but how is the passion of the mind of a person ever brought to an end?
"May this be mine, may that be mine"—this thought persists in his heart.
And since its root is firm in volitional construction (*saṅkalpa*), how can it be uprooted?
(10.44) Attachment toward objects already experienced ceases through knowledge; but as for that affection toward those not yet experienced, how can it be warded off? (10.45)
First, one should enjoy the objects of the senses to the utmost degree, provided they are not in conflict with dharma;
even that which is unobtainable, one should seek to know through seeing, hearing, and other such means.
Being himself composed, he should constantly dwell within his heart upon its true nature, as well as suffering, negligence, and fear;
he should observe many yogis who have fallen away from those very goals.
"One should maintain the effort with the thought, 'May I not come to be.
Having practiced yoga for a very long time through the meditative absorption of the knowledge of reality, one perceives those submerged in darkness by even a small seed of desire. (10.48–10.49)
For one who dwells in this way, whose intellect is prepared and who understands, there arises in the path of yoga a realization that is ultimate in its nature.
This occurs even as he perceives day by day those enjoyments as if they were not enjoyed at all.
Faith and devotion increase toward the worship of the Lord’s feet.
Then, with senses restrained, one should worship the God of gods tirelessly according to one's enthusiasm, by means of the sacrifice consisting of meditation alone. (10.51–52)
Having thus approached this field of merit with captivating materials,
one should worship the supreme deity as if he were the Buddha himself before one's eyes.
By his grace, no action performed by him shall ever go to waste.
Neither divine nor human obstacles approach him.
Even a person established in yoga, knowing that his own mind remains under his control, should not think, "This other [object] has been brought under my sway. || 10.54-55 ||
One should not reveal one's own spiritual detachment to common people;
if one is able, one should reveal that detachment only to the Lord.
Having practiced detachment sufficiently, being firm in resolve and unwearied, [one should act]. 10.56
One should constantly hold the Supreme Lord within the heart by means of meditative concentration (samādhi).
Just as one’s mind might find its dwelling in a jewel or gold, so should one settle [the mind] upon the Lord for a long time without deviation. (10.57–58)
Having thus trained his mind and established it on the path of yoga,
O God of gods, by your grace he attains that very state. (10.59) —
Brahmā.
Between the yoga consisting of action and that consisting of knowledge, which is distinct from the other,
for which person is which one praised as being superior? (10.60) Supreme.
But for a man of unrefined intellect who is striving on the path of the virtuous, the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) should be employed; for knowledge is indeed difficult for him to attain.
However, that person who is disciplined by learning and possesses a refined intellect—
For him, the yoga of knowledge is supreme, yet it falters when accompanied by ritual action.
For one whose mind is perfected through the application of both,
Viṣṇu becomes gracious in a very short time.
There is nothing beyond this for men that destroys sin, nor anything more dear to Viṣṇu than when the mind delights in yoga. (10.64) O Grandfather, even my actions bear fruit... (10.65)
One is not afflicted by calamities, nor does one fall into darkness, when the mind is joined with the highest good. This yoga has been proclaimed to you in brief, O Grandfather. (10.66–10.67)
Through the practice of yoga, a person may come to know his own true nature,
as well as the inherent character of the senses, the virtues and vices of the mind, the onset of fatal omens, and the significance of signs such as those of birds. (10.68)
The nature of the deities and the course of karmas—(69) A yogi should not let his body waste away through effort, nor should he nourish it with excessive exertion.
He should not feel pride even in suffering, nor arrogance in pleasure. (70)
One should sit steadily in a secluded place, with the body composed and at ease;

leaning against a pillar or similar support, and having restrained [the mind] by means of binding, one should there contemplate the chapters [of the scripture], as well as the self, the object, and the instruments. 10.71–72ab.
With dispassion, he should perform the highest worship of the Divine and cultivate supreme virtues;
he should constantly gladden his mind, which has been dormant due to concern for the world,
and he should strive to turn back its long-established attachments.
One should diligently practice breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) according to one's strength;
through the persistent application of these alone, yoga will certainly become his.
For as long as the vital breath flows within the body-cavity of embodied beings...
At that time, the cessation [of breath] is known as *prāṇāyāma*.
That cessation is proclaimed by yogis to be threefold: through suppression (*staṃbha*), through filling (*pūraṇa*), and likewise through exhaling (*recana*). (10.75–76)
One should practice the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇāyāma) by means of these three methods;
through this practice, the measure (mātrā) becomes increasingly firm.
Through these measures, the prāṇāyāmas of the yogi also increase.

Through this, there shall be an increase [in virtue] and the complete destruction of his sins. Having brought the fluctuations of the mind under control and exerting himself in breath-restraint (*prāṇāyāma*),
the devoted one attains the supreme, eternal Vaiṣṇava abode.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, named Yoga, in the Paramasaṃhitā of the glorious Pañcarātra.
Now begins the eleventh chapter: Brahmā.
"O Puruṣottama, you have described to me the *ariṣṭas* produced by bricks,
which are to be known by yogis through the practice of yoga once they have been attained.
But how is *ariṣṭa* known, and at what time?"
Tell me this, O God, for my curiosity is great.
The supreme [sign] is to be known as "ariṣṭa," while the other is its secondary characteristic.
Whether situated within oneself or in another, O Grandfather, by means of its own side:
prāṇa, apāna, udāna, samāna, and vyāna—
thus the wind is traditionally said to be fivefold in the body of an embodied being.
Exhalation, inhalation, mental yawning, coughing, hiccupping, and sneezing—
these are the various movements of the vital breath (prāṇa) as it constantly moves upward.
Exhalation, swallowing, and the discharge of feces and urine [are likewise its functions].
The downward-moving *apāna* is responsible for the activity of the lower body and the functions of the private organs.
*Vyāna*, however, residing in all the limbs, is said to cause fever and the like.
*Udāna* is the cause of activities involving strength and sacred power (*brahman*).
In this regard, a faltering line [of breath] always kindles the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) equally;
so too do the various distinct states of these very same winds. (11.8)
Vibrations are perceived in various locations, as well as sounds, in the ankles, elbows, and genitals, in the left side, and in the joints;
they are situated in the throat, at the edge of the ears, in the temples, and on the crown of the head.
And in other locations, one should observe throbbings:
within the throat, in the resonance, in the belly, and in the joints of the limbs;
and one should properly observe yawning everywhere as well. || 11.10–11.11 ||
Such are the primary modifications of the vital airs (vāyu) as they operate within the body:
when serene, they grant life; when not serene, they cause the destruction of the body.
The prāṇa moves alternately through the two nostrils.
One should know the time of transition for that [wind] which moves continuously:
one should know the northern [course] as the southern [solstice], and the southern [course] as the northern solstice;
one should know the time of the equinox (viṣuva) in the middle path according to the sequence.
Its transits are the months, and those twelve constitute a year;
one who knows yoga should understand the six-month solstice through subtle knowledge.
From five onwards, they increase by five each in due order.
For as many days and nights as twenty-five are produced,
from that point onward there is an increase by one day at a time,
until they sequentially reach thirty-three days and nights.
If the life-breaths of a mortal depart after the transit has been augmented by an intercalary month following the solar month, then hear his lifespan:
it shall be three, two, or even one year, as well as months. (11.18)
Two and one and a half months...
|| 11.19 || Three, two, and again one day and night in succession—one should understand life in this very way; of this there is no doubt. || 11.20 ||
At the very beginning of the time of the transition, one should first observe one's own [vital breath];
one should recognize its increase as a sign that death (ariṣṭa) is imminent.
One should observe its increase by means of the channels (nāḍikā), months, and years.
One should calculate their results, which become increasingly vast at each successive stage.
One should also calculate the distinct time of death that has arrived;
both should be known separately, like the sign and the omen.

A wise man should constantly reflect in solitude upon the month of the Sun; among these, he should examine the days deficient by a *nāḍī* or a month, in which there is the occurrence of *ariṣṭa*. O Grandfather, there is no knowledge regarding lifespan more subtle than this.
When the decrease and increase of the abdominal wind are observed and discerned,
and when the activity of the other winds also perishes, by that a wise man should know that the end is near. (11.25–26)

There is a decline in the powers of the senses, a change in one's complexion, and especially a weakening of vision for that man in whom these occur; furthermore, the throbbing in the big toes and the thumbs of the hands ceases. (11.27)
No more than six months remain of his life.
However, if the throbbing should cease above the lower part of the elbow,
death will occur for that man within three months.
If throbbing occurs in the genitals, the flanks, and the armpits,
his life will come to an end within one month.
If he does not see his own reflection for half a month, nor perceives the binding of sweat, [his life will likewise perish].

A disorder located within the stomach perishes in ten days. If the light in the eyes, resembling that of a firefly, does not allow one to see the tip of the tongue for five days, his life remains for only three more.
He who does not see the tips of his teeth, the tips of his eyelashes, or the tip of his nose, will meet death within two days.
Furthermore, there is ringing in the ears, loss of speech, negligence, and confusion of the mind. (11.33)
"But for one whose [faculties] perish in this way, his life lasts but a single day.
O Grandfather, a wise man should recognize such and other signs as these, and observe them as the indicators of the time of death.
Even in the future, one who is devoted to Viṣṇu shall be fearless.
One should not entertain excessive greed even when encountering a situation of calamity;
for actions and their instruments increase according to one's own nature.
When twelve years have passed in the life of men,
it is possible for yogis to thoroughly understand its subtle nature,
having perceived the attainment of isolation (*kaivalya*) within the elements of the exertion of the senses. (11.37)
Those Vaiṣṇavas who are ungrateful, even though they are associated with the virtuous—
for them misfortune is ordained, especially when it depends upon others;
for such a person does not behold the orb of the newly risen moon.
Or [he sees] a subtle line situated outside of what has been diminished;
likewise, he sees the lady Arundhatī, Dhruva, and the celestial rivers.
Within a year’s course, his death will come to pass.
In the eleventh month, seeing the moon and sun unilluminated, or fire devoid of radiance, one goes to the world of Yama;
[one sees] the celestial chariots and cities of the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas.
He who sees golden trees or a mountain of that same nature during the summer season lives for ten months. That man who, while standing on his own ground, sees such things lives for nine months.
If one sees gold, silver, or various kinds of gems being vomited out, he lives for eight months. If, while looking downward, he sees someone with a red head, he lives for eight months;
likewise, if dust, ashes, or mud are placed at his footstep.
If one's [reflection] appears fragmented for seven months, he lives;
likewise, if a red pigeon or a crow suddenly appears without a shadow,
or if something grows upon his limbs even though he has merely put on a garment, [he will die].

If a shower of dust should fall upon one's back without any apparent cause, O Lotus-born One, his life remains for only six months and no more. This is known by observing the "shadow-man" (chāyāpuruṣa) in the sky, which appears devoid of a head.
If he sees another person standing before him with the form of a headless trunk (*kabandha*),
or a man who is black in color and extremely terrifying, he will live for five months. If a black woman should pass by and strike his head, [he will die].
If he faints or falls asleep during the four-month period, he lives for that duration. If he sees a most terrible blue-colored Rākṣasa,
or a Piśāca of similar appearance, he lives for three months.
If one should wander alone at twilight in an unappointed cremation ground,
his life will last for only two months.
He whose urine has the smell of a goat even when he is otherwise free from disease [shall likewise perish].
Or he may see his entire body as a *brahmarākṣasa*;
or he may see three kinds of corpses and great deaths;
or there may be terrible suffering for one who is submerged in water in a dream. (11.53–54)
By such a sign, one may declare that his own death will be through various unmanifest causes,
even while seeing unpleasant things or even beloved kinsmen who wish him well.
Within one month from that day, his life shall perish.

He who sees the moon and the sun as if smeared with blood, or sees the sky as if anointed with blood, lives for only one year. Or he who sees his own reflection obstructed before him in a mirror or in water [lives for only one year].
Whoever sees a deformed figure or one who is missing a limb, or does not perceive the wick or the stand of a lamp that is not extinguished—
within twelve days, death shall also come to him.
The lip slips from its place and the nose becomes crooked;
the ear moves from its position— his life lasts but six nights—
for him whose tongue becomes black or whose face takes on the luster of a lotus.
He who has an aversion to food yet a great longing for life,

though he be endowed with splendor by means of punishment, will perish within three nights if he becomes devoid of that splendor and turns red. He on whose head grows a pale, blue-winged [fungus] shall likewise perish.
If one's reflection is not seen in a mirror, his life remains for only two nights. Wherever one’s reflection is not seen in a mirror or even in water,
his death will certainly occur within a day and night.
Perceiving that the time of his end has drawn near, a wise man, having become composed in mind, established in goodness, and free from feverish anxiety,
should resort to supreme detachment, remaining free from fear toward worldly objects.
Having renounced all ritual actions, one should practice mental yoga. Having reached a sacred place, with a tranquil soul and senses subdued,
one should worship the Supreme God with one’s whole being and take refuge in Him.
Having honored the Vaiṣṇavas who are established in Yoga and having deliberated with them,
one should practice the path of Yoga vigilantly and with a concentrated mind.
(12.67) Thus ends the eleventh chapter, named "Ariṣṭa," in the Paramasaṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the twelfth chapter:
O God of gods, what dharma is praised for the devotees of Viṣṇu?
What are the expiations, and likewise what are the occasional duties?
What duties are considered appropriate for one who desires liberation, and what for one who desires prosperity?
Explain all of this to me, for I have a great doubt regarding it.
That action by which the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, becomes most highly pleased and acts for one's benefit—that is dharma; of this there is no doubt. (12.3)
Furthermore, I have already previously described to you that it is threefold through its connection with mind, speech, and action; therein, I shall first speak of the mental [type].
Faith, mindfulness, and serenity—these three are all indeed mental.
All other [beings] are considered to be mental transformations of these very [elements].
(12.5) The person of faith attains knowledge; the person of faith is esteemed by the virtuous; the person of faith is disciplined; and the person of faith is honored by the gods. (12.6)
Through fortitude one does not fall away from the Dharma; through fortitude one is not afflicted by sufferings;
through fortitude one is not deluded by pleasures; through fortitude one does not undergo agitation.
One who is serene does not harm another; being serene, one does not envy.
One who is serene and not greedy for gain is always happy when serene. Wherever these qualities reside in one's mind— whether by nature or through effort— the god is pleased with that person.
Association with those possessed of virtue may be the cause of virtues,
or else the hearing of these qualities as they are proclaimed by great-souled men. Those who are the opposite of these, they declare to be unrighteous.

Attached to these, they experience sufferings in all their births. Therefore, a Vaiṣṇava who desires perfection should always, with every effort, practice the discipline of the mind through these three qualities.
When the mind is brought under control, everything indeed becomes controlled;
therefore, a person should first discipline the mind.
When the mind is established on the path of truth, speech remains on the path of truth.
For speech reveals that which has been conceived by the mind.
Truth, pleasantness, and wholesomeness—thus the duty of speech is threefold.
By establishing one's speech within these three, a human being attains success.
In all matters of profit, in all matters concerning virtues from every quarter,
and in the most excellent matters of dharma, one should speak the truth directly. Likewise, when the time is right, one should speak what is pleasing to one's teachers and great elders.
One should speak for the benefit of the wise and the children, the aged and those who are suffering,
as well as for those nearby, friends, disciples, dependents, and righteous devotees, each according to their respective needs. (12.17–12.18)
Through association with the elderly, through the study of meritorious scriptures,

and through long-term practice, speech attains the path of the virtuous. The faculty of speech, when not constantly engaged in improper company, becomes exceedingly disciplined through such application.

For it is impossible to restrain [speech]; therefore, silence is superior. (12.20) Silence is not considered the duty for one engaged in the affairs of the world. Therefore, a devotee of Viṣṇu of firm vows should always guard his speech. (12.21)

Deprived of these three, the speech of an embodied being leads only to unrighteousness; it should be known as a cause of suffering and calamity. Service, purity, and the very act of benefiting others—

The bodily dharma is threefold; by it a human being attains success. Whatever effort one exerts for the sake of propitiating the deity, through vows and through the exertion of material resources—that is traditionally known as *paricaryā* (service). || 12.23–12.24 ||
The vow consists of bathing at the three sessions of the day, sleeping on the ground,
celibacy, silence, and eating food free from pungent spices and salt; likewise,
sitting in the hero’s posture at night and avoiding sleep during the day.
"Going to sacred places and so forth, O Lotus-seated One—
whatever one personally gathers as materials for the worship of the Deity,
even when exhausted, that too shall be considered service. (12.26–27)

Purity of the self should be understood as the removal of impurities; for there are many impurities in the body, and by casting them off, one becomes pure. (12.28) Urine, semen, feces, phlegm, pus, and blood—

Sweat, tears, nails, and various kinds of secretions—these impurities, when internal, lead to no harm; it is when they remain outside that they become causes of affliction. Yet all these impurities arise from time to time for everyone.
Their purification is by means of earth and water, and cleansing is through washing;
however, upon touching the impurities of others, one should perform a ritual bath.
In the case of contact with a corpse or birth-impurity, and upon meeting those who are mentally distressed, [one should bathe].
After vomiting during a white [lunar] release, bathing alone is the purification for oneself.
Regarding one's own impurities that have fallen from the body, bathing alone is prescribed, excluding sweat, tears, and the like. (12.32–33)
Even there, he should perform ritual sipping of water (ācamana), but he should not sleep at all times.
O Grandfather, those implements for the performance of rites belonging to his own body are indeed defiled by the use of others.
O Grandfather, it is the established rule that the use by humans of divine implements, locations, and so forth, is a cause of fault; however,
this does not apply to whatever substance has been dedicated here for worship by those performing the rite.

It should be understood that *nirmālya* (the remains of offerings) is to be avoided in all ritual activities. The purification of gold, gems, parrots and other birds, the place of the fire, the *sruva* ladle, vessels, and images occurs through washing.
Purification through the washing away of impurities is also worldly purity.
Worship of the gods, ritual bathing, and the constant purification of one's actions are required for engagement in worldly affairs and according to other treatises on Dharma.
A wise devotee of Viṣṇu should accept only those pure offerings that have been duly prepared for guests, teachers, servants, or the suffering;
as well as for the great bridges of dharma and the temples of the deities. (12.40)
Whatever one assists with enthusiasm, gifts of wealth, and effort for the sake of mendicants, animals, and the many Vaiṣṇavas—
this is called "benefiting others" (paropakāra), the highest physical dharma. || 12.41-42 ||
Cows are to be honored more than other animals; likewise, human beings are to be honored even more than they.
Brahmins are to be honored even more than those, and yogins even more than mendicants.
Furthermore, those who are concentrated and desire liberation are to be honored even more than yogins.
The gift of food is the supreme dharma, as is the gift of wealth in every respect;
likewise, the gift of beds and seats to Vaiṣṇava ascetics is distinguished above all others, even those that are vast. (12.44–45)

Land, vehicles, conveyances, and so forth; wealth consisting of mastery over real estate and other riches; gifts that result in great fame—these are the middling fruits, according to the state [of the donor], the designation [of the gift], the recipient, and also the faith [with which it is given]. (12.46)
It is said that by means of time and wealth, various fruits are obtained.
In all cases, however, those who desire fame and the intellect, as well as their undertakings, are censured;
yet praise and the chanting of the names of a Vaiṣṇava are especially commendable.

Giving of land and other things is praised according to the distinction of one's desires; through that [giving], they pray for long life, health, sons, and so forth. One should also examine the objects, the time and place, and the recipient.
When an action is performed after due examination, every result is attained;
or rather, all things that ought to be given must be bestowed by a wise person.
When one aims for the God of gods, glory follows as a secondary consequence.
Even service is the supreme gift for the liberated and great-souled one;
by performing it with exclusive devotion, perfection is attained and not otherwise.
Thus has this threefold dharma arising from the body been declared to you.
Listen now to the supreme cessation resulting from the contraction of worldly activity.
That which is the opposite of these is declared to be unrighteousness (adharma). Furthermore, the turning away from unrighteousness through the actions of mind, speech, and body—
This dharma, consisting of cessation, should be known as the destroyer of sin.
(12.54,5) Thus, O Brahmin, this threefold dharma arising from mind, speech, and body has been described to you, specifically that of the Vaiṣṇava. (12.55,5)

For the wise one who has conquered the senses, the supreme dharma is threefold and mental; for even the ordinary devotee, the supreme dharma is recorded as being physical. But for all those of intermediate capacity, vocal dharma is considered the highest.
O Supreme Person, is it by that very threefold Dharma which was taught by you that those possessed of sense-objects are liberated from saṃsāra? (12.58) Parama.
Dharma is known to be of the nature of action, and it is also of the nature of knowledge.
Liberation is accomplished through knowledge; action is the purifier of knowledge.
Knowledge produced by action is never obstructed anywhere.
But hear, O Lotus-born one, the specific nature of that knowledge:
indeed, pure consciousness alone, without the support of Dharma, being permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of *saṃsāra*, does not become clear in any way whatsoever. (12.60–61)

Therefore, by propitiating the Lord of Gods through ritual action, the Vaiṣṇava, having transcended all obstacles by His grace, attains perfection. The God, when propitiated through ritual action, protects one even in future births.
It drives away calamities and extends prosperity.
(63) Not even a single sense-organ can be restrained by one's own powers alone without the grace of the gods; therefore, go to him for refuge. (64)
As long as they are unliberated, there would indeed be a distinction between the individual soul and the Supreme;
but for the liberated one, no distinction exists, because of the absence of any cause for distinction.
Therefore, seeking liberation, one should worship Viṣṇu alone day after day.
Having abandoned the fruit [of action], one should practice worship through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
Then, by his offering [and service], his knowledge increases;
however, through the growth of knowledge, the karma previously committed is exhausted.
Upon the exhaustion of karma, the pure-souled one desires supreme Nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, named Dharma, in the glorious *Pāñcarātra Paramasaṃhitā*.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
It is my conviction that, because the path to Nirvana is so profound, the inhabitants of this world are generally unable to remain steadfast with supreme fortitude. (13.1)
Those of little essence, devoid of effort, and enslaved by desire and anger—
being free from longing, they never go for refuge to the Lord of Gods.
Even when concealed, the desire of others remains situated within his heart.
That [light] shall always be the very manifestation of the God.

Therefore, for the sake of benefiting all, please describe in detail the sacrifices performed for specific desires, categorized by their divisions, according to the proper time and according to one's wishes.
O Lotus-seated One, among all men, various desires are supreme;
the first should be known as that which brings nourishment, while the second is the causing of suffering to others.
Through knowledge, wealth, and vehicles; through sons and indeed cattle;
through wives and attendants; through fame and victory; through health and beauty; and likewise through status, honor, and the like— (13.6)
O Grandfather, the nourishment of men resulting from such conjunctions has been declared;
likewise, killing, the onset of disease, expulsion from one's country, victory and defeat, the loss of wealth, and even forcible abduction [are determined thereby]. (13.7–13.8)
"Causing enmity, delusion, and subjugation, as well as the infliction of pain upon others— these and other such acts, O Grandfather,
one should never perform for the sake of another, whether they lead to one's own prosperity or involve the harming of others."

A Nāga may become so for the sake of a relationship or for the sake of wealth; likewise, one should exert effort toward the nourishment of one's own self when it is appropriate. Even in that case, success comes through moderation, and not otherwise.

One who always oppresses himself by force without any fault [of his own] should inflict suffering upon him; in this way, he does not become a sinner. The time for the first part of the lawsuit is traditionally held to be always that of one desiring prosperity.
The dark fortnight, however, should be understood as being for all kinds of afflictions caused by enemies.
(13.13) Therein, the deity is distinguished according to the division of the lunar days; one who seeks to accomplish results should always worship her according to the specific desire. (13.14)
There, one who desires the fruit approaches that deity;
he should apply himself to her lore and listen to her retinues as well.
He should also arrange her attendants appropriately.
For the sake of protection, one should assign the world-protectors (lokapālas) to all the directions.
Having fashioned a lotus alone, radiant and situated within the mandala,
with eight petals in the directions, blazing with a pericarp and filaments, [one should place them] in sequence.
Having visualized the deity situated there, surrounded by his retinue and equipped with weapons and vehicles, the wise practitioner should worship him.
For all deities, however, the maṇḍala shall be a celestial chariot (vimāna).
Whether circular or square, it was presided over by gatekeepers.
Their bodies were composed of splendor, blazing forth on all sides;
they possessed grace and a pleasant countenance, and were nourished by ornaments elsewhere.
Having performed the purification of the self in due order, and thereafter the purification of the site and so forth,
the wise one should worship the deity according to the sequence of the Single Hero (Ekavīra).
