All the mantras that were previously mentioned by me should be properly grasped.
O Lotus-born One, the mantras should have those [deities] as their presiding deities in all rites;
the sequence of ritual services for all of them is entirely the same,
including the invocation, the dismissal, and the fashioning of the image.
The deities are distinguished by name, form, time, and intrinsic nature, as well as by their retinues and various mantras. 13.24 Brahmā.
With what substances is the sacrifice performed, and at what time by the practitioners?
And what is the distinction between the deities? Tell me that now. 13.25 Supreme.
I shall now describe, in due order, the sacrifices to the deities according to one’s desire for the lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad);
listen to that, O Lotus-born One, regarding the Three-crested, the Three-footed, and the Seven-tongued.

[One should worship] Lohita, Aṣṭabāhu, Trimūrti, and Tejasāṃnidhi. Adorned with red perfumes, flowers, garlands, and garments, one should prepare an auspicious seat either in the midst of fire or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). || 13.27–13.28 ||
By that very same sequence of yoga, one should worship Jātavedas;
one should likewise provide for him a red seat and a red vehicle.
The practitioner [should do so] with the weapon-mantra, together with its limbs and sub-limbs.

One attains all goals and constantly enjoys auspiciousness. In the southeast, one should observe the vows with diligence; one must not blow on the fire with the mouth, nor place it beneath oneself, nor step over it.
One should not eat without having offered oblations into the fire, nor should one perform [the ritual] at the feet.
One should not lament over what has not been burnt; rather, one should go to that very [fire] for refuge.
With such auspicious substances, one should worship Brahmā, whose form is yellow.
On the second [lunar day], one should worship the four-faced Creator (Brahmā).
Many sons are born, the lineage of livestock increases, and the trees and medicinal herbs bear fruit for the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.
On the third day, one should worship Vaiśravaṇa, the king of the yakṣas, the lord of the conch and the lotus-treasure,
who has a large belly and a massive body, with devotion, using offerings of liquor, meat, sacrificial porridge, and oblations.
Endowed with a retinue and possessing full mastery over wealth,
he obtains all riches and attains sovereign power.
On the fourth [lunar day], one should worship Gaṇeśa, the leader of obstacles, who is white in color.

The wise practitioner, at the appropriate times, should worship the four-armed, pot-bellied, single-tusked elephant-faced one with various kinds of bulbs, roots, fruits, and foods, both solid and soft,
for the sake of pacifying obstacles.
No obstacles shall arise for him, and he shall be victorious in gambling;
in legal disputes and at the front of battle, victory shall be his.
On the fifth [lunar day], one should worship her who stands in the midst of a lotus and holds a lotus in her hand.

One should worship the goddess Śrī, who is nourishment personified and attended on all sides by all the female deities, with lotuses and sacrificial offerings (*caru*). For the sake of Brahmanical prosperity (*brahmaśrī*), one should offer all white items; for royal prosperity (*ājaśrī*), one should offer red items. (13.41)
A king obtains a kingdom; one who desires victory attains victory.
One who desires sovereignty gains sovereignty, and one who seeks wealth acquires wealth.
On the sixth lunar day, one should worship Skanda with devotion—he who resembles the flower of the pomegranate tree.
One who is youthful, holding a spear in hand, six-faced,
having a cock as his banner, riding upon a peacock, never abandoning the Caitya, and the leader of the hosts—
by him one obtains knowledge, intelligence, strength, and beauty; of this there is no doubt.
On the seventh day, one should worship that god, the seven-horsed one of great majesty,
who is devoted to the welfare of the world, who stands upon the single-wheeled chariot,
the lord of the planets, the radiant Bhānu, adorned with armor and earrings.
With *karavīra* and red lotuses, one should worship Rudra in his red form;
even a poor man shall become wealthy, and a sick man shall attain health. On the eighth day, one should worship Rudra in his white form with four arms.
He will become radiant, powerful, eloquent, and free from obstacles.
(13.48) By beholding Ambikā on the ninth day with red flowers and offerings of meat, a man crosses over difficulties and attains the glory of victory. (13.49)
On the tenth day, one should worship Yama, who has the luster of collyrium and a massive body;
thus one overcomes untimely death and shall become invincible.
On the eleventh day, one should worship the thousand-eyed one, whose form is white.
One attains sovereignty as well as abundant splendors.
On the twelfth lunar day, one should worship Vāsudeva with white substances;
thus one’s prosperity increases constantly and becomes invincible to enemies.
On the thirteenth day, one should worship Kāmadeva in the form of a jewel;
one obtains supreme good fortune regarding sons, wives, and servants.
On the fourteenth day, for the sake of knowledge, one should worship eight-armed Rudra.

By offering milk-rice with clarified butter, one obtains supreme knowledge. On the fifteenth day, however, one should worship the full-orbed Moon with white, pure flowers in water; thus one becomes free from disease and endowed with nourishment.
In the same way, the deities of the lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā,
when worshipped, certainly bestow fruits corresponding to their own nature.
Incense made of guggulu mixed with clarified butter is prescribed for all of them.
The primary scent of sandalwood, combined with camphor and aloe-wood, is recommended for one desiring nourishment. The lunar days (tithis) arising in the bright fortnight are praised,
while those of the dark fortnight are considered suitable for causing harm to others.

The practitioner [should perform] the visualization of all desirable forms and the materials for worship, as well as the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the essential nature of both himself and the deity; he should also consider the place, the time, the necessary provisions, his own enthusiasm, and his inner strength.
In all appropriate cases, the desired object is accomplished, and not otherwise.
In cases of enmity, malevolent rites, and subjugation, the practitioner should always employ the names of those to be acted upon [in place of his own]. (13.60–13.61)
At its conclusion, one should offer the form of one's desire to the deity;
the knower of mantras should perform the binding of mudrās in all sacrifices.
And by performing self-protection everywhere, no fear arises for him.
Thus, having become pure and composed, one should mutter the mantra in this manner—
one thousand, ten thousand, or a hundred thousand times— and in this way, success will be attained.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Sacrifice for Desired Objects," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
"O Vaikuṇṭha, tell me what this 'mudrā' is that you have mentioned, whose binding is prescribed, and explain it along with its defining characteristics. (14.1)
O Brahmin, they are known as *mudrās* because they cause the supreme joy of those who strike [the enemy] to flow away; thus, these captivating gestures of the deities are remembered as *mudrās*. 14.2
O God, it is always performed with the seals (mudrās) of direct perception and supernormal knowledge, especially during acts of worship; therefore, the seals yield great fruit.
Furthermore, that form of the deity which is manifested is grace itself.
O Brahmin, that mudrā is declared to be the supreme secret of the deity.
The heart, the head, the crest, the armor, the weapon, and the eye are to be known as the limbs of all, approved by everyone. 14.4–14.5

Having extended the thumb between the ring finger and the middle finger, one should form a fist at the heart; this is known as the Heart Mudrā (hṛdaya-mudrā). Having formed the fist, one should strike the index finger with the tip of the thumb.
Having placed it at the edge of the forehead, this is called the *śiras-mudrā* (head seal). Having thus formed a firm fist, one should raise the thumb;
having placed it at the region of the topknot (*śikhā*), this is desired as the *śikhā-mudrā*.
Having entered within and encircled the thumb on all sides, one should then contract the index finger; that is the mudrā of the armor (*kavaca*).
Having drawn back the forehand and formed a fist like a *nārāca* arrow—
Having released [the fingers] and bent them sideways, this is called the *astra-mudrā*.
Then, having placed the *śikhā-mudrā* facing forward between the eyebrows, the *netra-mudrā* should be employed; in all cases, the right hand is used.
These six mudrās have been taught for the rite of the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
By means of these, practitioners always perform self-protection.
[One should place them] on the heart or the forehead, with the hands joined in the *saṃpuṭāñjali* gesture pointing upward.
This mudrā is said to be known as that for bowing to the Parameṣṭhin.

Having placed the two thumbs together pointing upward and having joined the hands with one another, this is called the Yoga-sampuṭa mudrā; it is prescribed for placement during the ritual installation (nyāsa).
In the same manner, having made [the hands] with the gaps [between the fingers], one should place them on the head and then on the face;
at the conclusion of the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should perform the supreme purifying consecration (abhiṣeka).
With the fingers extended upward and the wrists raised, [one should join the palms].

Having inserted the two thumbs inside, one should form the lotus mudrā (padmamudrā). On a seat in the form of a lotus, and during meditations on emanation, one should gradually place the hands level with the wrists and rotate them crosswise like a wheel.
The mudrā of the wheel, which brings great success, should be employed in its various forms;
it is applied at the time of visualizing the wheel and for the purpose of protection.
Having formed a fist with both hands, both thumbs should be bent inward.
Having joined and whirled them, they are released; this is proclaimed as the *gadāmudrā*.
It is excellent for warding off obstacles and for the protection of the earth.
Having bound the right thumb into the fist of the left hand... [14.20]
Having joined the thumb and forefinger together and extended them evenly,
one should form a fist with the other three fingers of the right hand pointing upward;
this is designated as the Śaṅkha-mudrā, which is supreme for the placement of ritual substances.
The four mudrās are the lotus, the discus, the mace, and the conch;
one should present these very four to the God.
For the bow, there is the bow-grip, and for the arrow, the arrow-grip.
The separation of the scabbard from the sword is the seal of the shield;
it is formed by joining both little fingers and likewise both index fingers.
Both hands are turned back, with the thumbs and the tips of the fingers joined together below.
One should form the middle and ring fingers on both sides like a pair of leaves;
this is called the Garuḍa-mudrā, which, when bound, brings manifold fruits, is primary for the installation of Garuḍa, and is used in all fears of serpents. (14.25–14.26)
Having extended all the fingers, sparse and pointing upwards,
and having made the span of the hand [wide], it is prescribed as the *anta* mudrā. When used while lying down or when binding, it will provide protection for oneself.
It always destroys the poison of rats and worms.
Having raised both hands with their fingertips joined and extended,
one should perform the *prārthanā-mudrā* (gesture of supplication) during the invocation of the presence [of the deity] and other rites.
The wise one should perform the touching upon the chest at both places:
for the sake of the Śrīvatsa on the right side, and for the sake of the Kaustubha gem on the left side.
This has been declared to you as a brief description of the characteristics of the mudrās.
And their application in worship has been demonstrated here and there.
O Brahmin, it is impossible to describe the characteristics of these [mudrās] in their entirety because of their infinity;
however, due to the multiplicity of deities, the mudrās are distinct for each one.
Therefore, the worship of all [deities] should be performed with the general mudrā;
the name and the prayer—these two mudrās are approved for all.
One should employ those very same [mudrās] for the deities who constitute their limbs.
In the worship of Acyuta as well, one should arrange those two for the principal deity.
The wise know that for those seeking liberation, the mental application, the visualization of form, and the mudrā are prescribed;
however, for others, the manual application with the hands is recommended by the learned.
One should never display the mudrās in a gathering of many people;
for this is a secret among mantras, therefore one should employ them in private.
One should not reveal the characteristics of the mudrās to anyone who has not been initiated.
"The deities become angry with him, and his deed shall be rendered fruitless.
(14.37) Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, named "Mudrās," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
O Brahmā,
explain the general ritual procedure for an embodied being engaged everywhere in rites performed with desire, by means of which those who possess desires may achieve success.
"O Grandfather, this supreme [teaching] has been declared by me to you with certain omissions;
however, I shall now speak without omission the compendium of the ritual for desired objects."

At the outset, a wise man should resolve upon only one desire, in accordance with his birth and character, by which he himself may become fulfilled. Having made this resolution, he should go far away from his kinsmen and the city.

He should resort to a hermitage situated in the mountains and rich in water. (15.4) With his hair, nails, and beard kept trimmed, and clothed in rags or bark garments, having bathed at sacred fords, he should offer his own desires to the deities. (15.5)

Having constructed a single hut, he should dwell in it himself; if unable to do so, he should have it built by others, or he may enter a dwelling for all purposes. (15.6) He should stay there for a single period of time, with a limit of one year.
One should first perform the *puraścaraṇa* for the sake of accomplishing one's desires.
*Puraścaraṇa* is held to be the purification of the body and the mantra;
without it, even for an ascetic, the desired goal is not accomplished.
One should sustain one's life with wild herbs that have ripened naturally,
as well as bulbs, roots, and fruits that have ripened in their own time, according to one's ability.
Having bathed in the morning, one should worship the deity of the mantra in a pure place.
At the time of recitation, one should mutter the mantra neither too quickly nor too slowly;
a thousand times, or a hundred times, or for as long as one has the energy. Facing the deity, remaining silent, and with the senses restrained. (15.10–15.11)
One should recite the mantra while counting the repetitions and eating with focused attention.
When midday arrives, one should perform the ritual bath according to the rules.
Having bathed and sipped water, and having offered the *arghya* libation, one should again recite the mantra from that [point].
Having offered the *arghya* in the afternoon, he should unite with the mantra-deities.
Having bathed again and taken his meal, he should worship the *saṃdhyā* and go to rest. In this very manner, the practitioner should perform the rite on the following day as well.
Having gone outside for the purpose of voiding excrement, one should invariably perform a bath;
then, with great effort and preceded by the observances, the wise person should recite the great mantra twelve thousand times according to the rule. 15.15–15.16ab.
One should recite one hundred thousand syllables for Sudarśana, Nṛsiṃha, Vārāha, and Aparājita,
omitting the twelve-syllable [mantra].
Among the auxiliary mantras (aṅgamantra), the primary [mantra] is the portion belonging to each respective region.
In the case of single-syllable mantras, one should fashion the limbs (aṅgas) with that very same syllable.
Having stated the entire purpose, the garland-mantra (mālāmantra) is concluded.
For the success of the mantra, however, one should place the *praṇava* (oṃ) at both the beginning and the end.
When the mantra has been mastered according to the rule, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) ending with "svāhā.
Whether with clarified butter, fuel-sticks, or fruits,
the wise person should regularly perform the oblation at least ten times for the sake of attaining success in the mantra.
But one who is unable [to perform the fire sacrifice] should simply recite [the mantra]; he should perform a mental oblation (*mānasahoma*).
A wise man should always perform at least the end of the oblation and recite the mantra.
Having churned the fire for the purpose of the oblation, he should maintain it so that it does not go out.
When that has perished, one should hold it once again by means of churning alone.
While the great mantra is being recited, the deities cause fear;
they assume a terrible form and make a great noise, yet one should not become agitated therein.

Without confusion or agitation, the deities deceive him by presenting seductive objects such as the pleasures of the "jewel of a woman," while others do so under the pretext of explaining causes, like kinsmen appearing in a dream.
The deities cause the firm resolve of the practitioner to waver.
The wise practitioner who does not fall into delusion there—
his intentions, which are constantly present in his mind, will be accomplished.
For the wise and resolute who perform their work incessantly,
various desires are fulfilled, O Grandfather, and not for others.
Even without a companion, a wise man may accomplish his desired goal.
One should employ an unafflicted assistant; when one is incapable, no other should ever be used.
(15.28) Once the mantra has been mastered, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) for the accomplishment of the task;
one should offer oblations (*āhuti*) up to ten thousand times. (15.29)
Then, for the sake of the weightiness of his resolve, he should offer oblations once again;
a man desiring the glory of Brahman should offer white lotuses.
One who desires the glory of royalty should offer red lotuses.
One desiring a kingdom should perform a fire-oblation with fuel-sticks of the *aśvattha* tree.
One who desires the increase of longevity should offer *dūrvā* grass smeared with clarified butter.
One desiring a daughter should offer fruit ripened in due season, while one desiring land should offer earth.
A man desiring a stable position should offer oblations of *nyagrodha* fuel-sticks;
for all-encompassing peace, he should offer *audumbara* fuel-sticks.
One desiring a son should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and [one should also offer it] for the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*).
One should offer oblations of apāmārga when cattle are in great distress.
A wise man desiring knowledge should offer fuel-sticks of palāśa;
one desiring food, [fuel-sticks of] food-grains; and one desiring wisdom, fresh ghee.
One desiring sovereignty should offer *bilva* fruits; for the pacification of disease, one should offer sesame seeds.
One who is stained with blood should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*) provided with thorns.
Filled with wrath, he should destroy his enemies and all evils at the time of a solar or lunar eclipse.
Having fashioned an effigy out of powdered black gram (māṣa) and offered it into the fire starting from the feet,
the practitioner seeking to perform sorcery against an enemy should offer an umbrella into the fire.
Desiring to cause enmity, he should offer salt mixed with sesame seeds.
A practitioner desiring gold should offer *nimba* flowers;
one desiring rain, however, should offer fuel-sticks of the reed (*vetasa*).
It is traditionally taught that the utterance of "svāhā" is invariably required at the end of the mantra in all oblations.
Accompanied by the sounds *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, it is intended for the affliction of others;
in all rites, one should contemplate the various conditions of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*).
In a rite of subjugation, [one should visualize them] as having become submissive; in a rite of inciting hatred, as having come to a state of enmity.
One who has disciplined his mind should bring peace to all instances of causing pain to others;
otherwise, a very great fault is shown in the Viṣṇudharma-s: having performed an action for the sake of desire and having obtained its fruit [only leads to further bondage]. 15.42–15.43a.
Furthermore, the wise man should strive for the fulfillment of desire;
yet he should avoid both despondency and haste regarding actions performed for the sake of desire.
Success comes through speech and mind when there is self-restraint; otherwise, there is only the wasting away of life.

Therefore, with a view toward his own abundant welfare alone, the wise man should perform rites for specific desires; he should not be content with what is meager. Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, named "Rites for Specific Desires," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
O Lotus-born One, I shall speak of certain mantras that accomplish desires; listen with focused attention to those which possess great heroism and great power. 16.1
The Vārāha, Nārasiṃha, Śrīkara, and Sudarśana— these four, the Vaiṣṇavas declare, are the most excellent among mantras. Indeed,
these highly auspicious mantras bring success very quickly.
Since [the results] of others are achieved only after a long time, these [mantras] possess preeminence.
O Grandfather, there are thirty-three syllables in the Vārāha mantra;
one who desires land should especially accomplish this mantra.
Having reached a Vaiṣṇava site and having worshipped that Lord,
one should meditate upon Him in the form of the Boar and repeat this mantra twelve thousand times; thus, the perfection of the mantra will be attained.
Furthermore, whatever extent of ground he wishes to attain mentally,
having reached a location near that ground, he should constantly recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times,
fifty thousand, twenty-five thousand, or thirty-seven thousand times, as the case may be.
As long as one recites it, so long is it obtained; there is no doubt in this matter.
This mantra of four hundred syllables is known as the Nārasiṃha.
It is unfailing, invincible, of great heroism, and of great success.
By that, every accomplishment pertaining to the realm of Pātāla is obtained.

Whether it be the power of *siddhi*, wealth, elixirs, the earth, heaven, or rejuvenating alchemy (*rasāyana*), there shall be the abundance of desired objects through a chariot; one becomes possessed of success through the substance of accomplishment.

Through the elixir one gains long life; through heaven, one finds bliss. Having resorted to the western gate of the temple of the God of gods, one should repeat this mantra exactly twelve thousand times.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*, he went to the mouth of the cave.
Remaining there according to the prescribed rite, he should constantly mutter this mantra; having repeated it one thousand times, he entered without hesitation.
But if the practitioner should at any time not wish to enter Pātāla,
he should perform the recitation of the mantra while staying near the cave.
When the recitation has been performed extensively, the inhabitants of Pātāla become terrified.

They create many kinds of obstacles for the practitioner from all sides. Desiring to know the thoughts of one whose mind is steady, they come again and again and ask about his purpose there according to their pleasure.
Having taken that which was brought by them,
let him dwell according to his desire in his own country, or live happily wherever he may be, as is most pleasant to him.
They know that the mantra of Śrīkara is the eight-syllabled one.
By the practice of which the practitioner attains all desires,
having reached a secluded and most delightful Vaiṣṇava abode,
he should worship the Blessed One and chant the mantra without ceasing.

One should certainly recite five thousand [times], and thereafter as much as desired. Thus one should mutter [the mantra] for twelve days for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa). One who desires long life should offer oblations of dūrvā grass anointed with ghee, or not.
Having offered ten thousand oblations and consumed the sacrificial porridge with the remaining clarified butter,
one whose soul is purified should give gold to a Brahmin;
thus, having transcended untimely deaths, he lives for a hundred years.
One should hold a wheel strung with thread after touching it with the mantra;
from all sentient beings, protection becomes unshakable. In battle, being well-disposed, one should consecrate flowers with this mantra.

One seized by a planet is easily released, for he quickly liberates them by selling *śatapuṣpa* by the thousands as a "hero's purchase. One should offer oblations with sweet substances; thus, even a poor person shall become wealthy along with his entire family.
With arms raised, one should perform recitation; facing the sun, one should recite constantly. (16.26) For him, there shall always be an uninterrupted supply of food in his dwelling.
One should offer oblations of cremation-ground ashes for twenty-one days. (16.27)
Having visualized the enemy with focused awareness, one certainly destroys him by drawing Viṣṇu on all sides with a paste of *āsuri* flour;
having repeatedly touched it with the mantra, the enemy shall become afflicted with fever.
Having bathed the deity with cow’s milk, one should release [the ritual].
Having fashioned an image of the enemy out of cow dung for the sake of stability,
and having stepped upon its heart with the foot while reciting the mantra, one destroys him.
Having smeared the sacrificial ground in three ways, one should have water-pots placed in the cardinal directions;
having consecrated each one individually twenty-one times,
one should worship the Lord of Gods in the center and fill them with milk.
Having worshipped with the mantra and bathed [her] in the auspicious *Amṛtoda* (Nectar-Water), she obtains long life and a son without doubt.
Even a barren woman shall obtain a son through this ritual application; of this there is no uncertainty.
The man who daily recites this mantra a hundred times encounters no obstruction in his undertakings, nor does fear ever arise for him.
Even when facing places of death, difficult terrains, or when danger has presented itself—
One who recites this mantra does not fail; the practitioner does not come to grief.
Even a mortal who is destitute in every respect, by reciting this mantra, attains his desired success even without exertion.
They say that the six syllables of the Sudarśana mantra bring about the attainment of every desired sovereignty through its practice.
One who desires a kingdom, having ascended to a mountain peak provided with water, [should recite it].
One should recite the six-syllable mantra; this constitutes the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*).
A person should daily offer lotuses or bilva fruits into the fire ten thousand or even a million times; thereafter, Śrī approaches him.
But one who is incapable [of performing rituals] should mutter this for a long time without weariness;
by constantly propitiating the God, his kingdom shall come to be.
However, a Vaiṣṇava who is being bound by enemies should always offer oblations.
By means of *vibhītaka* fuel-sticks, his faction of enemies is shattered.
Desiring to conquer his adversaries, the practitioner himself should perform oblations;
by this, he conquers the enemy up to a thousand times over, remaining fearless. (16.41–42)
Having made this twelve-spoked [wheel] with the six-syllable mantra, one should recite it;
or else, having placed a beautiful golden or copper [image] everywhere,
one should set it up in the house and constantly worship it.
And by constantly reciting the mantra, he shall have no fear whatsoever.
(16.44) The wise one who constantly recites the Sudarśana mantra shall have no fear whatsoever. (16.45)
Even when he has been utterly defeated, his enemies regard him as a lion;
meditating on himself as situated in the hub of a wheel, he should recite the mantra.
Even alone, he shall not suffer defeat in battle.
Holding the discus with his hand, he should constantly recite [the mantra] while whirling it;
facing that direction, the enemy army will retreat, even when an epidemic has reached the countryside or fear has been caused by rākṣasas. (16.47–48)
Through the oblation of *apāmārga* fuel-sticks, everything is completely pacified.
One afflicted by domestic troubles should meditate upon the Self situated in the center of a wheel and gaze [upon it].
If one recites the mantra with indignation, it quickly creeps toward [the enemy].
That eight-syllabled mantra which has been declared as having Nārāyaṇa as its refuge—by means of it, inconceivable perfections (siddhis) are accomplished by the best of practitioners.
One should mutter this eight-syllabled mantra; this constitutes the preliminary service (pūrvasevā).
Then, a Vaiṣṇava, always observing silence within his mind, should perform japa;
by performing japa for a full year with his senses restrained,
the practitioner, free from desire, obtains a vision of the form of the God of gods.
Meditating upon whichever deity he intends, the wise man should mutter this mantra.
Within six months alone, he beholds that deity’s form with his own eyes;
by muttering it for four months, he beholds the very form of Śrī herself.
Without a doubt, for yakṣas, kinnaras, and mortals alike,
whoever desires to bestow either a curse or a favor upon another,
he accomplishes every desired object simply through the recitation performed during the Cāturmāsya.

For the subjugation of deities and for the very sight of their forms, one should indeed recite the eight-syllable mantra; thus one obtains the desired perfection. Even one who is free from desire, being a Vaiṣṇava with restrained senses, should recite this.
He is worshipped by all people and attains knowledge of the [proper] time.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, named "The Desirable," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Paramasaṃhitā.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter:
What should kings or those of royal status—who are of wicked conduct and supported by evil people—do for the purification of the body if they desire the Vaiṣṇava initiation? 17.1
For they have no opportunity whatsoever to perform austerity;
indeed, one overcome by sin must not undertake the Vaiṣṇava initiation. 17.2 Supreme.
For one who is prosperous, devoted to Viṣṇu, and wise,
the consecration (*saṃskāra*) should be performed from birth onwards upon entering initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Indeed, at an auspicious time, through merit and with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, [the rite should be performed].
Then, one should have two equal cauldrons made of gold.
Having filled one of them with curd, honey, and ghee,
[one should place it] in a secluded, uninhabited spot adorned with all auspicious objects.
The teacher, having taken the bathed Lord by the hand with his own hand,
should contemplate the body in due order according to the path of withdrawal (saṃhāra-mārga).
But one who desires the soul's survival should meditate upon him as containing gold within and cause him to enter it.
He himself should cover it from above with another skull-cup (kaṭāha).
Then, considering the living being to have returned to its primordial nature (prakṛti), the Guru sits down;
having withdrawn his own self and then regenerated it in every respect.
Having fashioned a body for the living being through mantras in the proper sequence,
and having thus established it from the golden womb step by step, one should bring it back again.
O Lord, his birth may then be brought about, created through the power of mantra.
Then one should cause all his birth-rites (*jātakarma*) to be performed.
And a name should be given to him, belonging to the gods,
in accordance with his birth and character, with the permission of the Vaiṣṇavas.
He should have his tonsure and initiation performed according to the prescribed rites;
thereafter, he should cause that [image] containing gold within it to be given to the Brāhmaṇas,
especially to those devoted to Viṣṇu and particularly to those who are learned.
One should cause the members of the three higher castes to perform all rites with their own respective mantras.
However, for a Śūdra, one should use mantras derived from the Tantras; his name should end in the word "dāsa," and one should provide him with a sacred thread and a garment using the *guṇamantra*.
The upper garment and the sacred thread (upavīta) are required only at the time of worship, and not otherwise.
One should not employ the seed-syllable of another, nor that of a Śūdra, during recitation or meditation.
It is held that there is no fault in the utterance of mantras when they are employed for the sake of ritual action (karmayoga).
But one who is intensely devoted, pure, and delights in the Dharma and the Vidyā—
such a person, even if he be a Śūdra, may be employed everywhere without negligence.
Yet, even for him, there is no station of an Ācārya, whether in initiations or in the installation [of icons].
Whether officiating at a sacrifice or performing one for another, he should arrange himself in the middle of the row;
however, a Śūdra should worship the Lord through another Vaiṣṇava alone.
He himself should serve there and likewise satisfy [the deity] with worship.

Having thus performed worship day by day for twelve years, he should again perform the worship himself; in this way, he does not become a sinner. Then the preceptor [should initiate] the initiated one who is endowed with faith toward the Lord.
Having instructed everyone according to the prescribed rule, one should initiate them all according to the ritual;
in every case, one should employ a vessel made of gold or silver. Having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) there, one should again fill it with the weight of the balance.

Having fashioned an excellent golden image equal in size to his own body and having given it as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the learned, he becomes pure in every respect. Then the wise teacher should initiate him again and instruct him in the mantras and mudrās.
One should formulate the instructions as well as the conduct of the observances;
furthermore, one should fulfill any deficiency in those conducts through the granting of wealth.
All occasional rites should be performed in every respect by means of great gifts.
He who, being very wealthy, gives a load of gold equal to his own weight every year,
attains union with Viṣṇu through that practice for a full year.
And he who is capable and devoted, [should do so] month after month on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī).
Having bathed and facing the east, the teacher should cause the Brahmin to sit upon a black antelope skin, the Kṣatriya upon a tiger skin,
the Vaiśya upon a Ruru deer skin, and the Śūdra upon that same skin.
Having seated him there, he himself should perform the consecration with jars made of gold and filled with water from sacred fords, containing precious gems;
first withdrawing and then generating [the deity] through all the mantras in due order.
Having always consecrated him with the form-mantras (mūrti-mantra) in due order along the path of emanation,
the preceptor should perform his adornment with mantras. Once he is seated comfortably, the preceptor should instruct him thus in his presence.
"You are a Vaiṣṇava; you should worship Viṣṇu alone with a focused mind.
Endowed with supreme faith, you should proclaim only his virtues.
It is not possible for you to destroy your sin through austerities. (17.31–32)
If you are unable even to give and thus sink into blind darkness,
then it is clear that you merely guard what remains— namely, that which you give to the distinguished and that which you consume for the sake of worldly existence. (17.33)
But when [the offering] is being presented to the Brahmins during the ritual performance of the oblation,
one should mentally perform the placement of flowers directly upon the feet of Viṣṇu.
You must not place your trust in sons, wife, wealth, and the like.
One must place one's trust solely in the feet of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama),
whether in times of awakening or in dreams, in adversity as well as in prosperity.
I see no other refuge for you than that Supreme Person.

"Therefore, do not abandon your commitments, conduct, vows, and observances, nor the worship of the Vaiṣṇavas, even in times of distress. Having been addressed thus, the virtuous master prostrated with palms joined in reverence.

One should inform the guru, "I shall do everything in this manner," and then honor the guru with gifts of wealth and respect. One should place him at the forefront in all undertakings and conduct oneself toward him with reverence.

One should treat his other disciples as if they were companions; however, one should keep those who are devoted to Viṣṇu at a distance. For those who do come, one should act with kindness by providing food, clothing, and so forth.
Out of trust, one should listen to this [teaching] and likewise cause one's beloved to grasp the secrets of the *graha*.
One should constantly recite the supreme Vaiṣṇava mantra in solitude.
And if capable, the initiated master himself should worship the Lord.
Having had a golden image fashioned, endowed with all the auspicious marks,
as well as vessels made of gold and consisting of conch shells and pearls,
he should appoint only those who have been initiated as attendants for the worship.
At the conclusion of the worship, the king should daily perform constant giving— gold, food, drink, mouth-fresheners, and garments— every single day.
If he is unable to perform the worship himself, he should have the deity worshipped by another.
At the conclusion of the worship, gold should undoubtedly be given to him;
otherwise, the fruit of the deity's worship would belong solely to the worshipper.
During the preliminary consecrations for the Vaiṣṇavas, one should cause the materials for worship to be presented.

Intent on the suppression of the wicked, he should protect the enjoyments of the gods; having taken refuge at the feet of Viṣṇu, he may take an oath on some occasion. He should not practice any deceit whatsoever, though he may act according to his will in other matters involving oaths.
One should recognize that [the recipient] is empty even in regard to obligatory and occasional rites.
Having performed the gift prescribed by the teacher, one should honor it;
through giving, one dispels evil, and through honoring, one brings about health.
One should seek out a teacher through gifts; one should honor the supreme [deity] with gifts.
By acting thus day after day, whether as a king or one equal to a king, one enjoys happiness in this world and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. (17.51–52)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, named "The Lord," in the Paramasaṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter: Brahmā.
What kind of worldly existence would there be for those men who, though prosperous with wealth and grain, are devoid of knowledge,
yet possess devotion and great enthusiasm?
For they do not [worship] the Supreme God through action, mind, or speech.
Therefore, since they are capable of performing worship, speak of what brings them great benefit—
those men who are devoted yet lack learning, as well as those who are wealthy. (18.2)
Through the installation of the God of gods, supreme accomplishment is ordained.
(18.3) Even for the foremost among the learned, for men seeking the fruits [of their efforts], the highest accomplishment indeed comes to pass through the installation of the Supreme Lord. (18.4)
Those who establish the Lord of Gods in a temple according to the prescribed rites shall become kings, sovereign lords over other rulers of the earth;
or else, they shall be born into a preeminent lineage of great-souled men, perfected in virtues.
They are born learned, of virtuous conduct, and long-lived;
or else they obtain their desired success—of this there is no doubt. Yet, by merely installing a deity, a man does not necessarily find the fruit [of his labor]. (18.6–18.7)
"Know them, O Grandfather, to be bricks, wood, and stones gathered for the purpose of installation, as well as the ritual materials for the God;
and those who strive there for the sake of installation according to their strength. (18.8)
Or that sacrifice of theirs is said to be for the purpose of building a temple.
O Brahmin, those who assist with their ability and those who engage them with their speech— fruit arises for them as well from the act of installation.
How is that supreme god Brahmā established on earth by humans, as if he were a transmigrating being, like a householder who always dwells within a home? 18.11
This Supreme God is established by no one, nor even protected;
He merely accepts the worship offered by His devotees. (18.12)
Various kinds of *kiṃkaras* dwell separately in these places—
those men who have attained perfection through yoga by means of their meritorious deeds.
The Blessed One himself settles them all within those abodes.

Out of compassion for his devotees, [he manifests] those who arise with various virtues and moral qualities. Being pleased by their worship, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, grants success to men according to their conduct and according to their qualities.
Therefore, I shall describe to you the supreme method of installation;
through sacrifice, the Vaiṣṇava attains perfection and the highest benefit.
The site is said to be of two kinds: the temple (prāsāda) and the dwelling (bhavana).
Wherever that deity is installed, he is gracious toward men. When installed in a temple, he bestows grace upon all worshippers;
when installed in their homes, he nourishes their own lineage.
One should have a temple for the Lord constructed with bricks, wood, and stone;
and within its center, one should establish Mādhava in the inner sanctum (garbhāgāra).
Various types of temples have been described by those expert in the science of architecture.
They are square and circular, both symmetrical and asymmetrical.
Among them, O Brahmin, the great and powerful ones are to be known as eternal and fixed;
they are declared to be middling and inferior according to the duration of their stability.
From wood come baked bricks, and from bricks come solid stones;
these endure for a very long time, and their fruit is established in due order.
Having caused a statue to be made according to the rules and endowed with all the proper characteristics, [one should install it].
One should install [the image] for the sake of attaining the fruit when an auspicious time has arrived.
Gold, silver, copper, wood, stone,
or clay— these are the materials for an image, each according to the previous [prescribed] order.
Having first constructed [the main structure] adorned on all sides,
the wise practitioner should cause a temple for Garuḍa to be built in the east;
he should also arrange a pavilion for the Mothers to the south.

One should have stone pedestals constructed for the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the various directions. Between Īśāna and Soma, one should construct a pavilion for Viṣvaksena; and having built an enclosure wall outside, one should place a gate-tower at the entrance.
Thereafter, one should select a preceptor who is of excellent conduct and has mastered the Tantras.
Having performed all this in due order and having chosen the guardians of the images (mūrtipās),
one should examine the lunar mansions, as well as the lunar day, the zodiacal sign, and the planets.
If these [omens] occur for the patron and portend auspiciousness,
then the Bhāgavata preceptor should commence the consecration (adhivāsana).
If there are many patrons, they should proceed as preceders of the Sthāpaka.
There too, one should determine the increase of auspiciousness through the application of the *jāti* [of the planets];

the strong signs (*rāśis*) are to be accepted when they are situated in the strength of the benefic planets. The lunar days (*tithis*) should be free from the *viṣṭi* and *rikta* [inauspicious] periods, and the asterisms (*nakṣatras*) should be the fixed ones.
Having first examined the omens, auspicious birds, and favorable sounds,
one should acquire an image endowed with the proper characteristics by means of a gift of wealth.
One should then construct a consecration pavilion in front of the temple.
An auspicious place should be prepared everywhere, provided with a bathing platform;
one should also designate another location for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the water,
enclosed on all sides and furnished with a vessel filled with water.

When available, one should perform the ritual installation of water according to the rules in rivers, natural pools, tanks, springs, or lakes. One should determine the measurement of the image according to the measurement of the temple door.

Or the wise man should have a temple constructed in proportion to the size of the image. He should appoint twelve, eight, or four Brahmins endowed with virtuous qualities as Vaiṣṇava *mūrtipās*, who remain steadfast in the instructions of the *ācārya*.
One should prepare the sacrificial substances for all [deities] individually.
Having done this, one should arrange the water-dwelling for the image;
one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) for three nights or one night beforehand.
The preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, having adorned them with garments and ornaments,
should observe a fast on the day prior to the installation.
When the afternoon has arrived, he should wash the image with water.
Having correctly examined the characteristics and having had the Brahmins recite auspicious benedictions,

the preceptor should cover the site on all sides with fresh grass and unwashed cloths; then, together with the presiding deities (mūrtipas), he should lead it to the place for the preliminary immersion in water.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon oneself in due order, as well as the rite of making oneself complete (*sakalīkaraṇa*),
and having stationed the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) all around the outside of the site,
one should cause the image to enter the river water by means of the path of reabsorption (*saṃhāramārga*).

One should thus perform protection on all sides in sequence with the five mantras. Then, when the night has passed, one should arrange the archways at the entrances of the directions of the pavilion, accompanied by all auspicious rites.
One should cause water-pots, completely filled with surrounding [offerings], to be placed at the sides of the doors;
they should be provided with smeared sprouts everywhere by means of the water-mantra.
One should arrange the placement of banners and flags by means of the wind-mantra.
Having done this and having brought the image from the midst of the water,
he should enter the bathing pavilion to the accompaniment of the sounds of musical instruments.
Then the preceptor, having placed the image upon the bed with its head facing east, [proceeds].
First, the teacher should pierce the eye with this sharp needle;
afterwards, the honored artisan, skilled in his craft, should perform the procedure with the surgical instrument.
Having properly opened the eyes, [he should treat them] with ghee and likewise with honey.
Having worshipped [the deity] for the sake of purification, one should cause a bath with water to be performed.
Facing north, one should bathe him— who is seated on a bathing throne facing east—
using white mustard seeds, ground rice, and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in succession.

Having covered [the image], one should subsequently bathe it on all sides with the five mantras, taking earth dug up from a riverbank, a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), the summit of a mountain, an anthill, the horn of a bull,
the tusk of a boar, or the tusk of an elephant.
Alternatively, having prepared earth consecrated with that [mantra] as far as possible,
one should smear it [on the image] and perform the bath with the water-vidyā;
thereafter, one should cause the bath to be performed with scented water using the earth-vidyā.
Having bathed [the image] on all sides with the waters of sacred fords, with water, and with the [purifying] splendors of the winds and divine [rays],
and having bathed it, he should worship it with fresh and auspicious perfumes.
With the *sparśa* mantra, one should offer two garments and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
One should offer all ornaments with the *puruṣātman* mantra,
a garland with the *viśva* mantra, and an upper garment with the *guṇavidyā* mantra.
Having offered a lamp with light, an umbrella with the knowledge of the earth,
a canopy above, and fly-whisks with wisdom,
and having done so, one should lead the image to the consecration pavilion.
Provided with a soft bed, equipped with incense and lamps,
and adorned by Vaiṣṇavas with the various implements for the sacrifice,
one should then place the image upon the bed facing the south.
One should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), conjoined with the dissolution and emergence [of the universe],
including the self-satisfaction and the Māyā, endowed with all mantras,
and joined with both effects and causes according to the prescribed rule.
Having formed the hand-gestures (mudrās) of the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus,
one should perform the invocation of Viṣṇu with five mantras while keeping the hands joined in reverence.
Having prayed for his presence at all times, one should worship him.
Having offered the *arghya*, *pādya*, and *naivedya* with the mantras according to the prescribed rule,
and having thus worshipped the God, one should then perform the *parihoma*.
Having prepared three sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) in the cardinal directions and having appointed the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipāḥ*), [one should proceed].
One should offer twelve, eight, or even four of the best oblations.
One should have the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) made everywhere either circular or square;
having constructed the pit in the center, the preceptor (ācārya) should then perform the oblation again.
Having spread out the *kuśa* grass and prepared the vessels according to the rule,
and having consecrated the sacrificial offering and the clarified butter, they should offer oblations to all the deities.
It is ordained that cooked portions be offered for the twelve guardians of the forms (*mūrtipāla*).
In the center, however, one should offer the oblation with the mantra of the God of gods.
The ritual procedure for all [the deities] is similar; the difference arises from the presiding deities of the directions.
Having meditated upon a great lotus with filaments and petals in the midst of the fire—
Having meditated upon the deity residing therein, the twice-born should then perform the fire-oblation (homa).
All of them, facing eastward, composed and wearing upper garments, should offer the oblations.
Then, at the conclusion of the homa, they should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to them.
Having offered the *arghya* to the deity, one should cover [the image] with auspicious garments.
Having fashioned a canopy above and enclosed everything on the outside,
one should worship both the pedestal and the *brahmaśilā*, and then perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*).
There, one should keep a vigil at night with dance, song, and other such performances;
and one should provide protection on all sides within the consecration pavilion (adhivāsana-maṇḍapa).
The preceptor (ācārya), however, should spend the night by the side of the deity while observing a fast.
Thus, the entire supreme consecration (adhivāsana) has been explained to you.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the installation (sthāpana) as enjoined by the ritual rules.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, named "The Consecration," in the glorious *Paramasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter:
How was the god Brahmā established in various locations by men according to the prescribed rite?
In some places and in some way, he will exercise his sovereignty and presence;
he is supreme with respect to the qualities and defects of the country, the time, and the person.
The installation of the temple and the image exists upon the earth.
When the installation of the deity is considered amidst these defects,
it becomes empty everywhere, or it is overcome by Rākṣasas.

A wise person should not install a deity in a region abounding in wicked people, one where water is far removed, or one infested with various diseases. Nor should one install a deity at night, nor during the influence of malefic planets.
On an inauspicious lunar day or asterism, or when the sun’s orb is invisible,
one who is not a householder, nor unlearned, nor a non-Brahmin, nor one who lives by a profession [unfit for a priest],
nor one with missing limbs or redundant limbs, should not install Puruṣottama.
When it has been completed, settled, and aged, one should establish it firmly in a dwelling that is not lacking in dignity, is suitable for livelihood, and is largely free from other activities;
it should not be moved, nor broken, nor devoid of proper proportions.

One should not install an image that is pregnant or decayed; one should act [only] with such [proper images]. (19.8) If an installation of the deity is performed with these defective [images], it will become an abode for yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas. (19.9)
If one should consider that which was performed for the sake of the God of Gods,
then that shall become both endowed with faults and endowed with virtues.
When these [materials] are endowed with virtues, the consecrator, having risen in the morning—
Having bathed, sipped water, and become pure, adorned with garments and ornaments,
he comes together with the image-keepers (mūrtipas) and performs a circumambulation of the pavilion;
then, being pure, he sits on the right side of the deity, facing the east.
One should employ the method of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) together with mantras upon one's own body;
thereafter, one should purify the temple both inside and out in every respect.
One should then arrange the archways and banners, complete with flags.
Thereafter, one should place water-pots at all the locations of the doors.
One should collect the substances for the purpose of worship and for the fire-oblation,
having gathered the gems, minerals, and seeds separately.
He should gather men skilled in playing musical instruments;
having brought all these together and observed the auspicious signs,
he should duly worship the abodes of the deities.
The preceptor, together with the image-keepers, should perform the rite of installation. When a bad dream has occurred or when an ill omen has appeared,
he should kindle a fire in the pavilion and cause the expiatory rites to be performed.

One should offer clarified butter with the five mantras, step by step, ten times, a hundred times, or even a thousand times according to the sequence. This should be accompanied by the auspicious proclamations of "A day of merit! (puṇyāha), the sounds of victory (jaya), and the voices of the Brahmins.
One should fill up what is deficient or excess, or restore what is scattered.
Then, having circumambulated the God of gods with palms joined in reverence,
and having received permission, one should perform the circumambulation outside the temple.
Then, having surveyed the inner chamber with the Āntra-visualization,
one should again scatter unbroken dūrvā grass all around it.
Furthermore, one should wipe it clean with the Astra-mantra and the Vāyu-vidyā.
Having had the purification performed with *kuśa* grass by auspicious image-keepers,
and having set aside the broom, he should wash his hands with pure water brought in a new vessel all around the temple.
One should have it smeared with cow-products by initiated attendants;
one should personally sprinkle that house with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra.
One should scatter the tips of Kuśa grass, unbroken rice, and Dūrvā grass with the five Śaktis.
The practitioner should employ incense everywhere with the eight-syllable mantra;
he should also provide lamps with light in all directions.
Having done so within the inner sanctum and having displayed the mudrā, [he should proceed].
To the south, at the outer gate, the preceptor,
having kindled a fire upon a sand mound (sthaṇḍila), should offer clarified butter with the five Upaniṣads—
either a thousand times, or a hundred times, or continuously— for the sake of the pacification of the site.
For the pacification of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas, one should again offer oblations of fuel-sticks of apāmārga, śamī, and khadira;
having also offered with the three "mouth-mantras" (mukhamantra), one should complete the remainder of the rite.
One should not take a thread directly smeared with sandalwood paste;
by means of that [thread], one should perform the measurement of the directions within the inner sanctum according to the rule.
Having laid out the thread for the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions along with their sub-divisions, [one proceeds].
Immediately after [marking] Someśa, one should cast a thread toward the south and southwest. Having divided the circular image of the unenclosed [space] into twenty-five parts,
one should indicate the site for installation by proceeding to the point where the threads intersect.

Thus, men who are Vaiṣṇavas declare that [the image] is a source of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) through its installation; however, those of middling capacity desire the sought-after middling accomplishment (*siddhi*) through the application of the proportions. (19.34) If the installation is performed with measurements that are either deficient or excessive, [the result is likewise diminished].
There would be destruction for the one who establishes [the image] and for the patron every day.
Even for a deity facing west, the ritual procedure is the same; it should be performed with great care according to that very same method of laying out the lines.
Having thus established the site and measured the circular area for the image,
one should designate the place for the installation of the external deities.
Then, having gone to the side of the deity and offered a handful of flowers at the spot, [one should proceed].
The consecrated ones should bring the pedestal, which is encircled by the Brahma-stone, into the house.
Having led it around the house clockwise and all the way to the inner sanctum, one should cause all the materials to enter; otherwise, the installation of Hari cannot take place.
Having himself turned toward the west, he should place that stone, which consists of Brahman,
in the center of the site for installation by means of the threefold self (triguṇātman).
Having worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings, he should deposit gems and seeds.
The officiating priest himself, taking the substance with his hand while reciting the mantra, should deposit it into all nine pits— in all directions and in the center—
and then he should place the *tejorūpaka* (the effigy of radiant energy) before them.

One should place, in sequence, a diamond, a ruby, lapis lazuli, and sapphire; as well as a pearl, a topaz, a conch shell, and an emerald; and likewise crystal, in the cardinal directions and in the center.
One should deposit [the substances] with the eight-syllable [mantras] and with the entire [mantra]:
mercury (tāla), realgar (śilā), collyrium (añjana), green vitriol (kāsīsa), and likewise copper sulfate (pātara); as well as saurāṣṭra, gorocana, honey (mākṣika), and coral (vidruma).
One should place rice, mung beans, cow-peas, sesame, wheat, barley, [grass?], millet,
and green gram in sequence as before.
One should never prepare any substance that is more or less than the measure of a hollowed-out tree.
The skillful preceptor should deposit the entire collection of materials in the center according to the dimensions of the stone slab; some say this is for the sake of prosperity,
but a Vaiṣṇava who is expert in the Pañcarātra should certainly not do so.
The depositing of wild seeds is not recommended;
likewise, there would be no growth for the village if one were to deposit them while living in the forest. Having prepared a space for the seat with stones or bricks, [one should deposit them there].
One should establish the pedestal with the pedestal-mantras in their proper sequence.
Having meditated there upon the infinite carpet and other items along with their mantras,
one should prepare the path for the water of worship, starting from the east toward the directions beginning with the moon (the north).
Having worshipped the established pedestal in this manner with perfumes and other offerings,
having covered it with new, unwashed cloths, and having performed protection on all sides,
the *sthāpaka* (consecrator) shall go outside together with the devotees of the Lord.
One should worship the auspicious abode of Vighneśa and Śiva as well;
to the south of those two, which are situated to the east and west,
one should also arrange the shrine of Garuḍa in proximity to the temple door.
One should arrange the stations of Ananta at the rear, those of the Mothers to the south,
and those of the Guardians of the Quarters in their respective directions. Between the enclosure wall and the temple, one should worship with perfumes and flowers.
One should establish the abode of Viṣvaksena between Someśa and Īśāna;
near the enclosure wall, one should provide a place for the bearer of the deity’s remains (nirmālya),
and outside the wall, a pedestal for the purpose of offering oblations.
One should prepare a worship-seat equal [in height] to that of the deity, situated in front of the god.
Having thus established the positions for the deities with a well-composed mind,
one should approach the side of the deity and perform the most venerable worship.
Having first performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon oneself, one should subsequently perform it upon the deity.
There, having invoked this [deity] in its manifest form (*sakala*) by means of the mantra, one should worship with unbroken grains, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and ornaments. (19.59–19.60)
Having worshipped Hari according to the rules with offerings of various foods and delicacies,
one should completely encircle him with unwashed garments marked with auspicious signs.
Then, having fashioned a single yantra before the Great God, [one should proceed].
Having requested permission, one should place Hari upon the mechanical palanquin adorned with arches and attended by initiated image-bearers;
then, having recited hymns of praise, one should perform a circumambulation of the temple.
With yak-tail whisks, water-pots, umbrellas, canopies, and flagstaffs;
with lamps, incense, and the sounds of conchs and drums; and with dancing, singing, and laughter, they should make the festival vast.
The teacher should proceed with speech restrained, supporting himself on a vehicle with his hand.
With his mind, he should meditate upon the gods themselves and the attendants of the gods—
the Ādityas, Maruts, Sādhyas, Vasus, Rudras, and likewise the Ṛbhus.
Having thus meditated with vigilance upon the Aśvins, the serpents, the Siddhas, and the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, and having led them clockwise around the house,
one should offer the *arghya* according to the prescribed rule once they have reached the doorway.
One should place two new sandals before [the deity] with the *sparśavidyā* mantra.
Having offered the *arghya* water at the door of the inner sanctum (*garbhāgāra*) preceded by the mantra,
one should then cause the deity to enter within by means of the *vyomavidyā* mantra, accompanied by those who have received initiation (*dīkṣita*).
Having circumambulated the divine pedestal by way of its general outline and having performed a circumambulation from left to right,
one should carefully lower it and exert effort in its installation upon the mechanical base.
When an auspicious moment has arrived, one should act with the permission of the Brahmins.
Amidst the resonant sounds of musical instruments and the abundance of incense and lamps,
the preceptor, standing in front, should establish Hari in the east,
within the pit situated in the center of the pedestal, according to the position of the image-pilaster.
Just as the stability [of the image] is equal to that of another by means of a vertically suspended thread,
so too, having established the deity and displayed the various mudrās,
one should request its presence with wisdom, bowing at all times.

With palms joined in reverence, he should offer a garland to him with an eight-syllable mantra. Having designated a seat and a pedestal, and having offered water for the feet and water for sipping according to the rule, he should offer the guest-water (arghya) and then present mouth-freshener.
One should offer yak-tail whisks, a canopy, and likewise a handful of flowers; then,
having performed circumambulations, one should cause gifts of affection to be given—
namely, articles of worship, ornaments, a vehicle, and even land.
If one should give a gift of affection after the installation of a Vaiṣṇava image has been performed,
thousands of such gifts arise for him in a future birth.
Then, having covered the Lord of Gods with fine silk, linen, and cotton cloths...
Having closed the door in front and gone out together with those who have been initiated,
the preceptor should station his attendants all around him.
Both Vaiṣṇava deities, Vainateya and Ananta, are seated upon their pedestals.
Having fashioned each respective image with faces created by the divine feet,
one should install Gaṇapati with the face of an elephant and Śaṅkara in the form of a *liṅga* in the southern direction, both facing southward.
All the pedestal-stones should be installed, remaining immovable and level on all sides;
they should be diligently worshipped with perfumes, garlands, and ornaments.
Having covered them all with cloths, they should be arranged according to the sequence starting from the east.
One should install the lords of the directions with stones or bricks;
having installed Vīrabhadra and Vighna on the two sides at the end,
one should duly install the seven Mothers in a row according to the rules.
Having worshipped the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) and the remaining external deities,
the preceptor, having mentally invoked them, should instruct the patron:
"One should satisfy both the Vaiṣṇavas and the learned scholars with gifts given out of affection."
One should bestow all kinds of food, both solid and soft, as well as drinks, upon the entire multitude; one should distribute garments and mouth-perfumes according to one's means,
and one should diligently satisfy the entire retinue as well.
The patron (yajamāna) should also perform all of this, as instructed by the preceptor,
with devotion to the deity, continuously day and night. Having closed the door, the practitioner (sādhaka) should perform the protection rite (rakṣā) and the offering of flowers (puṣpakalā).
Having gone outside, one should cause food, drink, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to be given.
For three nights, a wise man should not perform worship of the God of gods once He has been installed in His new abode; instead, the giving of sacrificial fees is prescribed there.
Whatever wealth this man gives after examining whether the recipient is worthy or unworthy, Hari is pleased by that through the common offering of food and drink.
But as for those who will suffer from diseases and great fear for their kinsmen... [19.91–19.92]
Therefore, for the sake of the increase of Acyuta, the wise man should cause the installation to be performed with abundant food and adorned with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Installation," in the Paramasaṃhitā of the glorious Pañcarātra.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
Brahmā said: O Puruṣottama, please explain the procedure for the fire-ritual (agnikārya) applicable in all cases.
O Grandfather, I shall explain in general terms the supreme fire-ritual (agnikārya), its connection with worship, and its necessary implements. || 20.1 ||
In the initiation ceremony, as well as in the installation, and likewise in the daily and occasional rites:
the vessel for clarified butter, the pot for the sacrificial porridge, the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling vessels, fuel-sticks, *kuśa* grass,
sand, rice, water, the large ladle, the enclosing sticks, and the small dipping-spoon.
Embers, a fan, a brush, dry wood, a stirring-stick,
and fragrant flowers and the like— this is the sequence of materials and implements for him.
Having thus brought these materials to the side of the fire-place:
The practitioner should begin the worship of Hari according to the path of Tantra.
Having invoked the deity, offered the arghya, and presented the mouth-perfume,
and having received permission, he should turn back and go to the south of Hari.
One should prepare a charming place for the fire directly in front; however,
for initiation, one should make a circular fire-pit (maṇḍala) or a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) made of sand, measuring one cubit.
Having extracted that earth with a mantra and sprinkled it with water heated by fire,
one should spread sand over the ground, level on all sides in every direction;
having first drawn [the lines] with the *ahaṃkāras*, one should draw them from the north with the *guṇas*.
Having washed his hands with water, he should take up the fire with his splendor;
having placed pieces of wood upon the earth, he should kindle it by means of the Vāyu-vidyā.
Then, having sprinkled it all around, he should take water in his hand.
One should have the kuśa grass placed in the various directions with the Vāsudeva and other mantras.
Having deposited it to the north of the fire with the Sparśavidyā,
one should prepare all the ritual substances there in pairs.
Having gathered in pairs the vessels for the *caru* and its two pots, the *darvī* ladle and the *sruva* spoon,
the vessel for clarified butter (*ājya*), fuel wood, flowers, rice, and likewise the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*),
he should prepare the *camasa* cups separately.

One should place the *kūrca* grass-bundle to the south of the fire with the *brahmavidyā* mantra. To the north, having fashioned a complete purifier (*pavitra*) by tying two *kuśa* blades together at their tips with a *vikhena* [loop], one should place a vessel of water there with the *nivṛtti* mantra. (20.14–15)
Having sprinkled water into a water-vessel and purified it with the three qualities,
one should turn the vessels face upwards and sprinkle them with that water.
Taking the vessel for the sacrificial oblation (caru), one should throw rice grains into it with a handful.
Having sprinkled water with the hand four times using the *dharmādi* mantras, one should place the food over the fire with the mantra and fan it with a fan;
having placed it over the fire with the *yantra*, one should fan it with the air from a fan.
Having poured the clarified butter into the vessel for the ghee with the splendor of the *pavitra*,
and having placed it to the north of the fire, he should kindle *darbha* grass and touch [the butter] with it;
he should also cast two tips of *kuśa* grass right there with the *parameṣṭhi* mantra.
Having kindled it further with brilliance, one should envelop those two oblations;
having caused them to be burnt in the fire and purified that clarified butter by its qualities,
one should loosen the strainer in the fire and cast it away by the Supreme Lord.
Having ignited the *darvī* ladle, the *sruva* spoon, and the tips of the *kuśa* grass in the fire with its brilliance,
he should wipe them inside and out with the *dhruva* [or *dhruvasruva*] using the *sparśa-mantra*.
Having likewise washed the *sruva* spoon, he should cast the *darbha* blades into the fire.
Having sprinkled clarified butter over the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) with the *sruva* ladle, one should remove the *caru* toward the north.
There too, one should perform protection against the interruption of the ritual on all sides.
Having approached the side of the deity, one should carry out the sequence of worship.
Having offered water, one should present the water-vessel and the tooth-stick.
Having given water again, one should assign the perfume, unguent, and garland with that same [water].
Then, having meditated upon the discarded flower-offering (nirmālya), one should offer it to Viṣvaksena at the side.
Having raised the Lord of Gods from the pedestal with his two sandals,
the worshiper should lead him to the bathing area and offer a mental bath.
He should sprinkle him with the power of the *rajas* and bestow the garment by means of touch.
One should apply a coating of fragrant paste all around to cover it with darkness (tamas).
Then, having sprinkled [the image] again with twelve other jars,
one should perform the pacification rite (śānti) five times with the five Upaniṣads.
Having offered water for the feet and water for sipping, he should place [the image] upon a pedestal;
then, having consecrated it on all sides with eight jars using the three root mantras, he should subsequently perform four hundred recitations for the sake of peace.
One should cover all his limbs with garments by means of their touch.
Then one should give him a sacred thread (*upavīta*) made of three strands and tripled;
thereafter, one should give him a yellow upper garment (*uttarīya*) with the *sparśavidyā* mantra.
Having offered water for the feet and other offerings, one should apply fragrant substances for the bath to the head;
having offered water, one should smear the body with that very same unguent.
Having offered water again, one should present two new garments as before.
Then one should give twenty-seven [units] of gold; for the threefold [set], not less than one unit of gold:
earrings, ear-seals, a waist-band, armlets, bracelets, both types of finger-rings, and rings, in due order. (20.33–20.34)
Then one should bestow the girdle for the belly, the binding of the ankles, the binding of the arms, the crest-jewel, the turban, the long thread, and the garment;
as well as flowers, garlands, and wreaths— all by means of the Rūpavidyā.
One should likewise mentally offer him the Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha, and the eternal forest garland; and with the appropriate mudrā, one should offer the conch, the discus, and so forth,
as well as the mirror with the Rūpa-mantra, and the collyrium for the eyes.
Having offered incense and a lamp to him, one should present water for the feet and water for sipping. Having offered him the sandals, one should lead him to the seat.
One should offer the *arghya* according to the rule, and likewise water for sipping again.
Having mixed honey, sugar, clarified butter, curd, and milk as the fifth ingredient together on all sides with the *parameṣṭhi* and other mantras,
he should present the *madhuparka* to him with both hands along with its essence.
Having offered water into a clean new vessel upon which the *upastaraṇa* has been performed,

one should take a third part of the sacrificial food (*caru*), sprinkle it with clarified butter (*ājya*), and present it. Having offered water with other vessels, one should separately present the various kinds of foods, both solid and soft.
When it has ripened at the proper time, he should offer it just as before.
There, the wise one should pause for a moment while reciting five mantras;
having offered water with other vessels, he should present mouth-perfume.
Having composed a hymn of praise and bowed down to him, having performed a circumambulation while keeping him to his right,
and having worshipped Puruṣottama like one who is afraid and yet like a king,
he should request permission with the *satva-mantra* and protect [the site] with the *astra-mantra*.
Having placed the fire-vessel nearby and having made the requests in due order,
he should again place the three enclosing sticks (paridhis) upon the ground to the south and north,
adorned with perfumes and flowers, and [invoke] the lords of the directions gathered in their respective quarters.
With his own pairs of prostrations, he should request permission from the twice-born;
then, taking twenty-five fuel-sticks sprinkled with clarified butter,
he should offer them once with the eight-syllable mantra ending in *svāhā*.
Having performed the sprinkling with the three *ahaṃkāras* and with *guṇa*,
and having meditated upon a lotus with its pericarp within that blazing [receptacle] made of jewels,
one should invoke the Supreme Deity by means of the path previously described.
Having offered the *arghya*, one should mentally offer clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle,

using the *pīṭha-mantras* in their proper sequence, accompanied by the utterance of "svāhā. Then, having spread a base of ghee in the *darvī* spoon and placed a portion of the sacrificial food (*caru*) upon it, [one should proceed].
Having thus held [the vessel], one should offer oblations with the mantra without wavering.
(20.51) With that same [mantra], one should offer twelve spoonfuls in succession;
likewise, one should offer eight with Vāsudeva and eight with the eight-syllable [mantra]. (20.52)
Furthermore, one should offer a ball of sacrificial porridge mixed with clarified butter using the ladle, reciting the Rudra mantra; then, having washed the ladle, one should release it again.
Taking a single fuel-stick, one should offer clarified butter with the dipping-spoon (sruva).

One should offer oblations for atonement with the mantras beginning with Mūrti and Śakti and ending with the Lokapālas; then, again, one should offer them five times with the five Upaniṣads, and finally, one should cause a stream of clarified butter to be poured out.

A learned Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya endowed with virtues, or even a Vaiśya who is well-versed in the scriptures, is qualified to perform this fire-ritual (agnikārya). A Śūdra, even if he is learned, should never perform the fire-ritual under any circumstances.
An initiated person, a scholar, or a learned man may, at his will, have [the rites] performed by another. Even a Brāhmaṇa of evil conduct, or likewise a Kṣatriya of such character,
incurs the highest calamity if he performs the fire-ritual himself.

One should perform the fire-rite (agnikārya) during occasional rites, those performed for specific desires, initiations, and installations; it should not be performed elsewhere unless one is unable [to do so].
This very rule is considered applicable for all subsidiary oblations (parihoma).

One should offer oblations of clarified butter with the individual names of the guardians of the directions.
