The best of the twice-born, having been initiated and having ascended to the status of preceptors, should perform the supplementary oblation once they have been gratified with sacrificial fees.

Only those [disciples] should be appointed by the teacher as attendants for the initiation and the installation ceremony, and no others, because of the defects found in other tantras. The practitioner,
performing the fire-ritual incessantly according to the rule, [attains success].
"He destroys all evils and attains the eightfold perfections.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Fire Ritual," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
What rite is prescribed for three nights for Mukunda once he has been installed by Brahmā?
And how should the worship be performed at its conclusion? Tell me that.
Having established the supreme deity and performed the ritual offerings,
he should bestow food, drink, wealth, and other gifts, preceded by a festival.
And one should scatter food outside at all the junctions for all [the beings].
Upon the passing of three nights, one should diligently perform the ritual bathing.
Between the two doors, one should construct a square altar.
Everywhere strewn with sand and adorned with a canopy,
the teacher should prepare new jars for that [altar],
made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, and well-decorated.
Having spread out cloths upon the sacrificial altar, he should prepare the vessels upon them;
having set them down and purified the water with a strainer,
he should sprinkle the jars three times while they are turned face upwards, using the Parameṣṭhin mantra.
Then, having invoked them through the presiding deities (mūrtipas), the preceptor should fill all [the vessels] with tested substances purified by cloth,
beginning first with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the five Upaniṣads in due order. || 21.7–21.8 ||
Furthermore, one should fill one jar with all [the aforementioned substances] together, and another jar with *kuśa* grass water;
then, one should fill [the jars] with honey, oil, sugarcane juice,
and waters from various sources, such as fields, sacred fords (*tīrtha*), mountains, and the burrows of boars and mice.
Having taken earth from an anthill and from the horn of a bull, one should fill [the jars].
Then, having filled those jars, one should fill them with flowers,
sprouts, perfumes, gems, and garlands, or according to one's means.
One should provide all the ritual substances for worship that have been purified by attendants who are initiated and not engaged in other tasks. Then,
having reached the inner sanctum, one should open the door with the wind-mantra.
One should remove the garment and other offerings from the deity outside with the *viśve* mantra.

Having first dismissed the deity and removed the floral remains (*nirmālya*), the preceptor (*ācārya*) should cause the materials to be bathed; having invoked [the deity] again, he should have it invoked by those who are initiated.

Having first removed those items that were previously arranged in order upon the altar for the purpose of bathing, one should bathe the divine image for its purification with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the five Upaniṣads in succession.
21.15 First, with the five products of the cow, and then in sequence with the five Upaniṣads.
Subsequently, [the elements] such as honey and so forth, along with the qualities (guṇas) and the two-fold essences of the trees;
the five beginning with the subtle element of smell (gandha-mātrā), mind (manas), ego (ahaṃkāra), and intellect (buddhi);
the mantras of the eight groups are remembered, and those of the six groups begin with the number six.
The three qualities, beginning with *sāttvika*, are proclaimed as the virtues;
the five *upaniṣads* are remembered as the collection of all substances.
Having first bathed the deity slightly and invoked him, the knower of mantras—

Furthermore, one should perform the consecration with all the substances for bathing. One should effect peace (*śānti*) with waters from sacred fords (*tīrtha*), as well as with water mixed with perfumes and flowers;
and finally, one should effect a most weighty peace with water containing gems.
With these very substances [of the water-offering], one should bathe the deities of the limbs.
Having thus performed the bathing, the preceptor should perform the entire course of worship as before, together with the fire-ritual (agnikārya).

For the purpose of offering oblations to the spirits (bhūtas), one should cook a different sacrificial food (havis) in the common fire (laukikāgni) without mantras; by that, it is known as the external offering (bāhyabali).
It should be accompanied by fire-rites and charming articles of worship.

One should perform the propitiation as arranged according to one's means, offering various kinds of food, both solid and soft, as well as fragrances, flowers, and so forth. One should employ radiant substances for the bathing of the Supreme Lord.
At its conclusion, one should perform the offering of the bali according to the prescribed rule.
Taking a vessel made of gold, silver, or copper, one should place it upon the altar within the mandala;
it has been prepared and sprinkled with water containing a pavitra-grass ring.
Having prepared that [base], one should fashion the seat with the second oblation;
upon it, one should complete the image of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
In the absence [of the prescribed materials], the teacher [should use] gold, or pure gemstone, or even silver.
Having performed a delightful worship of him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
the Guru should place that vessel upon the head of the initiated disciple.
Another person should fill the vessel with the remainder of the sacrificial oblation (havis) submerged in water.
Others likewise should take up handfuls of incense, banners, and parasols;
having circumambulated the inner sanctum to the right amidst the sounding of conchs and drums,
they should proceed to the place of the deity and scatter an offering with their hands.
Outside the palace and likewise outside the enclosure wall,
having thus circumambulated the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha) clockwise,
one should scatter the offering (bali) upon it while saying, "Salutation to the spirits (bhūtas)."
Having performed circumambulation once more and entered the inner sanctum,
one should place that image upon a portion of the worship pedestal.
With this offering of oblations, one should worship the external deities.
One should perform this at the three junctions of the day or at a single junction, but one must not let it lapse.
Where the offering of oblations (*balidāna*) to Hari who has been installed is neglected,
one should not eat in that place, provided that a Vaiṣṇava is available [to inform one].
Those lowest of men who create obstacles to the offering of the bali-oblation acquire a heap of sin equal to that of killing a cow.
The worship of an installed deity, however, concludes with the offering of the bali.
One should not neglect the ritual bathing according to one's ability when a specific occasion arises.

[This applies] on the fourth day after the image has been installed, on the twelfth day, on the equinox, at the conclusion of a festival procession, during the conjunction with Rāhu, and likewise upon the occurrence of an ill omen. (21.37–21.38)

When an epidemic has broken out in the countryside, during a famine, when oppressed by enemies, at a festival, when the ritual practice has been interrupted, when there is an increase [in population], or when worship has long been neglected;
and upon touching thieves, outcasts, Caṇḍālas, or those who are contemptible— [in these cases, one should bathe].
If death occurs while [the deity] is situated in the temple, such infamy would arise;
therefore, in that event, and in other such circumstances as these,
one should cause the bathing of the God of Gods to be performed according to the prescribed ritual.
For this indeed brings about all peace and destroys all evil; those who seek merit should perform the ceremonial bathing of Padmanābha.
One should offer everything—vessels, garments, and so forth—to the preceptor.
And whatever else may be available, as well as offerings for the Vaiṣṇavas, he should give on the right side.
From the fourth day onwards, he should constantly worship Hari;
and the preceptor should perform the fire-rite and the offering of oblations.
In whatever place Hari is constantly worshipped by devotees of Viṣṇu,
there the piśācas, grahas, and rākṣasas never approach.
Where Hari is perpetually propitiated with pure ritual implements, [there they do not come].
There, delicate people are born, free from disease. Those Vaiṣṇava men who, being afflicted by illness, take refuge in that place,
they too are liberated from their ailment, as if they had obtained medicines.

One should never reveal the deity installed in the temple except during the time of worship; for Hari is not pleased by that [revelation]. Nor should one allow contact with impure substances or even contact with common people.

In the temple of Viṣṇu, one should avoid [using] the articles for the service of the world. A Vaiṣṇava should always worship and protect the materials for worship. Having closed the door of the temple, he may go outside at his own will.

He who thus installs Viṣṇu in a temple according to the prescribed rite does not fall from his station as long as that [image] has not perished. If there should be many builders of the temple, they likewise do not fall. (21.51)
"Because of the abundance of ritual acts, the fruit therein also increases.
All this has been told to you regarding the installation of the Supreme Lord.
Hereafter, O Grandfather, I shall describe his procession."
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Bathing Ceremony," in the Paramasaṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter, the Supreme.
O Brahman, hear now from me the procedure for the procession of the installed deity, according to the rules and accompanied by the observation of omens.
O Lotus-born One, the procession of the deity is remembered as being of two kinds.
The first [image] is for the purpose of bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), and the second is for the sake of establishing the site.
The lotus-eyed Lord, having been installed in the temple by Vaiṣṇava men,
should be led to whatever river exists there for the purpose of bathing at a sacred ford.

"Even if he has been installed, the Supreme God becomes pleased only after reaching the festival, bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha), and returning home; it is not otherwise, O Lotus-born One. This sacrifice, as enjoined by the rules, begins from the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsa)."
This concluding rite at the end of the pilgrimage is indeed to be known as the Vaiṣṇava.
At the very beginning there, one should perform a festival accompanied by dance and song for twelve days; however, one may perform it for longer if desired.
Having heard the secret counsel, having observed the omens of the birds,
and having understood the auspicious signs, he should undertake the commencement of the expedition.
When lunar days, constellations, and days of the week are found to possess excellent qualities, [then he should set out].
When these [omens] are auspicious in every respect, both in accordance with the sacrificer's inclination and the direction facing him,
then one should undertake the expedition according to the prescribed method of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
On whichever lunar mansion (nakṣatra) one recites [this], and which is endowed with all these qualities,
on the day before that, one should perform a very extensive festival. With umbrellas, white banners and cloths held at the tops of flagstaffs, and with standards...
One should adorn the quarters of the directions with archways and lamp-pillars.
And in that place, one should especially perform a grand worship for all the deities, as well as with sacrificial porridges (caru) and offerings (bali).
There, at the edge of the village, he should perform a great bali offering in the evening,
preceded by a great multitude of people and accompanied by the sounds of conchs and drums.
He should scatter various kinds of food, edibles, grains, and drinks along all the paths.
In gardens, at the edges of forests, and in temples of the gods—
having thus offered the great oblation and performed the great festival at night,
the preceptor, having risen in the morning and bathed, should worship the deity.
At its conclusion, one should bring an image for the purpose of the deity’s procession;
it may be made of gold, silver, or copper, but no other material is prescribed therein.
It should be joined with a conch and a discus, small in size, and beautiful.
One should bring for him a chariot or an elephant as a vehicle for his journey;
many attendants skilled in various musical instruments;
and parasols, banners, canopies, as well as kettledrums, tabors, and cymbals.
Having thus assembled artisans, servants, courtesans, and temple-servants at an auspicious moment, the Guru,
accompanied by four disciples and having received permission from the best of the twice-born, [proceeded].

Having circumambulated the deity and prostrated before him as he stands in front, one should gently request his purpose, saying, "Perform a pilgrimage. Then, having withdrawn that image and prepared it according to the prescribed rites, || 22.20-22.21 ||
At the time of worship, one should invoke the deity into that [liṅga] as prescribed;
having invoked Him and recalled Him to mind, one should offer the *arghya* according to the ritual rules and cover [the deity] with a great cloth having ten fringes.
Taking him by the right hand himself while remaining silent,
he should go out from the inner sanctum surrounded by his disciples;
one disciple should carry a vessel of water, and another should hold aloft a parasol.
One person shall hold the sacrificial implements, and another shall hold the oblation;
having gone outside, he himself, remaining silent, shall announce with a loud voice upon reaching the vicinity of either an elephant or a chariot.
Having caused Garuḍa to carry him, they should mount it without agitation. There, all of them, restrained in speech, wearing upper garments and well-adorned,
surrounded by a great multitude, should proceed to where the rivers flow.
Having performed a circumambulation from left to right outside the village with the *diṅmantra*, one should depart;
having gone for a distance of one *yojana*, one should avoid traveling further.
In the interval, [one should avoid places] resounding with loud shouts, songs, dances, and music.
They should also perform [offerings] with various vehicles for the satisfaction of the deity.
Having reached the vicinity of the sacred ford (tīrtha), one should first have an altar constructed;
having caused [the image] to descend from the vehicle, one should place it upon that very altar.
And one should have an offering of milk-rice prepared there in some secluded place;
having given him water for his feet and water for sipping, and having presented the respectful offering (arghya),
one should take the elephant with all [the offerings], mount it, and lead it to the river.

Having invoked the sacred fords (tīrthas) there from all sides with the water-mantra, one should take hold of that [liṅga] and immerse it three times in the water while identifying with the Supreme Self (parameṣṭhyātman). Then,
having returned to the altar, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) as well as water for sipping (ācamana).
With kuśa grass in hand and composed in mind, one should sprinkle [the image] with the five mantras;
then, taking it up once more and performing the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite in water,
one should go forth together with great crowds of people, desiring the favor of the Brāhmaṇas.

Having crossed over and brought the deity, one should worship him with perfumes and flowers. Having offered water for the feet, the respectful oblation (arghya), and the food offering according to the prescribed rule, one should then take the deity from there and lead him to the vehicle as before.
Having mounted it, he should return without delay as before;
on the very day of his departure, he should bring Hari back to this palace.
For otherwise, a great fault will certainly befall those who perform the rite.
Having arrived and performed [the rites] as before, and having gone into the interior of the sanctum (*garbhagṛha*),
one should re-install the supreme deity in the primary image (*mūlabimba*) with everything [required].
Having awakened and invoked the deity with mantras, [one should worship] the god with perfumes, flowers, and water.
One should bathe that image with it; then, having performed the rites of the procession (yātrā) at the very end,
and having thus completed the ritual, worshipped, offered the arghya, and prostrated,
one should close the inner sanctum and exit outside at will.

Outside, he should satisfy the Brahmins with various kinds of food, both solid and soft, as well as drinks. Having gratified them with the gift of food, he should have the Brahmins recite benedictions.
Then, having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) right there to the teacher together with his disciples—
Thus have I described to you the bathing at sacred fords (tīrthasnāna);
now I shall describe to you the second expedition of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
for which the construction of a dwelling was designated as the primary purpose from the outset.
When the temple of Hari has become dilapidated or broken, or even when the inner sanctum,
the image, or its pedestal is shattered or decayed, one should perform a festival for the Lord;
having constructed a new house facing either east or north with auspicious fresh timber.
Having gone outside, one should place a well-guarded, quadrangular,
and beautiful wooden pedestal in its center. Upon that, one should place a small-sized, four-armed image made of metal.
Having fashioned the painting and placed it upon its stand, one should again make it motionless.
Then, when an auspicious day has arrived, having honored the best of the twice-born, caused them to proclaim an auspicious day, and performed a rite of peace for the sake of purification; 22.47–48.
One should take a large vessel made of gold or silver,
or else of copper, and having placed therein gold and gems according to one's ability,
as well as perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and all other purifying substances from every side.
Having first filled [the vessel] with pure water and having adorned it on all sides,
one should again perform the worship of the deity with great effort.
At the conclusion of that, the preceptor should go out to a new dwelling.

Having adorned it on all sides with perfumes, flowers, sprouts, and so forth, one should enter within and perform the bodily meditation upon the Self. There, having meditated upon a seat consisting of yoga and the [divine] image as before, || 22.52 ||
Having performed the invocation within and having established protection, he should go outside.
Having reached the door of the palace, he should ask its builders:
"For how long has Janārdana been in this small house? (22.53–54)

A wise person should not desire anger while dwelling in a defiled abode; therefore, even before that, the time for instruction must be indicated by those men. Beyond one month it should be indicated, but before that, it is not accepted.
Then, having taken that vessel and entered the inner sanctum,
he should invoke the God, the Supreme Person, within it;
and having meditated upon them with his mind, he should promptly announce the time as they dictate.
Placing that bowl upon his head amidst the sounds of conchs and drums,
and having performed a circumambulation, he should go to his new home.
Having circumambulated that [home] as well, he should enter within with a concentrated mind.
Having also obtained the permission of the Brahmins and announced the time previously mentioned,
one should meditate upon Hari with all the five Upaniṣads;
and having requested His presence, one should offer water for the feet as before.
One should perform everything with mantras, accompanied by fire-rituals;
at its conclusion, one should cause food and drink to be given to all.
One should also give sacrificial fees according to one's ability and likewise cause benedictions to be recited.

The knower of mantras should not perform the depositing of treasure-vessels and the like here; rather, the primary installation alone should be performed according to that path. Therefore, [the site] should be devoid of hidden treasures and provided with minor ritual implements.
For the sake of accomplishing the task, one should imagine him as having entered his dwelling amidst the afflictions;
then, once a beautiful palace or inner sanctum has been constructed,
one should likewise invoke him into a water-vessel and establish him there once more.
But when the image has been destroyed, with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas,
the preceptor himself, facing eastward and with his mind fixed on Viṣvaksena,
should go and cause the image to be raised up, accompanied by attendants.
One should personally take all the primary jewels and,
having placed that image upon a vehicle, carry it to a body of water; there,
while recollecting Viṣvaksena, one should cast it into the middle of that water.
Having had another new image fashioned, endowed with the [auspicious] marks,

the preceptor should perform all the consecratory rites for the image as prescribed in the Tantra, beginning with the preliminary ritual of the water-consecration (*jalādhivāsana*), but excluding the invocation (*āvāhana*).
Having prepared the pedestal, one should fill it with deposits of jewels and precious minerals;
having installed the image there, one should then cause it to be made immovable.
Then, having meditated upon the yoga-pīṭha and the very form of the deity, [one should proceed].

Then, from the outer chamber, one should summon the deity into a water-vessel when an auspicious moment has arrived; however, one must not clean that image. While the original image remains undisturbed, one should construct the site (vāstu) on all sides.
Having washed [the image] on all sides with substances such as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and others,
one should invoke the deity into that very vessel of water and unite it [with the image].
[This applies to] images that are broken, decayed, or defiled by impurities.

One should perform the ritual of dismissal (udvāsana); otherwise, one must not remove the image. Thus, O Brahmin, the two-fold procession of the Lord has been described to you in due order; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Procession," in the Paramasaṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter. Brahmā:
Tell me the characteristics of the images together with all their measurements,
as well as the arrangement of the limbs and sub-limbs, along with the characteristics of the pedestal. 23.1 Supreme.
Gold and other materials for the image have been described to you;
having purified them, one should have them fashioned firmly by artisans before [the deity].
Having melted gold—which is wealth in every respect—it should be poured out all at once.
The image of the deity should be made of [these materials]; otherwise, it will not be auspicious for me.
(23.3) Acacia, jackfruit, and also madhūka, as well as sandalwood;
sal tree, deodar, and likewise jasmine wood and *āsana* wood. (23.4)
The *timisha* and *candana* are esteemed species of trees;
their cuts should be straight, smooth, and even in form, neither jagged nor uneven, and dense.
Whether fully ripened, fresh, or dry, such tree-cuts bring about auspicious results.

In a highly auspicious and pure place, having dug the earth, one should take up a cool stone that is free from evil characteristics. One should know that a stone which is hollow is "pregnant" (defective); it breaks with a weak sound. || 23.6–23.7 ||
Indeed, it is proclaimed that there are three types of circles (*maṇḍala*) of various colors:
those marked with the signs of a crow, a vulture, a monkey, a dog, a snake, a scorpion, or a mouse; if these are observed on the sole of the foot, that is not auspicious.
If, when examined by another, they appear to be marred in some part, that stone should be known as having eight internal cavities; it causes the destruction of the lineage. [The auspicious marks are:
the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the parasol, the archway, and the elephant.
If a lion, a boar, a deer, the śrīvatsa, a goad,
and a water-pot are seen upon a stone, then it will be auspicious for us;
likewise, other [marks] that are indeed auspicious or inauspicious [shall be noted].

If, when the stone has been washed, nothing at all is perceived, that stone should be known as mediocre; it is smooth and dense throughout. If, by its appearance, sesame seeds, rice grains, or sand are visible, [it is inferior].
Nor should that [image] be understood as being merely of the middle size in its linear dimensions;
for, due to the negligence of craftsmen and the influence of wind and heat, stones, wood, and even sand may suffer from blows. (23.14)

If anything at all is perceived in smell, color, touch, or sound, it cannot be seen anywhere; that [nature] is auspicious in all colors. Even clay would be exactly like this, according to the action as it has been described.
But that which has been extracted from an irreproachable source is indeed beautiful.
Thus, the form of the deity which has been fashioned by means of these auspicious materials—
whether it be called a *bimba* in the *tantra*, a *bera*, or an *pratimā*— [is so designated].
In palaces and dwellings as well, its measurement varies.
O Grandfather, in the scripture it is declared that for everything—whether mobile or fixed in a painting—the measurement is of three kinds. || 23.18–23.19 ||
That by which the image is measured vertically, horizontally, and all around is declared the first, *unmāna*; immediately after that is *vimāna*;
and the third, O Lotus-born One, is *parimāṇa* in this scripture.
Whatever is correctly determined by these three means of knowledge should be known as "wonderful" (citra) and is to be honored by the wise;
that which is produced with less than the full measure is considered "non-wonderful" (acitra) and is not to be praised.
They say that what is called a "variegated appearance" is devoid of actual dimensions;
it is made beautiful for the sake of the vision of devotees. That which is created with pigments on cloth, walls, and so forth, they call the "enhancer of devotion. (23.23)
It should be pleasing to the hearts of children, the elderly, and women.
One should have a non-painted image made of wood or even stone and install it;
for the sake of prosperity, one should install a painted image in a temple or a residence.
Or one should constantly worship the mobile [deities], having invoked them and then dismissed them;
for those rays of the sun which shine after reaching the path of the window,
the atoms (paramāṇu) that spread there as subtle particles of dust— [these are the mobile deities].
Eight atoms (paramāṇu) make one hair-tip (keśa); eight hair-tips make one mark (likhyā).
Eight marks make one nit (yūkā), and likewise, eight nits make one barley-corn (yava).
They say that an inch (aṅgula) is precisely measured by eight barley-corns.
They say that a *tāla* is equal to twelve *aṅgulas*, even as much as a *vitasti*;
two *tālas* they desire to be a *hasta*, and five *hastas* a *puruṣa*.
An image (*bimba*) is desired to be no larger than the measure of five *hastas*.
Indeed, in my palace, nothing less than one cubit in height shall be installed.
But that which is to be installed in the residence shall not exceed one cubit;
and likewise on the Vindhya... 23.31.
At the time of laying down the body, during the salutation, and at the libation, one should observe silence with great effort; otherwise, one does not obtain the fruit.
(23.32) The wooden ladle (*sruva*) may be made of gold, silver, copper, or *khādira* wood.
The first [staff] made of silver is for the sake of attaining sovereignty and increases fame;
that of copper is said to bring peace, while that of khadira wood increases wealth.
Its length should be twelve finger-breadths, and its girth at the base should be three times that.
The circumference is double the diameter; half of the diameter is the neck (*gala*).
Both pits are one *yava* in measure; each pit is circular and distinct.
The boundary of the womb (*garbha*) should be either one-quarter less than the diameter, or half of it.

The wise one should have the handle made like a cow’s tail and the cavity like a nostril; the *sruk* and *sruva* should be equal in length. The circumference should be three times the diameter, and the neck twice the diameter.

One should again divide [the face] into five parts, and the mouth should consist of two parts. The remaining portion shall be the measure of the staff; from the mouth, a petal-like shape for the circular cavity should be made.
One should fashion the tip to resemble both lips and provide a channel for the clarified butter.
The root [of the blade] should be one barley-corn in measure, and the tip is desired to be half a barley-corn.
In all matters such as eating, the one who has transcended the senses should offer the tip;
having consecrated it by sprinkling and touching it, he should also mutter the eight-syllable mantra.
Having spoken the *paramahaṃsa* mantra, one should place [the food] upon the pure ground;
one should offer the remainder according to the ritual rule, by which all impurity is destroyed.
Having performed the *upasthāna* rite, one should touch the food with the *rasa* mantra and likewise with water.
The wise one should eat while offering the five oblations to the vital breaths (prāṇāhuti) with the Vāyu-mantras.
Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna—these five mantras are to be known by their respective names along with the Vāyu-mantra. (23.42–23.43)
Having eaten, one should drink water and thereby perform the purification of the hands;
having worshipped the Supreme God with a mind always undistracted, when the time for praise arrives, one should recite this hymn. (23.44-45)
Victory is yours, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
Salutations be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, Great Being, Primordial One!
You are the common supreme deity of both gods and demons.
At all times, I go for refuge to your pair of feet.
You alone are the creator and likewise the destroyer of the world;
you are the supervisor and the permitter, enveloped by the *māyā* of the *guṇas*.
Having taken refuge in you alone, the wise cross over the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, that vessel of endless afflictions. [The high-minded. 23.49
[The portion from here until the end of the manuscript fragment is found in the twenty-ninth chapter, in the section on the remainder of the ritual (*karmaśeṣaprakaraṇa*);
its presence here in the chapter on the characteristics of the image (*bimbalakṣaṇādhyāya*) appears inappropriate, and therefore it should be consulted in that very place.]
You have no form, nor appearance, nor weapons, nor abode;
nevertheless, you manifest in human form to your devotees.
Nothing is hidden from you, yet you are not perceived by anyone.
Nothing whatsoever is unestablished for you, nor are you established for anyone.
You are the primordial cause of all effects, the supreme object to be expressed by words;
you are the ultimate perfection of yogis—those who know the Supreme do not perceive anything beyond you.
"I am afraid, O Lord of Gods, in this terrifying cycle of existence;
protect me, O Lotus-eyed One, for I know no other refuge.
Even at all times and in all directions, O Acyuta..."
Great fear increases within me regarding both my body and my destiny. Apart from your lotus feet, there is no other cause for my welfare even in future births, by which I might go to a happy state.
O Lord, may this consciousness which has been attained and this state which has been secured not suffer destruction for me even in another birth.
Even if I am born in an evil destiny, may my heart’s desire remain fixed upon you.
If I do not meet with destruction, by that alone I shall always be content. My mind, defiled by desire, does not dwell at your feet;
rather, I desire only the state of being a Vaiṣṇava in all my births.
Having praised the God thus day after day with this hymn of praise,
he should announce himself to the God, saying, "I am your servant.
With all the materials for worship, he should worship his own body.
One should sit oneself upon a seat near the altar of worship (pūjāpīṭha). Just as one would diligently propitiate the most excellent among men or a supreme guru,
so too should one worship the Lord.
O Lotus-born One, for the fire-rite of the oblation there are three substances:
fuel-sticks, sacrificial food, and clarified butter; with these one should perform the daily oblation.
Flowers for the world-protectors [should be offered] in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The materials for worship should be prepared, and one should always perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
In rites performed for specific desires (kāmya) as well as occasional rites (naimittika), the cooked sacrifice (pakvahoma) is prescribed.
Beyond this point, the manuscript is missing.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Image," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter: "If [the image] is afflicted by sleep or if it assumes pride..."
"Just as my desired goal is accomplished by this very vehicle,
even so, though performed according to my own will, it is able to destroy evil.
As he reflected thus, his mind did not dwell upon unrighteousness.
By their very nature, the senses pursue only pleasure;
therefore, the wise person should not worship that which is not the ultimate reality.
Why should one recollect anything as being beyond the reach of the Imperishable? 24.3–4.1.
A wise person should please him with a form that is truly beneficial;
and while reflecting upon this, he should speak in such a way that his mind remains delighted—thus, a learned man should not abandon the prescribed outward appearance. (24.4–24.5)
One should worship the Supreme God for the sake of liberation or for the sake of a fruit;
one should constantly worship that very nature of His which has been described by me to you in this Tantra, and not that which is imagined by the intellect.
During the consecration of one’s own body, one should employ the peaceful *ājñā-mantras*.
For the sake of secrecy, for self-protection, and for the purification of substances through sanctification,
one should not employ sacrificial fuel (*samid*) or clarified butter (*ājya*) in the fire-offerings (*homa*), because they are the refuge of the deities.
One should meditate upon Him day and night in the very form described;
desiring His grace, one should serve Him constantly and steadfastly.
Through practice these [qualities] arise, and one should never fail to contemplate Him.
One should always cultivate familiarity with the form of Hari through meditation alone.
From that, his devotion increases; from that, affection for him arises, and he becomes truly inseparable from the feet of the God of gods.
The worshipper falls from his station at all times otherwise;
however, by means of the mantras revolving [in the mind] which are centered upon the feet of Viṣṇu,
his own true nature is perceived in the intellect, and his devotion becomes such [as it ought to be].
All mantras have devotion as their purpose, and constant worship is for the sake of devotion;
meditation and formal resolve—all these are held to be for the sake of devotion.
If one’s heart is intense, it suddenly takes refuge in Hari.
Whether it be unpleasant or even pleasant,
that man who contemplates things given by the God as dear to him,
and does not consider them as obtained solely through his own power— he is a devotee of the Supreme Lord.
"This unpleasant thing has come about because of sins committed by me in the past"—
he who perceives things in this way regarding what is disagreeable is considered a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Thus, even wise men [should worship] Janārdana for the sake of increasing their devotion.
Those desiring success should worship Him who possesses form, and not otherwise; for they would not attain it.
These entities beginning with the Unmanifest and ending with the body have been described by me.
Even though this God stands transcending them, He is to be meditated upon as possessing a body.
One should know that his form, consisting of all things, is composed of yoga-māyā;
it is manifested out of compassion for devotees, but is not established as ultimate reality.
It is endowed with weapons and ornaments, clothed in fine garments, and possesses resplendent arms.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Person as if he were the very embodiment of truth,
especially for the embodied soul engaged in the midst of ritual action;
this alone is the form of Hari to be meditated upon daily, and no other.
Or rather, when the mind has turned away from actions and finds delight in self-restraint,
then one should worship the subtle body as Puruṣottama;
the powers (śaktis) or shouts of "well done" (sādhukāra) are to be known as his arms and the directions.
The sky is the head of this embodied being, space is his belly, and the earth is his feet;
the sun is his sight and the moon is his mind; and his breath is the wind.
He is eternal, all-pervading, and immovable—he is to be worshipped by the wise. (24.24–24.25)
That supreme form which has been created is indescribable and without defining marks;
even a wise man should not desire to offer worship to it. Having meditated upon the Supreme Deity through the highest and most sublime [mantras] beginning with the *praṇava*, [one attains the goal].
Meditating on that which is beyond the senses, he should turn back [from external objects]; he is a wise man.
Whenever he attains clarity within the range of the intellect, then, being self-restrained, he should meditate upon the subtle body of the God.
One who has mastered the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the sciences, and is deeply learned,
surely comes to grief in his undertakings through mere doubt, O Lotus-born One. Therefore, a self-possessed man should make the meaning of the scriptures firm by means of all branches of knowledge.
And through pure discernment, there is no subversion of the scripture itself.
For this wise man, whose scripture has been completely purified and who remains in control of the machine of the body, where could he despair, having found no other refuge? (24.30–31)
This gross body has arisen from the subtle; for it is the instrument of this [soul].
Even a god is similar to him and ought to be an object to be accomplished by him.
Therefore, how could he [attain] the subtle reality of Hari through the sequence of the gross alone?
For indeed, even his physical form becomes beautiful through auspicious births.
O Grandfather, I shall describe in brief the procedure for that wise man who, desiring prosperity, should worship the Supreme Lord.
Having meditated upon a palace made of gold, surrounded by a golden rampart,
and upon a ground consisting of jewels presided over by deities;
and in its center, Vaikuṇṭha, seated comfortably upon a red lotus.
One should meditate upon him as four-armed, exceedingly gracious, and seated comfortably;
with four gatekeepers stationed at the entrance, the gateway is radiant with arches,
and he favors those nearby, bestowing the fulfillment of desires upon his worshippers.
By worshipping the attendants as previously described by me,
one attains stable prosperity in a very short time.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Worship of the Learned," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter:
O Brahmā, those men who are unable to worship you through the yoga of knowledge—
And for those who are always endowed with devotion, what is their supreme benefit?
O Lotus-seated One, what is ordained as their supreme attainment of Dharma?
By the path of the Vaiṣṇavas, which is the cause of purity for sacred fords,
one should visit the purifying holy sites everywhere— those sought by the wise who are never separated from [the Lord] and who desire the supreme dharma.
In whatever place the senses of this embodied being find serenity,
that should be known as a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) which destroys the sins of men;
by visiting them, there will be an increase in their merit.
Thus, out of a desire to favor the world, I shall describe to you those sacred fords (*tīrtha*) that can be accomplished in one day or two days;
however, from the third day onwards, they become purifying. (25.5–25.6)
A sacred ford (*tīrtha*) does not become fruitful if it is more than ten *yojanas* away;
rather, the increase of fruit is ordained precisely through [the excellence of] the time and the place.
Even if the place and time are distant, if there is a desire for another purpose, [the result follows]. (25.7)

A sacred ford may become a place of play, yet one should not hold it in high esteem out of delusion. If a foolish man goes to sacred fords either through incidental association or secondary connection, or while being supported by another, he shall obtain no fruit whatsoever. (25.8–25.9)

Even if one frequents a sacred ford, if one does not hold it in high regard due to delusion or increased atheism, no fruit shall accrue to that person either. Therefore, having established firm intelligence and abandoned desire for other activities, [one should practice].
A man should go to a sacred ford independently and with a steady mind.
Being capable, he should eat his own food; being incapable, he should practice begging for alms. He should never eat at occasional (naimittika) feasts.
His conduct is prescribed so as not to cause injury to the body;
for they know that for mortals, visiting sacred fords is indeed a hardship.
Rivers flowing to the ocean, sacred bathing places, and the confluence of the Sindhu and the Gaṅgā—these are the sites.
They saw ponds frequented by gentle creatures, mountain dwellings, abodes of deities, difficult passes, dense forests,
hermitages of the perfected ones, and the signs of the celestial inhabitants.
The sacred fords of the Bhāgīrathī and of the Sarasvatī everywhere,
as well as those extending to the ocean, are especially purifying for human beings;
likewise, the sacred fords in Kurukṣetra and the lake of Sālagrāma.
And at Śrīparvata there are sacred fords, as well as Kumārītīrtha;
the Setubandha of Rāma, Gokarṇa,
and likewise the sacred ford of Śūrpāraka, as well as Puṣkara and Naimiṣa.
The primary station of Viṣṇu is considered the supreme among sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having reached such sacred fords as these, a man of great intelligence should first observe a fast for three nights or one night.
In the event of inability, he should subsist on alms, or on bulbs, roots, and fruits.
He should always perform the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*), remaining silent and devoted to meditation.
Having bathed, sipped water, and become pure with the water of a sacred ford, the knower of mantras [should proceed].

Having meditated upon the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha) in the water and invoked the deity with the mind, one should offer water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya) using that very water. Then, one should meditate on a stream of water issuing from the deity's feet and falling upon one's own head.
A man devoted to the Lord should plunge into the sacred ford in silence.
Having sprinkled himself with the five Upaniṣads a hundred or a thousand times,
and having performed the entire ritual of bathing, he should satisfy the deities with libations.
Having given away wealth according to his ability, he should take up a sacred-site seal-ring (tīrthamudrikā).
By constantly smearing his body with the clay from that site, he becomes pure.
And having collected the water of the sacred site, he should sprinkle his own body with it.
For one night or three nights, a devotee of Viṣṇu, desiring purification,
should diligently listen to the Itihāsas at sacred fords—
those traditional accounts that exist there as causes for devotion.
One should also observe the characteristics of the perfected ones of old,
as well as the wondrous deeds of the deities and the sages.
There, one should contemplate the deities of the sacred sites both internally and externally within oneself.

The wise Vaiṣṇavas abide by their own vision of duty and not otherwise. By whatever ritual procedure one has approached that sacred ford (tīrtha), it should be served accordingly; they declare this to be the rule for visiting sacred fords, and one should not concern oneself with a ritual that causes distress.
A man should make his path (tīrtha) level with those who are superior or equal to him;
he may go with one, two, or at most three companions, but not more than that, nor with those who are inferior.
He should travel only with those who have renounced the world and are free from desire and anger.
A wise man should undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords and perform their worship.
Those men who have renounced all possessions, who are shaven-headed and clad in saffron robes,
and who wander over the entire earth— they are my most beloved beings.
Therefore, a devotee of the Lord should always offer service to them alone;
for worship rendered to them is indeed worship rendered to the God himself.
Having given them alms, conduct, shelter, and so forth with devotion, [one attains the same merit].
The learned man who has received instruction shall become most dear to Viṣṇu.
He should not do anything unpleasant to men dwelling at sacred fords,
nor to any deities, nor to any living beings whatsoever.
At whatever time a particular sacred ford (tīrtha) ought to be visited by the wise, one should go there at that time; if unable to do so, one should go on a festival day (parvan).
Likewise, on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), under the asterism Śravaṇā, or during the sun's transits (saṃkrānti).
One should resort to the primary sacred site; there is no fixed time for others. Alternatively, for those devotees of Viṣṇu who wander this earth as yogis on pilgrimages, no time is restricted.
Having reached whatever sacred site (tīrtha) his mind finds serene,
there a wise man, firm in his vows, should remain for a long time,
O Lord, wherever he goes and his mind attains clarity.
Even if he were to dwell for a long time at a preeminent sacred ford (*tīrtha*), a Vaiṣṇava who practices there—
even in the midst of dire calamities—
should never accept even the slightest amount of wealth from anyone, however insignificant, at that sacred site.
A wise man should not beg for alms at sacred sites; rather,
having gone outside, he should beg only as much as is required to sustain the body,
avoiding the throngs of great crowds and the assemblies of the wicked.
In cases of severe threats to life, one may somehow maintain one's livelihood.
A wise man should always proceed while reciting Vaiṣṇava mantras;
and how could he ever perform a Vaiṣṇava rite out of a desire to please his friends? (25.44–25.45)
Even having attained prosperous and excellent positions in the assemblies,
one who desires success should not remain for long once his purpose has been fulfilled.
Even while enjoying himself at sacred fords, the wise man should avoid excessive play.
Slapping one's arms, shouting, laughing, gambling, and sexual intercourse—
if anyone who has set out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords should perform such acts as these,
the Brahmarākṣasas take away all the fruit of that pilgrimage.

There are indeed two great gains for men who go on pilgrimages to sacred sites: the gain of faith through devotion, and the abundant knowledge of yoga. For he who performs a circumambulation of the earth by means of a pilgrimage to these sacred sites—
He attains supreme perfection and is not afflicted by sin;
he obtains great knowledge as well as the recollection of past births,
the destruction of obstacles, and grace from the Lord of the Gods.

Therefore, with every effort and desiring spiritual perfection, a Vaiṣṇava should undertake a pilgrimage; that alone is the supreme benefit. Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, named "Pilgrimage," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter:
What is the root of this worldly existence, what is its summit, and what is its middle?
O Supreme Person, tell me that in detail and according to the truth;
O Lotus-born One, you alone are the ultimate and supreme root of saṃsāra.
Having established [the world] up to the realm of Brahmā, that which is first among them is great;
these worlds are considered its middle, and hell its tip.
This tree has its roots above, its branches in the middle, and its head below.
In this machine of the process of saṃsāra, wherein embodied beings transmigrate,
its worlds are recorded as branches consisting of seven distinct levels:
the earth, the intermediate space, and the heavens— Svaḥ, Mahaḥ, and Janaḥ.
Austerity and truth—these seven worlds have been described to you in order.
Furthermore, below these, the regions of hell are proclaimed.
Among them, O Grandfather, I shall first describe this earth to you.
Endowed with length and breadth, and possessed of various characteristics,
the seven continents of the earth are recorded as being situated in the shape of a circle;
each is twice the size of the preceding one in extent and contains diverse abodes for living beings.
Encircled by oceans of equal length and breadth,
they are characterized by the distinctions and non-distinctions of both regions and mountains.
Jambūdvīpa stands in the center, and beyond that is Śākadvīpa.
Then there are the two islands of Kuśa and Krauñca, as well as Śālmali-dvīpa;
Gomeda and Puṣkara—these are the seven islands in order.
First is the ocean of salt water, and on the other side is the ocean whose waters are like sugarcane juice.
Surā, Dadhi, Ghṛta, Iḍā, and Kṣīrasāgara, as well as Svādūdaka— these seven oceans stand like islands. In these islands, situated in the center, are various peaks of great height.
The mountain ranges extending as far as the ocean are to be known as the boundary-mountains (varṣaparvatas).
Between them lie the regions (varṣas), as well as various inhabited districts,
cities, villages, and rivers by the hundreds and thousands.
In the center of Jambūdvīpa stands the great mountain named Meru,
with peaks composed of various jewels and a body of gold;
it is the playground of the gods, endowed with many wonders.
A river named Jambū stands encircling its base;
on its southern side, the Jambū tree is situated—
exceedingly tall, very wide, and bestowing all desired fruits.
Know that the region Ilāvṛta extends all around Meru.
There, the inhabitants of that region should be known as those who subsist on the fruit of the jambū tree.
To the north of Meru, where those mountain ranges of the region are located, they should be known [to reside].
Nīla, Śveta, and Triśṛṅga are each slightly smaller than one another;
O Lotus-born One, the first region is Ramyaka, followed by Hairaṇya, and then the Northern Kurus— these are the three regions.
Likewise, to the south of Meru, there stand three mountain ranges:
Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat;
these three [correspond to] Harivarṣa, Kimpuruṣavarṣa, and Bhāratavarṣa respectively.
For slightly less than three years in succession,
to the east of Mount Meru stands the mountain Gandhamādana;
and to the west, between Nīla and Niṣadha, stands Mālyavat.
Beyond those two are the two regions of Bhadrāśva and Ketumāla.
This middle island has an extent of ten million yojanas;
within its regions dwell human beings of various forms.
O Lotus-born One, their lifespans, strength, and other qualities differ;
in the mountain ranges, yakṣas, pannagas, and rākṣasas dwell.
The southern region of Bhārata remains divided into nine parts.
O Brahmin, by means of the water of the salt-water ocean flowing inward,
and through the very divisions of those [regions], neither the mountains nor the rivers can be fully enumerated even in hundreds of years.

Situated in the midst of the salt ocean are many birds, mountains, and numerous small islands; these are known as the domains of the Mlecchas. Furthermore, in the six islands beginning with Śākadvīpa, there are mountains.
There are hundreds and thousands of years and rivers as well;
in them dwell men of virtuous character and stable lifespans,
along with beasts, birds, carnivorous animals, and reptiles.
The protectors of the earth were righteous and endowed with compassion and virtue;
they never harmed one another through desire, anger, or other such passions.
The subjects were devoted to charity, study, and moral conduct, and were not intent upon the wealth of others.
They do not engage in harming others, nor do they dwell upon the misfortunes of others.
(26.32) There, trees and medicinal herbs bear abundant fruit, and all desires are fulfilled; likewise, the cows there yield plenty of milk, and the people are free from calamity. (26.33)
In the center of Puṣkaradvīpa stands the mountain Mānasottara;
there, the world-protectors, headed by Indra, are stationed at the cardinal points.
In the oceans, however, live beings whose origin is the water.
Crocodiles, sea-monsters, sharks, tortoises, serpents, and elephants—
those that move in the water are far more numerous than the creatures that move on land;
feeding upon the waters of the ocean, they live free from restraint.
Beyond Svādūdaka lies the Brahma-world, and the Lokāloka mountain stands encircling the entire earth on all sides. On the side facing this world, however, the rays of the sun move.
"May that Lokāloka mountain, which is eternally formed from half of a parārdha, be so.
Thus has this earth been described, renowned for its beautiful elements,
wherein embodied beings perform auspicious and inauspicious deeds.
From the worlds and from the intermediate space, the realm of Vāyu is fashioned;
there the Maruts stand in sevenfold groups, one above the other.
Therein are the sacrificial houses, the stars, the lunar mansions, and the great seers.
They dwell in their radiant bodies, free from all affliction.
Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras likewise live there at ease, moving according to their will, unimpeded and blissful.
There, the great sage named Dhruva, stationed above, causes that wind-wheel— sevenfold in its layers and rising evenly— to revolve.
The third world of light is known as the heavenly world (svargaloka).
There, thousands of gods dwell rejoicing by the thousands,
accompanied by celestial nymphs and moving at will in their aerial chariots;
there, O Brahmin, the hosts of deities reside by the thousands.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, and Rbhus,
as well as the Kiṃkaras, the Karmadevas, and the various classes of Pitṛs,
staying in the center of the circle of the wheel, drank the supreme nectar.
There they live, protected by Vāsava,
blazing on all sides with bodies composed of splendor;
these gods, whose lifespan lasts for the duration of a kalpa, live in perpetual youth.
For them, cows are always milk-yielding wish-fulfillers and the Kalpa-trees;
their jewels, which grant the fruits of thought, fulfill all desires.
Thus, these three worlds are obtained through auspicious deeds.
"Those which I have described to you perish through the exhaustion of karma.
But there are four other worlds, O Grandfather, which are to be attained through knowledge,
where yogins dwell who have emerged by means of the practice of yoga."
In the fourth [Manvantara] called Mahā, however, men have a lifespan of ten kalpas;
devoted to Viṣṇu and having conquered their senses, they abide with their desires fulfilled by mere resolve.
In the fifth world-age, however, men have a lifespan of a hundred kalpas.

Subsisting on meditation, they rejoice, their senses brought under control. In the sixth stage of austerity in this world, those seeking mastery over the great elements dwell as perfected beings (siddhas), endowed with self-restraint and possessing a lifespan of a thousand kalpas.

In the seventh world, Satyaloka, there dwell the principal masters who have attained self-control; these perfected beings (siddhas), possessing a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas, live there free from all worldly desire.
It is in this very place that Brahmā, the expert in the creation of the worlds, resides.
Therefore, this is the world of Brahmā where you preside;
these worlds are the destinations born from the ripening of auspicious karma.
But as for the destination of evil, it is the low worlds—this is the certainty of the people.
Beneath the world of earth lie the grounds of the great hells;
there dwell six kinds of wicked Piśācas of various forms.
Of these, Raurava is the first, and Mahāraurava as well.
Naraka, Kālasūtra, Pañcakaṣṭa, Anantara, Tāmisra, and Andhatāmisra— these, O Grandfather, are indeed places of intense suffering that one encounters. || 26.59–26.60 ||
All embodied beings experience the terrible fruit of their evil deeds;
beneath these [hells] lies the one renowned as Avīci,
the dwelling place of the lords of the Dānavas who have been destroyed and cast down.

Thus, O Grandfather, has this creation been described by way of summary. After creating [the world] outside the cosmic egg, the Creator remains there. That which exists outside the egg is what is known as the external intellect (buddhi).
Beyond the intellect (buddhi) is the unmanifest (avyakta); beyond the unmanifest is the Puruṣa.
He is Viṣṇu, the eternal Vāsudeva, composed of the five powers.
O Grandfather, there is nothing whatsoever higher than Him, for that is the very essence of being.
He, however, is without beginning, without end, and devoid of measurable dimensions. By his will, this creation attains expansion; and by his will, it undergoes dissolution at the end of the eon.
Thus has this creation of the world been described to you in its entirety;
in this manner, and moreover in other ways, further creations are produced by him.
These are invisible to one another, yet they are directly perceived by that yogin.
Incalculable worlds remain, all arising and passing away;
various forms and transformations have been created by him for the sake of sport,
just as there are very many fruits upon the branches of a tree.
Understand that worlds arise within him in that same manner;
the supreme Lord, though changeless, creates the transformations.
Having observed the course of saṃsāra, he remains as if playing.
Thus has this creation of saṃsāra been described by me to you.
Within it, embodied beings revolve again and again;
having at times become superior, they are born once more as middling.

And later they become the lowest, bound by the nooses of their own past actions. O Brahmin, all the destinies within the sphere of saṃsāra for a person perish through the exhaustion of karma; yet they do not vanish completely, nor are they free from suffering.
There, those who consider the successes created by the gods to be self-created enjoy them until their very roots are destroyed; yet,
they encounter nothing but hardships and perils when they see them lying ahead.
Helpless, he regards the Lord as the creator and sovereign of the universe;
yet for one who is not a Vaiṣṇava and who hates worldly existence, liberation does not come.
For a mortal who is not a Vaiṣṇava, there is no lasting happiness even within the cycle of rebirth.

Having fallen under the sway of the senses, one does not transcend saṃsāra. By overcoming even those [senses], one transcends saṃsāra; and by overcoming even those, one reaches Janārdana, the God of gods, who arises from their conquest.

One should worship at all times; by that, success will be attained—for animals, humans, gods, and likewise for yogis. Devotees of Viṣṇu are distinguished above all others; this is certain throughout all the worlds.
As the gods are to men, and as Hari is to the gods;
as the Siddhas are to the Yogins, and as Hari is to the Siddhas—[so is he to this world]. This long-lasting, vast, and exceedingly difficult-to-cross stability of the world... || 26.80–26.81 ||
The Supreme God sits beholding, blissful in the highest heaven;
just as men easily see the dice held in their own hands,
even so does the Supreme God behold the seven worlds.
The lifespan of Brahmā shall last as long as the duration of the world.
When his life is completed, the entire world dissolves;
indeed, all created things always return to their respective causes.
They dissolve into that Unmanifest; it, in turn, dissolves into the Supreme Self.
Six thousand yugas less six constitute a single day of Brahmā;
his night is of equal duration, and this is known as his *saṃkalpa*.
A year for humans is not more than that for the gods.
By that measure, twelve thousand years constitute a [divine] year;
by this reckoning, the ages (yugas), the kalpas, and the manvantaras proceed.
But when, by that measure of time, the period of a hundred years of creation has come to pass,
then the Supreme Person, having withdrawn the creation, remains in himself.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, named "The World," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter: Brahmā [says], "Regarding those various actions described by you in various places as being mixed..."
"O Lord of Gods, you ought to tell me the compendium in its entirety.
"Very well, I shall indeed tell you the compendium of actions for you."

Having first spoken the name of Nārāyaṇa, one who has risen from bed should, remaining silent and facing the east, perform protection for oneself in every respect— whether for obligatory, occasional, or optional rites. (27.2–27.3)
Having contemplated everything by means of the mind through the path of emanation,
and having meditated upon the body's interior as a sealed yogic vessel in due order,
one should afterwards support oneself on the ground and emerge externally as before.
Having performed the acts of voiding and so forth according to the sequence of the path of purification,
and having cleansed the hands, feet, and face with water and earth, one should likewise properly clean the nose, eyes, and ears.
Having chewed the tooth-stick and having spat out [the remnants],
he should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules; thereafter, having drunk [water] and wiped his mouth once,
he should again perform the sipping of water in the same manner and sprinkle himself according to the prescribed rite.
Then, having sprinkled water over himself, he should release a handful of water [as an offering].
Having performed the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) once more, having washed his hands with water,
and having performed the recitation of the five mantras, he should also circumambulate the deity.
After conversing with the Brahmins, he should subsequently dismiss the initiation into silence;
even if he is poor, he must never neglect his own daily auspicious rites.
[He should perform] the two mantras for scents and flowers, the binding of the topknot, and the rite for prosperity.
A mirror, collyrium, protection, and mouth-perfume,
as well as weapons, ornaments, and so forth, according to what has been prescribed for each; having first performed these, one should carry out the worldly duties.
One should sit by means of the earth-mantra and move by means of the wind-mantra;
one should speak by means of the space-mantra and perceive form by means of the fire-mantra.
And at all times, one should touch water by means of the water-mantra.
Even in worldly affairs, a wise man desiring success—
when the time for sacrifice has arrived and the collection of materials has been made—
should cast off his garland, bathe, and offer libations to the deities.
Having reached the place of sacrifice and become himself composed of mantra,
he should meditate upon the site as consisting of jewels, as well as various vessels,
a golden palace, and waters born of sacred fords (tīrtha).
Designating the place for the floral remains (nirmālya) outside the outer enclosure, one should fill a vessel with water and fill another;

with one [vessel] one should provide water for the feet (pādya), drinking water (pānīya), and water for sipping (ācamana), and with the other, one should perform the ritual bath (snāna). || 27.17–27.18 ||
One should fill the *arghya* and *pādya* vessels, as well as other vessels, with the appropriate ritual substances;
furthermore, one should fill another large vessel for all purposes with water.
One should place the perfumes and other offerings into the vessels, either by means of a pillar-like support (*staṃbhana*) or, if that is not possible, [in another way].
Having placed the implements for the fire-oblation to the south of the fire,
and having properly prepared the seat as well as the two pieces of wood for friction,
one should take fragrant flowers in the hand and invoke the Supreme One.

One should place the seat (pīṭha) with flowers, designating it as the throne; then, from the beginning of the sacrifice until its conclusion, one should pray for the presence of the object of worship. Thereafter, one should perform the worship as appropriate, including the self-offering (ātmanivedana).
Having returned the Lord of Devas to his own abode according to the sequence of dissolution,
having purified the place and likewise offered the vessels and the *bali* outside, and having worshipped Viṣvaksena with the floral remains (*nirmālya*) and presented them to him— 27.23–24.
Having sipped water (ācamana), he should eat together with Vaiṣṇavas and others according to his capacity;
having become fire, he should consume the food which exists in the form of Soma.
Having sipped water, when his hands and feet are dry, he should contemplate [the deity] with his mind.
One may touch the sense organs and the elements while preceded by mantras;
one may touch other beings or even impure substances.
One should spend the remainder of that day with stories concerning the God alone.

Having performed actions that are not contrary to dharma and ritual duty, or else, when the time of twilight has arrived, the wise man should perform the twilight worship (sandhyopāsana). Furthermore, having eaten and sipped water (ācamana), the learned man should recite hymns at night as well.
Having established [the deity] in the space of the heart and worshipped it once more,
one should then resort to the process of dissolution and lie down comfortably upon the bed.
This indeed is the rule and the doctrine for householders who are devotees of the Lord.
This same collection and possibility is remembered as being equal for others as well;
however, for a Śūdra there is neither the fire-ritual nor likewise the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana).
Only the collection of the flower-sacrifice has been described to you.
O Lotus-born One, I shall also describe for you the procedure for others:
one who desires initiation should approach another virtuous and compassionate master who is knowledgeable in the tantras, honor him, and inform him of the desired undertaking.
The teacher, having ascertained both their moral conduct and behavior,
should first cause them to hear the commitments after having drawn a maṇḍala;
then, in a secluded and pure place, he should invoke the Supreme Lord there.
Having performed the sacrifice mentally, he should then withdraw the disciple. Then,
having made him consist of mantra again by way of emanation, the knower of mantra,
having shown him the mandala, should cause him to hear [the teachings] before him with devotion.

Furthermore, the Guru should cause [the disciple] to hear of the teacher, the commitment, and the various dharmas, as well as the mantra that has been transmitted through the lineage from former times. Having caused him to hear these, he should then perform the initiation of the knots with colored powders.
Then he should give the instruction as well as the sequence of worship (arcana).
He should cause the flower-sacrifice (puṣpayāga), the recitation (japa), and likewise the observances (niyama) to be performed.
Therein he should apply the initiation (dīkṣā) accompanied by mantra and fire-oblation (homa).
Furthermore, one should perform the rites with mantras and also with the fire-oblation (homa).
In the initiation (dīkṣā) and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), protection is prescribed first;
in the second and third [stages], it is performed extensively; and at the time of dismissal (visarga), it is done once each.
Having thus performed initiation, which is divided into three types with progressively higher limits,
the Vaiṣṇava who is well-composed attains perfection.
One who desires to perform the supreme, eternal installation [of the deity] should likewise proceed.
One should have a palace constructed in front, according to the extent of one's wealth,
made of stone, brick, or wood, and endowed with the proper characteristics;
having ascertained that the lunar mansion for the installation is imminent.
Having honored the artisans with wealth and having inspired their goodwill,
one should collect materials in every way for the purpose of installation.
First, however, one should receive the new image from the presence of the artisan.
Having honored him with gifts of wealth and personal gifts of affection,
one should personally choose as preceptor a man of virtuous conduct who has mastered the Tantras,
who is skillful and devoted, and whom one has sustained with wealth and other resources.
And there may be other various new materials;
having collected all of them, one should purify the ground and perform the opening of the eyes of the image according to the prescribed rite.
Afterwards, one should cause [the image] to lie in water and protect it on all sides;
then, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) according to the prescribed rule.
Thereafter, the wise man should install Hari under an auspicious constellation.
Having established this for all supplicants without distinction,
one should daily provide clothing and food in due order to all Vaiṣṇavas and to all learned scholars from every quarter.
One should perform worship, in due order, for the servants and the artisans,
as well as for the installers, the craftsmen, and the officiating priests in every respect.
Otherwise, indeed, a great fault will befall the establisher.
When the fourth day has arrived, having performed the supreme ritual bathing,
one should then undertake a pilgrimage to sacred sites accompanied by a festival for the deity; having completed and consecrated it, one should perform the daily worship.
One should offer the *bali* offering three times a day or once a day, day after day.
Know this, O Grandfather, to be the conclusion of the installation ceremony.
By performing the installation in this manner, one will have fulfilled one's duty.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, named "The Compendium," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter, [spoken by] Brahmā.
But when a time of distress has arrived, tell me all of this— the rule for the obligatory sacrifice, as well as for the occasional and the optional—
[which is] supreme.

Accompanied by the Śaktis, the Muktipālas, and the mantras of the Pīṭhas, this should be known as the Kṛtayāga; that is the supreme Nityayāga. (28.2) Even with the entire Pīṭha alone, without the external enclosures (āvaraṇas).
A sacrifice preceded by mantras is a regular sacrifice (nityayāga); that is the intermediate one.
It consists of the great elements and follows the proper method, being endowed with lotuses alone, as well as with ritual action, oblations, and ornaments.

Worship endowed with the purification of ritual substances (dravya-śuddhi) is the supreme worship. That which is performed without the fire-ritual (agnikārya), yet consists of offerings ripened by time and accompanied by all the ritual services (upacāra), is the middling worship.
Excluding various forms of splendor such as garments and ornaments,
the flower sacrifice alone is known as the lowest form of worship;
it is joined with concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and the like, and is united with the dissolution and emergence [of the breath].
The deposition of the body (*dehanyāsa*) performed with all mantras is to be known as the highest;

that which is performed merely through the dissolution and arising [of the breath] is proclaimed as the middling. The deposition by means of the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is called the lowest.
In all these cases, each preceding one is more important according to the sequence.
Practice performed through the union of power (*śakti*) and devotion (*bhakti*) is considered "unforgotten" (*aparismṛta*).
Furthermore, sacrifice performed at a sacred place and at the proper time is known as occasional (*naimittika*).
Furthermore, that [disciple] should be known as being of three kinds: superior, inferior, and middling.
Having observed the fast, he should diligently practice the vow among them.
The middling one subsists on milk, while the other eats fruits and roots.
That which is provided with food, drink, and so forth is considered the primary occasional [rite].
Merely by means of the completeness of the sacrifice, it is proclaimed as the middling;
that which is devoid of vows and fasting is proclaimed as the lowest.
Performing sacrifices for others due to another's request, or when there is a general obligation, or even in times of distress—
having observed the qualifications of the sacrificer, such officiating becomes intermediate.
From one’s own power [to officiate], it is the lowest form of officiating in sequence.
Fasting, sacrifice, eating, and giving—these alone are recommended on this very day for one who desires liberation. Having observed the fast on the previous day, one should worship... [28.16]
The very consideration of the magnitude of one’s action [determines its result]...
[28.18] ...the engagement with desire proceeds in due order;
that which is its course toward attenuation is the lowest... [28.19]
The isolation (*kaivalya*) of the sacrifice is desired...
by other learned ones there, in due order:
...by means of the letter *ḍha*, by the letter *ha*, and by the beloved letter *sa*.
Even if one is unable to give wealth, one should cause the worship of the deity to be performed.
One should fulfill all of that through service and pleasant words.
However, one who does not know the way of worship should have it performed by a priest.
...by these [mantras] employed, for the sake of the worship materials and the progeny;
for the gods, for the sake of their station, through the purification of wealth;
with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, through the rites of luster.
And by means of festive rites and propitiatory ceremonies (śāntikarma),
a sacrifice to the gods is considered supreme;
it is not common [to all], and it is new.
A Vaiṣṇava who hears [this] there, for him also...
having deceived and having stolen [wealth], [he becomes] Puṣkala.
There, his sin... he is excluded from the dharma of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing his desired goal, even at that time,
the practitioner ought to approach a teacher in order to receive the tantra—
the best by means of services, and the middling by means of offerings of wealth. (28.27–28)
One should satisfy the teacher with desired and pleasing actions.
In times of distress, without the teacher,
one should bestow the supreme tantra and the knowledge.

Devoted, virtuous in character, and free from desire to harm others; seeking knowledge and desiring spiritual accomplishment—such are the disciples who are worthy vessels. Having imparted knowledge to such a worthy vessel solely for the sake of Dharma.
The teacher attains great accomplishment; it is never otherwise.
The disciple who desires supreme accomplishment is considered the highest; he who desires prosperity is remembered as middling;
but he who desires trivial things is the lowest—thus are disciples described.
Even in times of dire distress, whether out of fear or even when fallen into misfortune,
one should never worship the God of gods for the sake of a livelihood.
A mountain peak is the supreme location, while a riverbank is middling.
The lowest [type of] place is situated in the middle of a village; such is the threefold characteristic [of the site].
Having mastered the teacher’s vidyās and mantras, one who is firm in his vows and invincible against obstacles is called a practitioner (sādhaka).
But he who undergoes hardship while practicing is a middling practitioner.
In this very way, the threefold destiny of all should be understood: for those who are capable, it is the highest; for him... [it is the lowest].
...the ripe [fruit] falls from both ends.
One should never act toward the youngest [member] as if he were capable [of independence].
Even my own devotion here becomes diminished by those who are devoted [only to themselves]. 28.38

If one has performed [an act] once during a time of calamity, or out of negligence, or even in a crisis, one should not do it a second time; this is the conclusion of the scripture. Whatever was done at the word of a guru, or whatever was done under the pressure of disease, [is not to be repeated].
That should not be known as a fault, provided one performs auspicious acts again;
this rule has been declared for times of distress merely by way of summary.
Because of the great abundance of calamities, however, a detailed exposition would never reach its end.
Famine, royal oppression, disease, and likewise fear of fire;
the harassment of bandits and robbery—these should be known as supreme calamities.
Even when these calamities prevail, one may overstep the [usual] time [for study]. || 28.42–28.43 ||
"One does not incur fault again after having performed even a small act endowed with merit.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, named "Grace," in the *Paramasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter.
"O Brahmā, if there are any remnants of karma remaining by you that have not been mentioned in this tantra,
then explain them now, for my curiosity is indeed great. (29.1)
O Grandfather, I shall now fully declare the remainder of those very rites, according to their proper application, without omission. (29.2)
Without the yoga-pīṭha, one should perform the lotus-seat (padmāsana) with the mudrā;
having fashioned the Śakti, the lotus-garlands, and [the deities] upon the filaments and petals,
one should again establish the guardians of the directions as external supports.
Having placed [the seed-syllables] in the seed-place, in the seeds, and in the names of the deities,
one should perform the sacrifice with the root-mantra;
having stated the purpose for oneself, the root-mantra is concluded.
One should visualize the principal deity itself within the heart and other locations;
this is the rule for the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) for the sake of accomplishing rites performed for specific desires.
At the beginning of worship, in places of fear, in wildernesses, and by rivers—[this should be done].
In life-threatening dangers and difficult situations, one should perform the six-limbed nyāsa (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
