[One should do so] during worship, eating, praise, bathing, sipping water (ācamana), offering oblations,
voiding urine or excrement, at the junctions of time (sandhyā), and during formal ritual worship.
At the time of laying down the body, during the salutation, and at the libation, one should observe silence with great effort; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
The *sruva* ladle may be made of gold, silver, copper, or *khadira* wood.
The first [type], made of silver, is for the sake of attaining sovereignty and increases fame;
copper is said to bring about peace, and that made of khadira wood increases wealth.
Its length should be twelve finger-breadths, and its width at the base one finger-breadth.
The circumference is double the diameter; half of the diameter multiplied by three [gives the circumference].
Both pits should be one *yava* in measure, and their circumferences around the pits should be distinct.
Or, for the boundary of the inner chamber (*garbha*), it should be one-quarter less than the diameter, or half [of the diameter].
The wise man should have the handle made like a cow’s tail, with a cavity for the nose and a small cavity [for the tip]. The *sruva* ladle should be made equal in length;
its circumference should be twice its width, and its neck should be twice its width.
One should again divide [the space] into five parts; the face shall consist of two parts.
The remaining measure shall be the staff, and the pit shall be as wide as a great petal.
One should mutter the eight-syllable mantra at the tips, which resemble the two lips.
Having spoken thus, one should indeed cause the Paramahaṃsa to be given on the pure ground.
One should give the remainder according to the prescribed rule; by that, sin is destroyed.
Having approached with the savory food, one should likewise touch it with water.
The wise one should consume [the food] with the Vāyu-mantras as five oblations to the vital breaths (prāṇāhuti):
Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna.
These five mantras are to be understood by their own names through the seed-syllable of Vāyu.
Having eaten, one should drink water and thereby perform the purification of the hands.
Having worshipped the Supreme God daily with an undistracted mind,
when the time for praise arrives, one should recite this hymn.
Victory is yours, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
Salutations be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Great Being, O Primordial One!
You are the common presiding deity of both the gods and the demons.
I go for refuge to you, whose pair of feet is ever accessible.
You alone are the creator of the world and likewise its destroyer;
you are the presiding overseer and the permissive witness, veiled by the power of your own *māyā* consisting of the *guṇas*.
Having found refuge in you alone, the wise cross over the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, which is a vessel for infinite afflictions.
Neither your form, nor your appearance, nor your weapons, nor your abode [are perceived].
Nevertheless, you manifest in the form of a person for the sake of your devotees. (29.25) Nothing whatsoever is hidden from you, yet you are not perceptible to anyone;
nothing remains unaccomplished by you, nor are you established as an object for anyone. (29.26)
The cause of all effects is the foremost; the object of speech is the highest;
the supreme perfection of yogas—these they know to be Your supreme state.
O Lord of Gods, I am afraid in this world of great terror.
Protect me, O lotus-eyed one; I know no other refuge.
O Acyuta, at all times and in all directions, as well as within my body and in my movements, a great fear increases within me.

Other than your lotus feet, there is no cause for my spiritual merit even in future births, by which I might attain a happy rebirth. This wisdom that I have attained and this state that I have secured— [is all due to you].
"O Lord, may there never be a loss of this [devotion] for me even in another birth.
Even if I am born into a miserable state, may my heart's desire remain fixed on you;
as long as it does not meet with destruction, I shall always be fulfilled through that."
"My mind, stained by desire, has never rested at your feet;
rather, I desire only the state of being a Vaiṣṇava in all my births. Having thus praised the God day after day with this hymn, [she continued].
One should offer oneself to the deity, saying, "What shall I do?
One should worship one's own body with various special materials for worship;
however, one should sit oneself upon a seat slightly removed from the seat of worship.
Just as one serves a superior king or a supreme guru with diligence, so should one worship the God.
O Lotus-born One, there are three substances for the fire-rite of the oblation.

One should always perform the fire-oblation with fuel-sticks, sacrificial offerings, and clarified butter. Having placed flowers scented with perfumes belonging to the world-protectors in the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should always perform the oblation.
In rites performed for specific desires as well as in occasional rites, the *pakva-homa* (cooked oblation) is prescribed;
however, neither the *idhma-homa* (fuel-wood oblation) nor the *sruva-homa* (ladle oblation) is performed elsewhere.
Having prepared each individual fuel-stick (*samidh*), one should offer them with all the mantras in their proper sequence.
One should offer clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle and the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) with the hand.
Having gathered the ashes from the fire at the end of the *homa*, mixed with water,
one should smear them over oneself for the sake of self-protection and for the destruction of evil.

A wise person should apply an anointing of ashes with the fire-mantra on the crest-lock, the forehead, the neck, the heart, the two arms, as well as the navel and the tips of the feet, never for the sake of mere ornamentation.

It should be shaped like a mace and uniform throughout, never exceeding [the prescribed size]. A man desiring spiritual perfection should not, however, make one who is inferior by birth his teacher; rather, he should choose a Vaiṣṇava who is superior even if he is ill-behaved.
If the preceptor should perform initiation for many people at one time,
there should be only a single ritual procedure common to all.
Furthermore, he should not perform both [the initiation and] the purification of the disciples simultaneously.
During the installation, the twelve guardians of the forms (mūrtipālas) shall offer oblations in due order;
the guardians of the forms should not offer the cooked food, but the Preceptor (ācārya) himself should perform the homa.
He should likewise offer clarified butter for the twelve forms and for their Śaktis as well.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for Vāsudeva and the others in due order;
having leveled the ground with water, one should diligently plant a ritual stake (śaṅku).
It should have an equal diameter everywhere and be twelve finger-breadths in length.
Having drawn a mandala on the ground with a karkaṭa [compass] all around,
having firmly established a gnomon (śaṅku) in the center so that it is perfectly level in every direction,
one should mark the shadow at its limit upon the installation mandala.

In the afternoon, however, one should mark the very point where [the shadow] has emerged; having laid the thread between those two, one should know the eastern and western directions. Then, by means of a compass, one should again produce a fish-figure in the middle of those two.
One should determine the south and north of those two [lines] by means of a thread;
thus one should always establish the measurement of the directions for a temple.
This is considered the subtle measurement for the drawing of a mandala as well.
Otherwise, the wise man should determine the direction by means of a coarse measurement,
using either the space between the stars of Citrā or the middle star.
Then, remaining celibate and composed, he should perform the flower sacrifice.
When available, he should also offer fruits that have ripened in their own time.

A forest-dweller (vānaprastha) should offer even wild-grown ripe foods. He should not go from the forest to the village for the worship of the gods unless he has performed the renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
Constantly performing the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), one should then practice the sacrifice of meditation (dhyānayāga);
one should observe the limbs of yoga and take refuge in sacred fords (tīrtha).
[One should dwell] in principal sacred sites and in the temples of Viṣṇu.
Having drawn a maṇḍala, one should observe the Cāturmāsya vow;
one should also undertake pilgrimages to sacred sites and worship the deity there.
One should listen to the Tantras along with their secret doctrines in the presence of the Guru.
When death is near, a man who has gone forth into the religious life should strive to constantly attend upon his secret sanctuary, even if it causes him great hardship; likewise,
a Vaiṣṇava should perform circumambulation of the temple of the deity.
One should not step between the deity and one who carries the remains of the offering (nirmālya).
Having gone that far, one should turn back; having returned forcefully, one should reach the temple door and again offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali).
Saying "namas," with a slight turning of the head and likewise with palms joined, one should pay homage with devotion alone to him and to all his attendants in every way.
This is the conduct for one who has been initiated; it may be done at will by other yogins as well.

One should perform the placement of the powers of yoga (yogaiśvarya) and so forth on the exterior of the yoga-pīṭha, following the same sequence as the placement of the forms (mūrtivinyāsa) in all sacrifices. One should then arrange Viṣṇu, Vīra, and the many guardians of the directions (dikpālas) outside [the pīṭha], in all their respective directions.
And during the initiation (dīkṣā), one should place them outside in the directions starting with the east;
their individual worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth is prescribed.
For this is known as the Great Sacrifice (mahāyāga), which bestows the fulfillment of all desires.
The detailed ritual placement (nyāsa) should not always be performed in sacrifices;
however, one should employ it especially on specific occasions and when they are possible.
In sacrifices performed for the sake of fulfilling desires, however, the full elaboration of the rite is required.
Even if this procedure is deficient in any of its constituent parts, it will not accomplish the desired goal.
Having invoked the deity, one should worship him with devotion by offering the *arghya* water;
and this should always be done at the conclusion of the ornaments and at the end of the worship.
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, clarified butter, sesame seeds, fruit, perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as dūrvā grass— these effect the destruction of all sins.
By collecting these five or more, the *arghya* offering is prescribed.
Having taken the *arghya* from vessel to vessel, one should present it with both hands;

one should constantly mutter the eight-syllabled mantra as well as the twelve-syllabled one. Even one who is uninitiated, if he is a constant devotee of Viṣṇu and firm in his vows, [attains the fruit].
One should mutter that Paramahaṃsa mantra; one who has not been initiated should never do so.
Even fools may mutter the other two mantras with the *praṇava* (Oṃ).
One should worship [the deity] for women, children, the deaf, and others, being at peace through the divine.

The wise one who always knows the Blessed One is supremely auspicious; the profound and supreme Lord will soon be pleased with him. An action once performed does not perish; therefore, one should remain undisturbed.
And he did not worship the God of gods in the presence of the great multitude.
He did not proclaim the worship already performed, nor did he recite a hymn of praise aloud.
It is not possible for me to describe the remainder of his actions in their entirety.
O Lotus-seated One, this instruction has been given for the most part:
those high-souled devotees of Viṣṇu who are devoted to the Pañcarātra—whatever they say regarding a matter of doubt, that should be done without hesitation. (29.78–79)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Remainder of Ritual Action," in the Paramasaṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
Now begins the thirtieth chapter:
"O Blessed One, O Lotus-eyed One, O Vaikuṇṭha, O Supreme Person!
By your grace, I have heard this knowledge in its entirety."
All my doubts that previously arose on every side have been destroyed;
O Lord of the World, today I consider myself as one who has accomplished his purpose.
Even if there were any secret here or some hidden knowledge anywhere, [I have attained it].
Tell me all of that as well; I have a supreme longing for it.
"Very well, O Grandfather, I shall tell you this most secret knowledge."
That which has never before been heard by others— the supreme benefit among all benefits—
a person should constantly worship me with a mind undistracted, according to the procedure taught in this Tantra, without looking for any other fruit whatsoever. (30.4–30.5)
Having thus performed worship, one should offer a counter-worship in the center; making oneself a servant, with palms joined and face turned downward,
[one offers] food, drink, wealth, sons, long life, sovereignty, and a dwelling place.
Even in times of distress, a worshiper should not beg from the Supreme Person. (30.7) "I do not give to one who is displeased, even if he asks day after day;
but to one who is well-pleased, I give all that, even if he does not ask. (30.8)
"O Lotus-born One, neither time is the cause there, nor the weightiness of the worship, nor the suffering of the worshipper;
rather, it is I myself who know the virtues and faults of the worshipper through my own grace. (30.9)
Regarding the worship, the excellence [of the ritual], and likewise the passage of time:
I am pleased of my own accord whenever I behold such excellence. Being thus pleased, I grant grace, but never with haste.
If it does not exist in this life, it certainly exists in another life;
if it does not exist in that other life, it certainly exists in a subsequent life.
Yet, even across hundreds of other births, I do not favor this [worldly existence].
Even if one worships me but once, having turned away from ritual service,
when other karmas are being ripened and others have reached their exhaustion,
I reveal myself to my devotees; what [more] favor of mine could there be?
Then, through this prosperity, he attends upon men;
his friends increase, and likewise his enemies diminish.
Fruits are mostly lost despite effort, while diseases vanish of their own accord.
There is no defilement regarding food and drink, and likewise, livestock increase.
Life spans become long, offspring are born fortunate, all people offer praise, and thieves do not steal. (30.16–30.17)
Sovereignty, free from calamity, shall either endure or even expand;
it will come about at a time of merit through happiness alone in the future.
Therefore, he shall obtain birth in a distinguished lineage of great-souled ones.
Even there, by attending upon me, he prospers through attainments;
from that, he obtains a birth even more distinguished in virtue than the former.
In this way, there shall indeed be nourishment for him in birth after birth.
Then he attains unblemished sovereignty consisting of eightfold qualities;
or, remaining there for a long time, he dwells with me as his supreme goal.
Alternatively, having resorted to knowledge, he attains nirvāṇa.
Even toward my devotee, my grace never fails.
(30.22) If a person himself seeks refuge in me alone, yet forgets me because of tainted, pleasant sleep, he is at fault. (30.23)
Then, misfortunes arise for him from all sides;
thereafter, this person is joined with the contrary current.
Then, various desires arise within his mind.
Then, through attachment to those things, he exerts futile human effort.
Frustrated therein, he strives again for something else;
thus, through the persistence of his undertakings, he encounters suffering in saṃsāra.
Devotion directed toward me alone is the supreme cause of his prosperity;
when that devotion has perished, ruin follows of its own accord.
Therefore, a man should indeed cultivate devotion directed toward me every day.
She must be especially increased [in strength], for she leads him along the true path.
Without effort, no boat moves of its own accord against the current in the waters; yet, when it does move, it carries him even upward.
In this way, through the yoga of devotion to me, his prosperity increases;
casting off the afflictions born of saṃsāra, he makes himself supreme. Just as a boat does not turn back because of the fault of the sailor, so too [does the soul not return].
Thus, through the loss of devotion to me, his cycle of worldly existence increases.
Therefore, unswerving devotion directed toward me is the refuge for embodied beings;
everything else, O Grandfather, exists only for the sake of its manifestation.

For one who constantly worships me, recites this hymn of praise, and meditates upon me alone, devotion increases. Even if devotion is not yet present, though one's effort be very great, [it will increase]. (30.33)
Worldly ostentation alone would be fruitless both in this life and after death.
Therefore, one should strive with all effort to increase devotion alone;
for when that has grown, it leads indeed to the supreme station of Viṣṇu.
The vision of reality itself has been declared to be the cause of its increase.
Always behold me as the reality; devotion toward me increases thereby.
I alone am born, having attained such a body.
Just as I am endowed with this form at this time,
so too was there a previous birth for me in some realm,
whether it was superior, inferior, or equal in its abundance of qualities.
There will be another birth for me, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious;
from that, yet another birth will certainly follow.
And as I am being born from the womb of my mother, there is no place from which [I could escape].
When one is dying alone, no one at all follows after.
No one else’s suffering arises from my suffering;
no one else becomes happy through my happiness; therefore, I have no friends.
I have come alone, I remain alone,
and I shall certainly go alone even into another body. Whether I live for a long time or whether I live for a moderate time—
That I live and that this body of mine is emaciated—nothing else is equal to that.
This has been enjoyed by others in the past, and it is being enjoyed by me now;
furthermore, even after my departure, this very same thing will be enjoyed by others.
"This is not my abode, nor is this wealth or sovereignty mine;
these are servants, these are wives, these are sons, these are dear ones. They act for their own sake, and not one among them is established in me. (30.45)
"This disease afflicts me; this old age afflicts me.
This fever is another's, yet this sensation is mine alone.
What was seen in the previous year, I see again in this year. (30.46–47)
There, work already done has here become something yet to be performed;
food eaten on the past day is still being eaten even today. In that very same way, action is performed, and in that very same way, one sleeps even now.
Even beasts, birds, and other creatures act in this way;
I never perceive any distinction between them and me.
Indeed, living beings take special delight in their own kind.
Therefore, whether birth be auspicious or inauspicious, it is indeed the same;
thus, I have no confidence in those born, nor in those who die. Neither in sciences, nor in forms, nor in friends, nor in kinsmen [is there any lasting reliance].
I do not know anything dependent on me, nor anything subject to my will, nor anything else.
I see only myself submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra,
like a traveler on a road [relying on] a friend, food, wealth, or a home.
In this very way, I perceive this life of mine as born;
just as a bird occupies a hollow and then abandons it,
even so my stay in this body is not to be trusted.
"From where did I come before, or where shall I go again? How long shall I dwell here? I know not all such things;
everything is directly manifest to me, yet it is entirely fruitless. (30.55–56)
Likewise, what exists for me in the interval between all that which has not yet come?
Therefore, I seek some refuge that is associated with absolute certainty;
otherwise, my fear will not be dispelled.
"By good fortune, through my past meritorious deeds, I have attained in this life the integrity of my faculties and likewise the solitude of my mind. Therefore,
in this very life, I must diligently perform what is wholesome."
I do not see a path to the highest good in these actions being performed, by which there might be an increase of my prosperity in a future birth;
for their fruit only increases further suffering and destroys knowledge.
Indeed, only ritual actions are seen in the Vedas, the Shastras, and the Agamas;
yet by means of them, the mental anguish does not perish at any time.
Therefore, one must find some support that is immutable and free from affliction.
"I must seek something, for there must be an object endowed with purpose;
yet I do not see any Person standing higher than Viṣṇu, whether in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, or in the worlds, the Vedas, and the Āgamas. (30.63)
Therefore, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, I take refuge in you alone.
With mind, deed, and speech, firm in my vow and indifferent to all else,
I shall never direct my thoughts toward sensual desires.
"What need have I for one desire, or even two, for the sake of attaining success?
Therefore, without desiring any fruit, I take refuge in Hari. With single-minded and firm devotion, my resolve in this matter is certain. (30.66)
Thus, with a pure mind, one should practice visualization in solitude;
seeking Vaiṣṇava perfection, one should practice with a concentrated mind,
and when the mind is serene, the wise person should contemplate Him.
For those overwhelmed by passion and hatred, the vision of reality is fruitless,
even when they have reached sacred places, wandering mendicants, and yogis;
yet the minds of ordinary mortals find some degree of serenity.
At the end of sleep and in solitude, especially for the wise;
in such matters as these, the learned devotee of the Lord, being himself composed, should always abide in the vision of reality.
Because of that, his devotion never falters;
he is neither tormented by desire nor does he experience despondency.
Indeed, a person endowed with devotion turns away from the ways of the world.
He does not become overly attached to enjoyments, nor does he hasten out of curiosity. He does not seek even what is difficult to obtain, and he is content with what he has acquired.
Furthermore, he remains equanimous in the union with the unpleasant and in the separation from the pleasant.
Beholding the ripening of karmas, he does not grieve over anything;
thinking "this is not fitting" or "this is fitting," he does not grieve.
Seeing sovereignty as merely a kind of performance, he remains equanimous.
He does not proclaim his duties nor does he feel any agitation;
for he desires nothing from the worship of the God of gods,
just as his mind remains fixed upon jewels, wives, or sons.
In this very way, his mind becomes endowed with devotion toward the Lord of Gods.
When such devotion has arisen, preceded by the vision of reality,
the wise man, free from attachment, should wander as a mendicant wherever he may be situated.
Furthermore, he alone should go there and circumambulate the ground;
he should daily visit sacred fords (tīrthas) and places belonging to me,
being my devotee, meditating upon me, intent on me, and having me as his supreme goal.
And by remembering me at the time of death, one attains union with me.
What eightfold sovereignty does Brahmā enjoy that a devotee of Viṣṇu enjoys?
Even having realized this, why does the embodied soul return?
(30.82) What is the distinction between this cessation [of rebirth] and that which is proclaimed as *sāyujya*? (30.83) It is the supreme.
The person who understands becomes minute in form;
the person becomes great in form as much as he desires.
By his will, he becomes light, like the down of a withered śalmali tree.
At the very time he desires, he attains the entire earth.
He always conducts himself at will regarding food and recreation;
by mere resolve, he brings all beings under his own control.
And he enters his desired body himself in an instant.
This eightfold sovereignty has been described to you, O Lotus-born One;
by attaining this alone, many people sport.
He becomes the lord of all; nothing whatsoever can obstruct him.
There is no fault in them, nor is there any cessation from birth, just as these men turn back from all worlds for my sake.
If these people, deluded by pleasant sleep, should forget me,
then in the course of time they will suffer ruin.
Because their devotion to me has been protected, they shall remain free from harm on all sides.
They proceed against the current once more upon the path of saṃsāra.
There, in that lineage of high-souled ones which is most excellent, they take birth;
there, desiring perfection, they resort to me alone once again.
Even while established in sovereign power, if the yogi follows me,
then like one who is liberated, he rejoices throughout all the worlds.
Those ascetics of intense devotion have attained union with me.
Those servants of mine shall be eternal and free from affliction.
Only through an offense against their devotion would saṃsāra arise for them again;
otherwise, by my grace, their state shall be eternal.
But those who have attained liberation are distinguished above all others as the Supreme Persons;
they have transcended the sphere of saṃsāra and are forever without distinction from me.
For them, there is no further rebirth nor any kind of negligence whatsoever.
This very state of Viṣṇu is declared by the Vedāntas.
For embodied beings, it is liberation, release, and indeed nirvāṇa;
this alone is the supreme perfection and the highest goal among all goals.
But all other destinies, O Grandfather, are accompanied by suffering for men;
yet, due to the diversity of individual natures, something specific is desired by each person. Therefore, both [the path of knowledge and the path of action] are here considered acceptable for men.
O Grandfather, whether it be sovereign power or liberation,
devotion directed toward me alone will accomplish both of these,
through the differentiation of the qualities that arise from one established in meditative absorption.
But when a person finds that his mind is directed solely toward what is undesirable,
then, with every effort, he practices the limbs of yoga.
Abiding in those, he worships me with a one-pointed mind.
Darkness (tamas) wanes, and by that, his passion (rajas) also perishes.
Thereafter, through successive births, he attains nourishment;
then, gradually, whatever slight remnant of passion remains in him begins to manifest.
When one abides in sattva and is not touched by rajas at any time, that sovereignty over the fluctuations of the mind stands fully before him; from that,
there shall be liberation for him— such is this twofold destiny.
Therefore, one seeking that goal should always be my devotee.
When devotion is present, the desired goal is indeed attained.
Brahmā.
"By what fault, O Supreme Person, does a man's mental devotion wane both in this world and in the next? Tell me that. (30.108) Paramaḥ.

Disenchantment, doubt, affliction, and false knowledge arise for one who is devoted to another [object] when the enjoyment [of that other] is present and his beloved approaches. But separation occurs through the illusory powers of the goddesses.
The binding of the snare of affection proceeds from association with friends.
Furthermore, when one's fame is being heard, intoxication arises in the heart;
a Vaiṣṇava should recognize this as an obstacle to the practice of yoga.
While these are arising, one should practice the vision of reality;
one should not exert intense force nor cause pain to the body.
One should also withdraw gradually and with effort from the sense objects.
One should not indulge in curiosity regarding food and drink (30.113),
nor regarding the union of the hips and the organ, nor the fickleness of the hands,
nor at the sight of the unprecedented, nor in relation to the abodes of the world-protectors (30.114).
A wise man desiring union with those who possess vain mental attachments,
as these objects of sense gradually turn away from him,
finds that devotion to me naturally increases within him.
And without first having tasted them, it is not possible for men to renounce sense objects entirely; therefore, one should resort to them as well,
following a path that does not contradict the treatises on Dharma, while remaining loose in one's longing.
Having experienced those faults in all circumstances, the wise and virtuous person [realizes]:
"These sense-objects are difficult to master, transitory, devoid of purity, always fraught with many dangers, and must be enjoyed at the cost of one's very essence. (30.118)
Having thus resolved with such an understanding, one should turn away from the sense objects.
For one who turns away from them, the mind becomes auspicious;
and for that turning away, purity alone is considered the supreme means.

When purity is being cultivated, a sense of revulsion toward sense objects constantly arises in the mind; by means of that, a person is protected. This applies to all foods, as well as to beds and clothing.
In ancient dwellings and in waters at all times,
the wise devotee of the Lord, perceiving purity in these with effort,
does not himself come into contact with impure things.
Through non-association with impurities, his mind becomes serene;
in serenity, his longing for sense objects gradually ceases.
Having turned away from sense objects, he certainly becomes absorbed in me.
Absorbed in me, one should practice yoga, unassailed by obstacles;
freed from former sins, one attains the supreme goal.
Thus, O Grandfather, I have declared to you all this secret.
Having heard this, a person will always be one who has fulfilled his purpose.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, named "The Secret," in the glorious *Pāñcarātra Paramasaṃhitā*.
Now begins the thirty-first chapter,
the supreme:
Thus has this been declared by me in various places in detail.
This knowledge must not be spoken by you in its entirety to one whose self is undisciplined,
nor to a non-Vaiṣṇava who seeks it out of pride and possesses a dull intellect;
yet the definitive conclusion has been stated there and there in particular.
But to him who is my devotee alone, firm in his vow through single-minded devotion, whether he be of noble birth or humble, to him I shall speak this knowledge of yours—
just as it was to the highly fortunate sages of rigid vows.
Having reached Śvetadvīpa, they worship me at all times.
By my command, you must speak this to them;
for these devotees, while worshipping me, do not pray for any other fruit.
"But I myself shall bestow this knowledge upon them in age after age.
Therefore, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me, approach him and communicate this knowledge to them in its entirety and in truth."
"And those yogins who come to that island by my grace,
O Grandfather, they themselves shall impart this knowledge to them."—
Mārkaṇḍeya.
"So be it," Brahmā said to that God of gods,
with palms joined in reverence and eyes cast downward, his mind filled with radiant splendor.
Then the Blessed Lord Govinda vanished right there.
Seeing that, the lotus-seated Brahmā was struck with wonder. Then, by the command of Hari, Brahmā reached Śvetadvīpa.
Then, seeing that Brahmā had arrived, they all [beheld him].
Filled with wonder, they gratified him with hymns of praise. Then Brahmā, with a serene inner soul, spoke these words to them:
"Listen, may it be well with you; O Siddhas, supreme devotees of Viṣṇu!"
"The supreme god, whose eyes resemble lotuses, is pleased with you;
filled with compassion, he himself desires to bestow knowledge upon you.
Go to them yourself and speak of this knowledge"—thus was he urged.
"I have come before you; therefore, I shall speak to you," having said this, Brahmā was addressed once more by all the Siddhas:
"Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sanandana, and Sanātana."
"Let these four listen, especially those distinguished by wisdom and intelligence.
We shall hear from them again and again as we please.
By your grace, O Grandfather, let them become masters of yoga."
Thus permitted by the Siddhas, those four great seers,
filled with joy for the sake of knowledge, attended upon Brahmā.
[He was] endowed with the creation and destruction [of the world], and endowed with the dissolution of liberation.

He bestowed upon them all knowledge in its entirety within five nights. Then, at the conclusion of that [instruction], the Self-born One, having been honored by those great sages while they were looking on, vanished right there.
Having attained that knowledge, those yogins of perfected intellect shall in turn bestow that entire knowledge upon those Siddhas as well. And those Vaiṣṇavas of firm vows who come to that island—
From them as well, through their grace, other yogins also obtained this knowledge.
By me too, through the favor of Viṣṇu, having reached that auspicious island,
this Vaiṣṇava tantra was received from the mouth of Sanaka.
Furthermore, O Devala, having seen Sanatkumāra, other Siddhas, and Vaiṣṇavas, and having followed the path shown by them, I have returned here; and having returned,
I shall proceed with zeal to the abodes of the Supreme Self.
"I shall dwell on this island for many years," he said.
"Having gone there again and again, I shall behold the Vaiṣṇavas who possess long lives,
and from them I shall hear those very qualities of Viṣṇu."
The king of tortoises, Akūpāra, the best among his kind and long-lived;
likewise Jaigīṣavya, the preeminent one who remains untroubled even during the cosmic dissolutions;
as well as Rāma the son of Jamadagni, Atri, and Aṅgiras.
I see these and other Vaiṣṇavas who have gone there at the proper time. Having reached that island, those sages of rigid vows attained the knowledge of reality and became perfectly composed.
Exclusively devoted, filled with joy, and intent upon devotion to Viṣṇu,
they worship Vāsudeva endowed with supreme faith.
O Devala, you too have thus obtained this Vaiṣṇava knowledge.
Shaking off all doubts, become a single-minded devotee of Viṣṇu.
There is nothing higher than this for a person that brings about auspiciousness:
that a person takes refuge in the Supreme Lord with single-minded devotion.
Indeed, in all the worlds and at all times,
there are no men anywhere who excel those devoted to Viṣṇu;
their birth in this saṃsāra is fruitful, of this there is no doubt.
Those men who devote themselves exclusively to the Supreme Person—
indeed, O Devala, I do not see anyone anywhere in all the lands who is a devotee of Janārdana, the God of gods, without being motivated by desire.
For him whose devotion does not waver toward the lotus feet of Viṣṇu, there is neither death nor fear, nor transition to another birth. Therefore,
although you have reached the further shore of all the Vedas and Śāstras, [you must cultivate this devotion].
"O devotee of Viṣṇu, may you always remain free from doubt regarding the true path.
Then, by that very time, a firm conviction will arise in your heart, through which all your doubts shall vanish of their own accord. (31.37-31.38)
And there, O Devala, they receive favors in various places;
furthermore, the resolve of the devotee never perishes at any time.
And even teachers obtain [disciples] from everywhere without any effort.
From whom one obtains complete knowledge endowed with devotion;
those embodied beings on earth who have set out on their journey by this excellent path become honored everywhere and worthy of praise.
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas,
and pannagas never do anything unpleasant for one who is devoted to Viṣṇu.
Those men who worship Viṣṇu with their mind, their actions, and their speech [attain the highest state].
For them, nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain in this world or in the next.
Mobile beings always excel over stationary ones by their own qualities;
among mobile beings, animals are superior, and humans are superior to animals.
The Vaiṣṇavas are superior to ordinary men; those who are deeply learned are superior to other Vaiṣṇavas;

those who have realized knowledge are superior to the merely learned; those with controlled senses are superior to those who possess knowledge; perfected beings (siddhas) are superior to those with controlled senses; and great seers (maharṣis) are even superior to the perfected beings.
"From the great sages [come those] who have lost their sovereignty, and from them, those who seek liberation. (31.46) Thus have the stages of conscious beings been fully described;
by knowing them, one attains the supreme state of Viṣṇu. (31.47)
The lordship of the gods, the wisdom of the learned,
and the Vaiṣṇava nature of mortals— none of these are the fruit of any other austerity.
For Vaiṣṇavas, both birth and death are endowed with fruit.
But for other mortals, both of these are useless.
Therefore, O Devala, having abandoned all other activities,
worship the Supreme Self, the Infallible One, with your whole being.
Thus, O sinless one, this Vaiṣṇava Tantra has been declared by me to you;
it is endowed with secrets and accompanied by the distinctions of ritual action.
And this supreme knowledge has descended from the mouth of the God of gods.
"O Devala, you must give this to one whose devotion has its root in ignorance.
Only that ascetic Vaiṣṇava by whom the three initiations have been performed is worthy to hear the entirety of Vaiṣṇava knowledge. (31.52–53)
O Devala, this knowledge of yours should not be given even to those wise ones who possess discernment and desire to hear it,
for among all gifts, the gift of knowledge is preeminent.
There is no counting the accomplishments of the fruits [of merit] because of the spreading forth of knowledge.
Just as knowledge is distinguished by the excellence of the recipient,
so too does the donor incur sin through the fault of the recipient.
Therefore, having examined the recipient, the supreme knowledge should be given;
for through the gift of knowledge, one obtains great merit without effort, as much as one desires.
Thus, O Devala, has this been told to you in brief for your benefit.

"Having extracted the essence from all [scriptures], I have [composed] this Pañcarātra Tantra. O Devala, this firm knowledge must be grasped, practiced, and contemplated at all times; by that, your desired goal shall be accomplished."
"O Devala, have you retained all this knowledge?
Have your doubts been destroyed? Has your mind reached certainty?
Thus was Devala addressed by Mārkaṇḍeya at that time.
Bowing his head to the feet [of the sage], Devala spoke these words:
"O great sage, this knowledge has been obtained by me through your grace."
I shall have accomplished my purpose; the darkness of my heart has perished.
All my doubts are severed, and a definitive conclusion has been attained.
Today, devotion accompanied by faith becomes firmly established within me.
"Just as this knowledge, the most purifying of all purifiers, has been obtained, so shall I act; I stand firm in your word. Having thus received this supreme Vaiṣṇava knowledge, Devala—
Having taken leave of Mārkaṇḍeya, he departed as he desired. Whoever, being a Vaiṣṇava of pure mind, should hear this tantra, his sins— even those committed in other births— are destroyed.
Having heard this tantra, whoever worships Puruṣottama,
the Lord becomes gracious toward him in a short time.
That man who recites this with devotion, or causes it to be recited, [attains the same].
Even his sin perishes; indeed, devotion is held to be supreme. Therefore, one should worship Madhusūdana by this path;
thus one attains sovereignty or liberation without effort.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Conclusion," in the Paramasaṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra,
within this very [text].
One should worship Karmahakṣmatu.
I have attained [this] through the effort made by the Compassionate One.
Having cut and having fixed the intestines.
The cause is the manifestation of the unmanifest;
this is transformation.
Because of transformation, because of avoidance, and because of transformation.
Kṣatatha kṣatatha kṣavaro.
O Kṛṣṇa,
even when you have not acted, [the world] is born.
Deluded,
O Khṛti-khṣakti!
By means of the knife,
[I cut] the sacrificial portion for the Lord of the Earth.
Khṇi kh.phalantaraiu khṃiva.
O Sadhvi, you are the essence of the wheel of space.

Having reached Khpatana Kḍhama,
he performed the Kṛtañjana rite.
These two half-verses are additional in the Kh manuscript:
"O God,
the mantra is *khṣastadeva*."
In this case, the negative particle (nañ) located in the preceding verse is carried over here.
People see only what is near at hand.
The two [deities] Khaskhasaila and Khyogya are endowed with wrath.
The portion from *khṃulani* to *k.punau ayamardhau* is missing in manuscript Ka.
O nourisher,
listen as if you were hearing us!
He pierces the supreme state of yoga.
Bound together by the jewels of the teeth, which are like razors, and are eternally sharp.
Kṣa and the others [the remaining consonants] are the lords of the sense organs (indriya).
The duty toward one's mother and father is the same as that toward a preceptor.
Having turned back the enemy with the *kṣarva* mantra,
[one should act] at the time of the *khṣarpa*.
One should worship KṢR.
with the syllable KṬAṂ.
If *khṣukṛta* occurs, there is *kha*; the practitioner attains success (*siddhi*) at the place of *kha*.
And likewise, Kha-vidha,
Kha-catu,
and Adhyakṣa.
But those who are attached to weapons and earth are [thus] overcome.
And one falls into impure wombs.
